noticias.texto:
Senator Thom Tillis, the outgoing North Carolina Republican who is due to be replaced by a Democrat, has reportedly blocked a confirmation vote on Donald Trump’s nominee to lead a key US cybersecurity agency, Michael LoSapio, after he denied during a hearing that the Capitol was attacked on January 6 2021.
Tillis, who declined to run for re-election and after repeated clashes with Trump’s, confirmed to HuffPost on Friday that he has placed a hold on LoSapio’s nomination to serve as a director of the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (Cisa). His block on the nomination will prevent it from being included in a package of nominees to be voted on next month, before the Republicans lose their majority in the Senate.
At his Senate confirmation hearing on Thursday, LoSapio, the chief information security officer for Palantir, a technology firm founded by JD Vance’s mentor, Peter Thiel, was asked by senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat: “Was there an attack on the Capitol of January 6 2021?”
After initially replying, “I don’t know,” LoSapio said: “No, I don’t believe it was an attack.”
Tillis told the Hill that the question of whether a mob of Trump supporters attacked the US Capitol in an attempt to overturn Joe Biden’s 2020 victory was not open for debate.
“It’s binary,” Tillis told the outlet. “The minute you pretend like it didn’t exist or you can’t even acknowledge it, I don’t have any time because it’s not a very thoughtful person.”
The agency LoSapio was nominated by Trump to lead, Cisa, plays a role in protecting US elections infrastructure from hacking.
The week after the 2020 election, as Trump falsely claimed that count had been rigged, Cisa was one of a number of federal agencies with oversight of election infrastructure to issue a statement calling the election “the most secure in American history” and noting that there was “no evidence that any voting system deleted or lost votes, changed votes, or was in any way compromised.”
After he returned to the White House last year, Trump signed an April 2025 presidential memorandum directing executive offices to take steps to address supposed “risks from Chris Krebs”, who led Cisa in 2020.
“Krebs, through CISA, falsely and baselessly denied that the 2020 election was rigged and stolen, including by inappropriately and categorically dismissing widespread election malfeasance and serious vulnerabilities with voting machines,” Trump’s memorandum claimed.

noticias.titulo: Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer
noticias.resumen: German company faced 65,000 claims from people who said they developed cancer after using weedkiller A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer ’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade. Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits alleging that its weedkiller Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade.
Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”.
He overruled objections that payouts to individual cancer victims would be too low because claimants who previously settled were paid more.
The judge also said delaying payouts could force victims, including those whose cancer is terminal, to wait “an indeterminate number of years” to be paid.
Bayer had faced approximately 65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from people who said they developed cancer after using Roundup at home or on the job.
The settlement announced in February aimed to resolve nearly all current and future Roundup claims in the US.
“The court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bayer’s CEO, Bill Anderson, said in a statement.
Bayer has faced extensive litigation over Roundup, and had seen its share price fall 46% since it bought Monsanto, which produces the weedkiller, for $63bn in 2018.
The company settled much of the Roundup litigation for $10.9bn in 2020, but was unable to win court approval of a $1.25bn settlement to resolve future Roundup claims.
Bayer has long maintained that Roundup and its active ingredient glyphosate were safe, and that decades of studies had shown that glyphosate did not cause cancer.
The settlement was approved five months after the US supreme court overturned a $1.25m jury award for a Missouri man, John Durnell, who blamed years of exposure to glyphosate in Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
In a 7-2 decision, the court agreed with Bayer that a federal law regulating pesticides barred failure-to-warn claims brought under state law, undercutting a central pillar of many lawsuits.
Christopher Seeger, a lawyer for many of the plaintiffs, said the Durnell decision narrowed the ability of Roundup victims to pursue claims in court.
“We look forward to getting this relief into the hands of all Roundup victims as quickly as possible,” he said in a statement.
Lawyers for some of the Roundup victims who objected to the settlement did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
The settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court. Bayer has said that about 200 of those cases were still being litigated, and that the supreme court decision gave it strong defenses.

noticias.titulo: US judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion cancer settlement
noticias.resumen: Bayer could end years of costly lawsuits in the US over claims that its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer. Tens of thousands of people could now receive compensation, although some lawyers say the payments are too low.
noticias.texto:
US judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion cancer settlement
November 21, 2026
A US judge on Friday approved German chemical giant Bayer's $7.25 billion (€6.60 billion) settlement of lawsuits claiming its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer.
Judge Timothy Boyer in the US state of Missouri ruled that the agreement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate."
The decision could help Bayer end years of costly legal battles over Roundup, which the company acquired when it bought US weedkiller producer Monsanto in 2018.
"The court's final approval is a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation," Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said.
The ruling could still be appealed.
How much money will Roundup cancer patients receive?
The agreement covers tens of thousands of people who say they developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, after using Roundup.
It also covers people who may be diagnosed with the disease in the future after previous exposure to the weedkiller.
Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion into a special fund over the next 21 years.
Individual payments are expected to average between $10,000 and $165,000. The amount will depend on factors including the patient's age, the severity of the illness and how long they were exposed to Roundup.
Some lawyers representing cancer patients have criticized the payments as too low.
But the judge rejected their objections, saying that further delays could leave seriously ill patients waiting years for compensation.
Christopher Seeger, a lawyer representing cancer patients, welcomed the decision.
"Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," he said.
Why has it become harder to sue Bayer over Roundup?
The settlement follows a major victory for Bayer at the US Supreme Court in June.
The court ruled that Bayer could not be sued under state laws for failing to put cancer warnings on Roundup packaging.
The judges argued that US federal rules did not require such warnings and that individual states could not impose additional labeling requirements.
The decision made it much harder for cancer patients to win lawsuits against Bayer.
In October, a Missouri jury also ruled in Bayer's favor in a separate Roundup cancer case.
However, some legal battles continue. Around 200 cases are still being fought in federal courts outside the new settlement, according to Bayer.
How much have the Roundup lawsuits cost Bayer?
Monsanto introduced Roundup in 1974. Its main ingredient, glyphosate, became one of the world's most widely used weedkillers.
Farmers use Roundup to kill weeds without damaging crops that have been genetically modified to survive the chemical. It has also been widely used in private gardens and on lawns.
Bayer inherited the legal problems surrounding Roundup when it bought Monsanto for $63 billion in 2018.
Since then, around 200,000 claims have been made against Bayer by people who believe the weedkiller caused their cancer.
The company already agreed to a $10.9 billion settlement in 2020. However, it failed to secure approval for a separate agreement covering future cases.
Some lawsuits have resulted in huge payouts, including a $2.1 billion award to plaintiffs in Georgia.
Bayer has already set aside $16 billion for Roundup-related legal costs. Its shares have fallen by 46% since the Monsanto takeover.
The company has also removed glyphosate from newer versions of Roundup sold to private consumers in the United States.
Does Roundup really cause cancer?
Scientists and regulators disagree about whether glyphosate causes cancer.
In 2015, the World Health Organization's cancer research agency classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" to humans.
However, the US Environmental Protection Agency says glyphosate is unlikely to cause cancer when used as directed.
Bayer has repeatedly denied that Roundup causes cancer, pointing to scientific studies and regulatory approvals.
The debate intensified last year when a major scientific study that had supported Roundup's safety for decades was withdrawn.
The journal that published it cited serious problems, including missing cancer research and previously undisclosed involvement by Monsanto employees.
The withdrawal raised further questions about the influence of chemical companies on scientific research.

noticias.titulo: Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation
noticias.resumen: Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.
noticias.texto:
Russian ornithologist jailed over donation to Navalny foundation
November 20, 2026
Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.
Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.
On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.
A biologist who dedicated her life to Arctic birds
Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album.
Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.
She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.
"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.
Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.
"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."
Protecting birds in Russia and beyond
Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.
Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.
"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."
More than 225 cases over donations to FBK across Russia
In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.
Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.
"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".
For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.
There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.
A year of court hearings and travel restrictions
Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.
Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with her colleagues focused largely on science: "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."
Leaving Russia was never an option
"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.
Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.
Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.
Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.
The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."
This article was originally published in Russian.

noticias.titulo: Repression against Iranian lawyers increases
noticias.resumen: At least 135 lawyers in Iran have been subjected to repressive measures over the past year. UN experts warn that this seriously jeopardizes the right of those accused to trial in a constitutional court.
noticias.texto:
Iran: Lawyers increasingly under pressure
November 20, 2026
UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers. They warn that limiting access to legal representation increases the risk of arbitrary detention, coerced confessions and unfair trials.
"Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts said in a statement in mid-November.
They said that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling. In January and February 2026, 23 lawyers, including five women, were reportedly arrested after nationwide protests.
Defending the politically persecuted is becoming dangerous
A current example is the case of Amirsalar Davoudi, a human rights lawyer who was arrested in October in the central Iranian city of Isfahan, where he was defending a client in the Revolutionary Court. According to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), he was taken to hospital on November 9 after suffering a heart attack in custody.
"There is a long history to the persecution of and coercive measures taken against lawyers," Sina Yousefi, a 41-year-old lawyer and human rights activist, told DW.
In October 2022, Yousefi was arrested by security forces in Tabriz during the nationwide "Woman Life Freedom" protests. Later, he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for "propaganda against the system." He has since left Iran, and now lives in the German capital Berlin.
"The pressure was already increasing on lawyers back then, because they were undertaking the defense of people who were arrested and publicly expressing their support for the demonstrators," said Yousefi. "The security services, judiciary, and criminal prosecution apparatus increasingly used targeted mechanisms to move against independent lawyers."
Even renowned and internationally known lawyers such as Nasrin Sotoudeh, who was co-awarded the Sakharov Prize in 2012, have been affected by this repression. In 2026, Sotoudeh was awarded the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prizeafter being repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.
Yousefi said arrests and threats against lawyers working on political and human rights cases not only curtailed the rights of those accused to a defense, but also discouraged other lawyers from accepting such briefs. This, he added, compromised the fairness of trials.
Criminal proceedings have also been instigated, or other measures taken, against lawyers who undertook to represent demonstrators. Comments on social media about the violation of civil rights can also be cited as grounds for investigation and judicial proceedings.
Restrictions on the right to choose a lawyer
Yousefi also warned against tightening restrictions on a person's right to choose their own lawyer. According to the note to Article 48 of Iran's Code of Criminal Procedure, for people arrested on certain charges, access to lawyers of their own choosing is already restricted during the investigation phase. Defendants must resort to lawyers approved by the head of the judiciary. In some cases, even these lawyers are not granted access to all the files and evidence.
According to Yousefi, in many cases in which charges have been brought against demonstrators, lawyers have only been granted access to the files "when the preliminary investigations have been concluded and the evidence for the prosecution has been gathered — including confessions made during their imprisonment." Even then, he said, "their access to the records is limited and they have little time to prepare the defense."
"In many cases," Yousefi added, "the judges ascribe greater importance to reports by security agents than to the defense. Verdicts are handed down predominantly on the basis of this."
Shabnam Moinipour, the program director at the Center for Supporters of Human Rights (CSHR) in the UK, sees the independence of the bar as a fundamental precondition for the effective defense of citizens. The organization monitors the situation of lawyers in Iran, documenting violations of their rights, and following up at an international level.
"A lawyer must be able to call into question the charges brought by the public prosecutor and the credibility of the security agencies' reports without fear of criminal prosecution," Moinipour told DW. "Because when a lawyer's freedom and professional activity are threatened, their client's right to defense is impaired."
Fear and self-censorship among lawyers
In Moinipour's view, when the decision as to which lawyers are approved is made by the most senior representative of the same court authority, it raises serious questions about the independence of the bar.
"This restriction has psychological as well as legal consequences," she stressed. "For the accused, it may reinforce a sense of being unprotected, as well as feelings of fear and mistrust. It can also prevent them from disclosing details of threats, torture, and illegal behavior."
Moinipour considers this practice incompatible with Iran's obligations as a member of the UN Human Rights Committee. International law stipulates that people must have immediate access to a lawyer of their own choosing, be able to communicate with them in confidence and be supplied with sufficient means to mount a defense.
Referring to a joint report by the Tehran-based Defenders of Human Rights Center and the International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI), as well as the recent statement by UN human rights experts, Moinipour said: "Even without mass arrests, the actions taken against a limited number of lawyers can send a threatening message to others and restrict their professional activity. This phenomenon is described as a chilling or deterrent effect."
However, Moinipour stressed that, despite this pressure, "many lawyers in Iran continue to defend the rights of their clients and accept the risk of arrest, criminal prosecution, and professional restrictions. In doing so, they are prepared, if necessary, to pay a high price for this resistance."
This article was originally written in Persian.

noticias.titulo: Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
noticias.resumen: Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.
noticias.texto:
Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
November 19, 2026
Ugandan Environment Minister Beatrice Atim Anywar has come to the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, seeking to secure more funding for her country as it grapples with climate change.
"This is a thing we are living with," she told DW on the sidelines of the COP31 summit, where she's leading the Ugandan delegation. "People are displaced, people are dying of harm, hunger. It has implications on food security and livelihoods."
In recent years, the East African nation has been hit by a series of climate-related disasters, from deadly landslides and floods washing away villages, to droughts damaging harvests and hydroelectricity production.
"When we come to COP and we talk of what the reality is on the ground, we Ugandans have suffered it," Anywar said, referring to the effects of climate change.
"It has an implication for the health of our people, on national budgets," she added.
Climate financing for developing countries to deal with the impacts of a warming planet has become a major sticking point at this year's climate talks. The gathering of some 200 states is seeking to close gaps on how to scale up financing from developed states and whether support should be provided through grants or loans.
Africa contributes less than 4% of the global greenhouse emissions that drive rising temperatures globally, but the continent is among the most vulnerable to climate impacts.
Ramping up electricity production
As it deals with the affects of climate change, including extreme weather, Uganda is also rapidly expanding investment in electricity production from renewables such as hydropower and solar.
In the country of some 53 million people, more than 90% of Ugandan households still rely on wood and charcoal as the most affordable fuel for things like cooking. Biomass accounts for 90% of the country's final energy consumption.
While using wood and charcoal leads to deforestation, Ugandans have little choice. Only around 2% of the country's energy comes from electricity — which is largely derived from hydropower — and less than half of the population has access to electricity.
"Now we are deliberately going into scaling up the production of electricity — hydropower electricity — and making it cheaper for cooking," Anywar said. "We have other alternative energy sources... to mitigate this charcoal use. But the use needs to be phased out in a systematic manner by giving them alternatives."
Drilling for oil
At the same time, the country is seeking to boost economic development by becoming an oil producer. Due to open in 2027, a controversial 1,443-kilometer (897-mile) pipeline is nearly complete. It connects two oil sites in eastern Uganda with a port on the Tanzanian coast.
Environmentalists have criticized the East African Crude Oil Pipeline project, which can transport up to 246,000 barrels per day. Environmentalists say it runs counter to the goal of limiting global temperature rise and could damage fragile ecosystems.
The Climate Accountability Institute said it would release 379 million tons of climate-heating pollution over its 20-year lifetime.
Oil wells for the project, operated by French energy giant TotalEnergies, are also located in Uganda's largest and oldest national park, Murchison Falls.
"That has been also a sticky issue. And actually, that is one of the challenges we are facing at COPs," Anywar said. She stressed that measures have been taken to limit emissions, and that the project was progressing in a "very deliberate way."
The minister also urged developed countries to cut less wealthy nations some slack for using the resources they have to drive much-needed development, saying oil revenues could help fund the transition to cleaner energy.
"You cannot tell us to cut off the umbilical cord that feeds us, as much as it has to be cut off," Anywar said, criticizing the lack of financing from developed countries to deal with climate change. "We are here begging for funds that are not forthcoming."
Anywar added that developing countries "need a just transition," referring to an equitable shift away from fossil fuels that focuses on protecting workers and communities.
Carbon trading 'breakthrough?'
Another way Uganda is looking to finance climate change adaptation is through carbon credits, Anywar said, describing them as a potential "breakthrough."
Carbon credits are tradeable permits representing one ton of carbon dioxide that has been reduced or removed from the atmosphere through initiatives such as forest protection, renewable energy projects or tree planting schemes. Companies or governments can buy them to offset emissions they have not cut themselves.
"Our country is rich with biodiversity. And that is what we are looking forward to — attracting investors into our natural setup so that we earn some finances," Anywar said.
Carbon credits have been promoted as an important source of income for developing countries. But they have also faced criticism, for a lack of transparency and allowing polluting activities to continue.
"We need to have a bankable approach to all interventions. Otherwise… it's not going to work for us," Anywar said, adding that her country also wants to attract investment and build partnerships in smart agriculture and the energy transition.
"If we rely on begging for funds which are not forthcoming, we shall go back empty handed."
This interview also appeared as a video.

noticias.titulo: No mention of fossil fuels in latest COP31 draft deal
noticias.resumen: One of the most fraught debates at the UN climate talks in Turkey has revolved around the future of coal, oil and gas. Now, all mention of fossil fuels has been removed from the summit's new draft agreement.
noticias.texto:
Fossil fuels dropped from latest COP31 draft deal
Published November 19, 2026last updated November 19, 2026
Climate negotiators have removed any mention of fossil fuels — the main source of greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet — in a new draft deal published by COP31 summit co-host Australia.
The latest text released Thursday at the UN climate conference in Turkey stripped out two references to a transition away from coal, oil and gas and a call for an accelerated phaseout that had been in an earlier draft.
This slimmed down version follows days of tough negotiations, with representatives from nearly 200 nations debating issues such as the future of fossil fuels and climate funding for developing countries.
The text still includes a call to increase the global share of final energy demand met by electricity to 35% by 2035 — up from around 20% today — a proposal that was pushed by host Turkey.
It did not specify whether that additional electricity needs to come from clean sources rather than fossil fuels, a point that has drawn criticism from some countries.
The draft did mention the electrification target alongside efforts to triple renewable energy capacity globally as well as other energy efficiency measures. But Jan Kowalzig, a climate finance expert with Oxfam Germany, said negotiators had failed to "meaningfully" link them.
Kowalzig also criticized the text for not referencing a transition away from fossil fuels in a gradual manner — something that had been mentioned in the final decision out of the COP28 in Dubai several years ago.
"This is insufficient for a climate conference that already decided several years ago to phase out fossil fuels and that presents itself as a conference focused on implementation," he said in a statement.
'Worst fears' on climate financing
Another hotly contested issue at the talks has been financial support to help developing countries deal with climate change. Divisions largely revolve around who should bear the costs and whether funding should come in the form of grants or loans.
The second draft called for further discussions on a tripling of funding for climate adaptation measures in developing countries. It also noted "with concern the gap between climate finance flows and needs," with the adaptation costs in developing countries estimated at $305 billion annually up to 2035.
The wording on finance prompted criticism from Meenakshi Raman, the coordinator of the climate change program at the Third World Network, who had been "hoping to see much more ambition on the side of finance from the developed world."
"Coming here really confirmed the worst fears that developed countries are not only backsliding but putting nothing in terms of real meaning on the table," said Raman.
The European Union has said it won't agree to higher climate financing pledges because it pays its "fair share" while others don't.
What else is in the draft text?
The draft text also expressed "deep concern" that global warming is projected to exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels — the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avoid runaway climate change.
It acknowledged that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems."
Australian Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen said the text aimed to communicate that "1.5 degrees of warming is not acceptable and will not be allowed to stand."
The draft also recognized the need for "deep, rapid and sustained" cuts to greenhouse gas emissions and called for efforts to ramp up action targeting the potent greenhouse gas methane.
The greenhouse gas emissions heating the planet are largely caused by burning fossil fuels.
The text additionally calls for the deployment of technologies that can remove carbon from the atmosphere to be sped up, many of which have yet to be tested and proven on a large scale.
Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign to boost climate finance for developing countries said the second draft "trims away inconvenient mandates and accountability while leaving behind lofty rhetoric that won't protect a single vulnerable community."
Talks in crunch time
The climate conference officially ends on Friday, but it's not uncommon for the annual talks to run on for longer than expected. The latest text is expected to face further revisions before it can be adopted.
Decisions on the language need approval from all countries, meaning an objection from one party is enough to scupper a deal.
On Thursday, Panama said it would block any agreement that does not meet its demands for a cap on oil production and steps to eliminate methane.
The country's environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, said Panama would "not lend its name" to "complacent or ineffective language" in the final pact.
Australian Energy Minister Bowen said he expected countries to bring forward their concerns, feedback and questions in the coming hours and overnight.
"We won't be leaving the rooms of Antalya until we have that consensus, until we have a plan we can put to the parties on behalf of the countries and governments they represent, and they can say, yes, we can do this: we can keep the world to 1.5 degrees of warming."
The stakes are high for this edition of the COP summit, which comes in a year of major climate-related disasters, from wildfires and deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.
It's also taking place against the backdrop of an intensifying "super" El Nino weather pattern, and geopolitical shocks that have sent energy prices rising globally.
The conference is the first to be held under the acknowledgement by the UN that keeping the average global temperature under 1.5C is no longer realistic. Instead, scientists are talking about limiting the time spent above this threshold and bringing temperatures back down rapidly by the end of the century.
Countries are at odds about how to acknowledge overshoot of the temperature threshold in the final agreement, with some worrying that fossil fuel producing countries such as Saudi Arabia and Iran are seeking to jettison 1.5C entirely, which could lead to "backsliding" on climate action, according to AFP.
"It's critically important for this COP to recognize, and this is really the first COP that will likely do so, that we are on the way to overshooting 1.5 degrees," said David Waskow, the director of the World Resources Institute's International Climate Initiative.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
noticias.resumen: Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI
November 19, 2026
Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.
Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.
The stock opened at $111.50 (€101.7) — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion. Anthropic stock ended the first day of trading at $97 per share.
The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.
The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.
This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
First of the AI giants to go public
Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.
Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.
Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.
That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.

noticias.titulo: Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend
noticias.resumen: World No. 1 tennis player Alexander Zverev is facing a new lawsuit related to a domestic abuse trial. The lawyer for his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea, told DW what the allegations are against the German player.
noticias.texto:
Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend
November 19, 2026
Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.
The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven."
As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."
However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.
"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.
"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.
However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights."
Zverev's lawyers: 'permissible expression of opinion'
Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.
"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.
The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.
Zverev's lawyers reject the allegations.
"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.
"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view."
The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press."
Patea's lawyer: 'We had no choice' but court
Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.
"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.
"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice."
Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

noticias.titulo: EU Commission confirms it was targeted in cyberattack using AI tools
noticias.resumen: The European Commission was targeted by an "AI-generated cybercampaign," a spokesperson has said. This is the first time the bloc has publicly reported an AI-based cyberattack.
noticias.texto:
EU targeted in an AI-assisted cyberattack, spokesperson says
November 19, 2026
The European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was targeted by a cyberattack through the use of AI tools.
The incident was detected on October 22 and there was no evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters.
"This was an AI-generated cybercampaign," he added.
Regnier did not elaborate on the attack or name a perpetrator. He said the Commission "has taken the necessary steps in response."
This is the first time the bloc reported an AI-assisted cyberattack.
Disruption reportedly lasted 10 days
Regnier's statement came after Politico reported earlier on Thursday that the Commission had been targeted. The report said the cyberattack disrupted several systems for 10 days and might have compromised large amounts of personal data. The European Commission has roughly 33,000 employees.
The Commission then convened its highest-level internal crisis management body for an urgent meeting about the cyber incidents, according to Politico.
"We temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored," Regnier said. He also stated that they did not detect any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff.
Recent hybrid attacks on supermarkets, air traffic controllers, blood banks and broadcasters across Europe have raised worries among leaders that this may be part of a coordinated attempt at hybrid warfare.
France summoned the Iranian ambassador last week over cyberattacks that caused supermarket freezers to defrost, but Tehran has denied any involvement.

noticias.titulo: Wadephul: 'Coalition of the Willing' talks in Berlin send strong signal to Moscow
noticias.resumen: German Foreign Minister Wadephul has said the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin sends a clear message to Moscow to take peace talks seriously. He also warned Ukraine should be prepared for peace talks to fail.
noticias.texto:
Germany's Wadephul: Berlin talks send strong signal to Moscow
November 19, 2026
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday's meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin sent a strong signal to Moscow that it was time to take negotiations to end the war in Ukraine seriously.
Speaking to DW during a visit to the South Caucasus, Wadephul described the summit as the largest meeting of Ukraine's supporters so far. The meeting represents the 18th set of high-level talks among the coalition's members.
He said it demonstrated that allies remained firmly behind Kyiv in the fifth year of Russia's war and were ready to do "what was necessary to ensure Ukraine could negotiate from a position of strength."
"The summit itself is already a success," he told DW.
Wadephul also welcomed the US initiative to restart peace negotiations. After nine months without progress, an initial meeting had taken place in Abu Dhabi, with a follow-up round planned and European participation expected.
Wadephul promises future support for Ukraine
"We are also preparing for the possibility that the negotiations will not be successful and that, over the coming winter, we will have to continue supplying Ukraine with heating, electricity and all essential supplies, including water," he said.
"And we will continue to stand by Ukraine militarily."
He stressed that any peace agreement must include security guarantees to protect Ukraine against future Russian attacks.
In earlier comments during his trip to the South Caucasus, Wadephul said that Ukraine and Europe must be involved in any negotiations over the future of Ukraine.
Wadephul did, however, welcome the trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.
"Every conversation that takes place is a good conversation," he told DW during a visit to Azerbaijan on Wednesday.
Later on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said he had invited Europeans to Moscow for talks on the potential structure of future talks to end the war.

noticias.titulo: Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
noticias.resumen: As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington.
noticias.texto:
Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure
November 19, 2026
As Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support.
For Iran, relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow.
Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran. But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington.
That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate?
China is now Iran's economic lifeline
China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil.
In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports, much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions.
As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs.
Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, says China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own.
"If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW.
But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter.
"The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost said.
Sanctions enforcement raises pressure on Iran
That distinction has become more important as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports.
In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny.
As a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets.
"A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said.
Iran prepares for the worst
This economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning. A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently said the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero.
That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks.
Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating.
What does Beijing want?
Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost.
But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies.
A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping. China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability.
Russia can help, but how much?
Russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation.
Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify.
Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, believes the summit should be viewed within a larger attempt to manage the wars in both Ukraine and the Middle East.
"Russia, China and the United States appear to be seeking constructive dialogue and results that could shape a new security architecture in the international system," Vakhshiteh told DW.
Russia supports Iran, but limits remain
Solhdoost also warns against overstating Russian support for Iran.
The strategic partnership between Moscow and Tehran provides for security cooperation and efforts to counter unilateral sanctions, but it does not require Russia to enter a war on Iran's behalf.
Since Russia is deeply engaged in Ukraine, it likely has its own priorities in negotiations with Washington, says Solhdoost.
"Russia would prioritize its own national interests in negotiations with the US over Ukraine and Iran," he said.
Moscow could support Iran while simultaneously using its relationship with Tehran as leverage in talks with Trump over Ukraine.
How much influence do the three powers have?
For Iran, ties with China and Russia remain essential. They provide alternative trade routes, export markets and diplomatic support that complicate Washington's efforts to isolate Tehran.
Yet neither Beijing nor Moscow views Iran solely through the lens of strategic partnership. Both weigh support for Tehran against their own economic interests, security concerns and dealings with Washington.

noticias.titulo: Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
noticias.resumen: The sharp sell-off in tech stocks after the US midterms and the Nvidia scandal has cast doubt on Anthropic's IPO. Yet with hundreds of billions still being invested, some think the AI party is still in full swing.
noticias.texto:
Is the AI bubble bursting just as Anthropic goes public?
November 19, 2026
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) giant, made its Nasdaq debut Thursday in the largest share sale on record.
The Claude maker offered 980 million shares for sale at $83 (€76), yet began trading 34% higher at $111.50.
The opening price values the five-year-old firm at around $2 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.
Anthropic's public listing is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.
2026 was meant to be the year Wall Street’s trillion-dollar bet on what US President Donald Trump calls superintelligence (SI) started paying off.
In the first half of the year, it did. Many AI stocks hit record highs as US hyperscalers like Google's Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft recorded bumper earnings.
AI doubts trigger market turbulence
The second half of 2026, however, has brought a lot more uncertainty.
While the stock of chipmaker Nvidia pushed even higher last month, many hyperscalers and chip or memory firms have seen erratic movements in their stock prices.
Then, after the Democrats won control of the United States Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, technology stocks sold off again dramatically.
The Magnificent Seven — including Meta, Apple, Amazon and Tesla — lost more than $1 trillion in value in a single trading day.
In a further twist, the AI sector took another hit last week as Nvidia shares plunged nearly 10% over two days.
The sell-off followed revelations that CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman reportedly suspected by US intelligence of being a Chinese spy.
Huang resigned from the chipmaker, sending Nvidia's shares lower still and prompting a campaign by current and former staffers, investors and other key figures in Silicon Valley to have him reinstated.
Questions over timing of Anthropic IPO
While OpenAI — the maker of ChatGPT — has delayed its public listing until next year, some analysts have been left scratching their heads at Anthropic's decision to proceed, even though the IPO is reportedly about six times oversubscribed.
"Is this the best timing?" asked Dennis Dick, chief market strategist at the Canada-based Stock Trader Network, in an interview with DW last week.
Dick said Anthropic's valuation depends on whether it can deliver on a forecast by Goldman Sachs of more than $600 billion in revenue by 2030.
"If you get to a company with $600 billion in revenue, [a] $1.3 trillion [valuation] doesn’t sound that bad," he told DW. "But when you’re talking about a company with currently $52 billion in revenue, it sounds like it’s overvalued."
Other analysts, like Vivek Seth, chief executive officer of Shaires Holdings, are more bullish about the Claude maker's prospects.
"Anthropic is a once-in-a-generation company," Seth told Bloomberg last week, noting how it has grown rapidly and has strong institutional backing. "Its IPO will establish a market-clearing valuation as conditions stabilize."
Amid huge spending, big returns remain elusive
Wall Street is growing increasingly cautious about the sheer size of the AI outlay, amid warnings that future earnings may not justify the huge spending.
In September, investment bank Goldman Sachs estimated that hyperscalers need around $300 billion in annual AI revenue to break even on their spending, leaving a gap of roughly $230 billion.
"We're not in Kansas anymore," Dick quipped, borrowing a line from the classic movie "The Wizard of Oz," which means times have changed. Now, he said, investors are telling companies: "Show me the money."
AI stocks needed a 'healthy correction'
Other analysts, however, think it's too soon to expect the AI bubble to burst, including Kit Rees, investment strategist at London-based wealth manager Quilter, who thinks the post-election rout was a "healthy correction."
"We’re still in the very early innings of the AI build-out," Rees told DW. "There’s still a lot of excitement around this technology and investors will want to have a slice of the pie."
In addition to the roughly $800 billion invested in capital expenditures this year, AI hyperscalers plan to spend a further $1.2 trillion in 2027 and $1.4 trillion in 2028, according to Goldman Sachs estimates.
Signs to watch, not reasons to flee
With many investors already running for the hills, Rees isn’t convinced the AI bubble will burst in the way skeptics expect. She thinks they should watch for stronger signs that the AI trade is maturing.
This could be "a slowdown in AI-related revenues for companies, or signs of less demand or less appetite for financing companies’ AI plans, be it through debt or through equity offerings," Rees told DW.
There are early signs that investors have less appetite for AI-related debt. Borrowing costs for AI infrastructure firms like CoreWeave and Oracle have soared recently. Even the cost of insuring Nvidia’s debt against default has risen 76% in a month, CNBC reported recently.
"They [Oracle] have been spending, some people say, like drunken sailors," Dick told DW. "They’ve compromised their balance sheet to a point where the stock’s fallen 65% from the highs."
That has not stopped Oracle, along with Meta, Microsoft and Alphabet, from continuing to issue new AI bonds. Since the end of last month, the four AI giants have announced deals worth $67 billion.
Rees said another sign could be any new regulations that make it harder to build out US data centers, due to pressure on local water and electricity supplies.
Is AI next in a long line of bubbles that burst?
In his upcoming book "AI Mania: Blather, Bluster, and the Bubble of All Bubbles," economist Gary Smith compares the AI boom with earlier frenzies around railways, automobiles, television and the internet. He warns of a "frightful crash" when the AI bubble eventually pops.
When the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, the tech-heavy Nasdaq stock market index lost nearly 80% of its value. Yet, previous bubbles have often lasted far longer than expected, making the timing of any crash hard to predict.
Joachim Klement, head of market strategy at UK-based investment bank Panmure Liberum, believes a reckoning could happen as early as next year.
"My core conviction is that the AI bubble will either burst in 2027 or in 2028, so sometime in the next two years,” Klement told Bloomberg last month.
Editor's note: This article was first published on November 13, 2026 and was updated on November 18 and 19 to reflect the latest developments.

noticias.titulo: S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
noticias.resumen: AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
noticias.texto:
S&P 500 sinks 3.7% and the Nasdaq composite goes negative for the year
NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7%, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year.
The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a "correction," having fallen more than 10% from its Oct. 6 all-time high.
The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3%, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9%.
Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1%.
The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each fell more than 5% overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well.
AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market's direction. They were responsible for Wall Street's big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market.
The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks' big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data center construction winning at both the federal and state level.
"The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that's what's being priced right now," said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. "But I don't think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over."
Much of the AI rout was centered among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centers. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3%, Micron Technology slid 13.9% and Broadcom fell 12.1%. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7%.
Corning slid 10.9% and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3%.
Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8% lower. The chip company's stock was caught up in the market's anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25%.
The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1% to $88.30, but remains above its IPO price of $83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing $2 trillion in value.
Anthropic's share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23% decline from its brief peak of $115.10 a share set the day prior. That's an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO.
Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50% in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later.
Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7% and homebuilder Lennar gained 1%.
All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73.
While the stock market's mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year.
The University of Michigan's latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists' expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93% from 5.04% late Thursday.
Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6% to settle at $92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil.

noticias.titulo: MLK's handwritten draft of iconic speech on display for the first time
noticias.resumen: The only known handwritten draft of The Reverend Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech is on display in his hometown. The iconic phrase, however, never made it on the page.
noticias.texto:
MLK's handwritten draft of iconic speech on display for the first time
ATLANTA – The only known draft of one of the most famous speeches in American history is on public display for the first time: The Reverend Martin Luther King Jr.'s remarks at the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom in 1963. And it's written in his own hand.
"Just for a few days we have this incredible artifact here, which is Doctor King's handwritten, final draft of what became known as the 'I Have a Dream' speech," said Jill Savitt, CEO of the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta, King's hometown.
"Nothing has given me chills like this handwritten document, where you see him crafting one of the most iconic speeches in U.S. history."
It's written in cursive, blue ink on yellow legal paper. King scratched through entire sections and reworked them, or changed a particular word or phrase.
"You see him on the page wrestling with the words," Savitt said. "He's struggling with: How do you make this case to America that we're not living up to our own ideals?"
The seven-page document, which will be on exhibit here through Sunday, is enclosed in a glass case in a gallery dedicated to the March on Washington. Above the display, footage plays of speeches and the crowd of 250,000 gathered on the National Mall on Aug. 28, 1963.
Savitt said King originally titled the speech "Normalcy Never Again." Notably, the manuscript does not include what became the most famous lines from that day, "I Have a Dream."
"Doctor King improvised that," she said. "The preacher in him connected with a crowd in a particular way. And when you watch footage, you can almost see this electric charge go through him."
His rousing words that day on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial included:
"I have a dream that my four little children will one day live in a nation where they will not be judged by the color of their skin but by the content of their character. I have a dream today."
Savitt says King sent the draft to be typed up in the pre-dawn hours from the Willard Hotel in Washington, DC, on the day he was to deliver it.
The handwritten copy of King's speech was discovered by Xernona Clayton, an Atlanta civil rights leader who worked closely with King and his wife, Coretta Scott King. Her late husband, Edward Clayton, was one of King's speechwriters.
Now 96, she said in an interview with NPR Thursday she found the papers tucked in a manilla envelope while cleaning out his old desk.
"I knew Doctor King's handwriting very well, and I said, 'Oh, this can't be the speech,'" she recalled. "Then when I started reading it, I knew that it was and then I got scared. Like, what do I do now?"
That was in the late 1990s, and she tucked it back into the desk. She rediscovered it a couple years ago, and it took her back to 1963.
"As I went through the speech, I was reading his words and hearing them in my head," she said. "Martin Luther King spoke to the world through that speech."
She decided it was time to share the document with the world. Clayton's charitable trust is offering it for auction through Christie's in New York in January, where the auction house says bids could top $10 million. Prior to that, the manuscript also will be on display in Chicago.
Clayton said she wanted it available to the public with the hope that people will find inspiration in King's words today.
"He used to tell me all the time how much he hated that we as a people can't live together," she recalled. "That was his preachment. All of the time he was preoccupied with what can we do to get people to love each other."
For former Atlanta Mayor Shirley Franklin, who visited the center last week, seeing the document was personal.
"Do you see me?" she asked, pointing to a photograph on display of the crowd at the March on Washington. "I'm sitting right there by the reflecting pool."
Franklin was Atlanta's mayor from 2002-2010, the first Black woman elected to lead a city in the Deep South.
"It's amazing that 60 years later this document has survived," she said.
Looking at King's writings, Franklin said she was struck by how thoughtful he was about each and every word.
"As brilliant as he was, as clear as he was about what he was trying to accomplish, it required enhancement and refinement," she said. "He was making this speech as good as it could be."
Yet even with all the reviewing and refining, what stuck from that speech never made it on the paper.
"What we remember is the part that came from his heart," Franklin said. "Gives me the chills."
Franklin is a living witness to the change wrought by the work of King and others civil rights pioneers, but she said seeing the speech is a reminder that the work is ongoing.
"Sixty years later, we've made some progress," she said. "Much of what he says is relevant today, because we've not really fulfilled the full promise of a free and a loving community."
Franklin helped found the National Center for Civil and Human Rights in Atlanta. She said it's fitting such a foundational document got its public debut here.
"This is one of my favorite rooms," she said, as the famous ending of King's speech played on the screen overhead:
"In the words of the old Negro spiritual, 'Free at last, free at last. Thank God almighty we are free at last.'"

noticias.titulo: Germany: Berlin student protest targets rearmament and compulsory service
noticias.resumen: Thousands of students marched through Berlin, on Friday 20 November 2026, protesting against the country's rapid military rearmament and fears of a return to compulsory military service. Their protest formed part of a wider wave of youth demonstrations across Europe.
noticias.texto:
Young protesters took to the streets of Berlin beneath the city’s television tower to oppose soaring defence budgets and the possible return of compulsory military service, chanting "Never again conscription" as smoke flares billowed above the march. Carrying signs emblazoned with "Hands off my future" alongside GTA VI-inspired posters proclaiming Generation Z’s readiness to push back, demonstrators warned that Germany’s drive to bolster its armed forces threatens their personal freedom and life choices. "We’re trying to resist this because it’s our future," one participant said.
The protest coincided with a broader day of youth-led demonstrations across Europe, with rallies also unfolding in Rome, Frankfurt and London. While local grievances differed, young crowds voiced shared anger at political leaders whom they accused of sidelining their generation’s priorities amid rising military expenditure and mounting global challenges.

noticias.titulo: Russian missiles over Poland, European troops in the mud: Ukraine’s defence force is taking shape
noticias.resumen: Just hours before the European war games in Poland began, Russian missiles and a drone tore through its Nato airspace.
noticias.texto: The air raid sirens came at around 6.30AM on Friday (20 November) near Nowa Dęba, a small town in south-east Poland, roughly 100km from the border with Ukraine. At least two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone had violated Polish airspace during the morning even as troops from 11 European countries had gathered in a large field surrounded by tall pine tree forests nearby. The Russian cruise missiles and drone hit areas in south-eastern Poland, one 50km from Ukraine’s border. Nobody was killed. “Common sense suggests there are no coincidences in such incidents. I think it was some kind of incident linked to our presence here,” Dariusz Mendrala, a major general in the Polish Armed Forces and the chief of the Armed Forces Support Inspectorate, told reporters. “It won’t stop us from preparing to carry out our mission. For us, for the Polish state, for the Polish Armed Forces, these things have not been entirely exceptional for some time now,” he added. Behind him, some 48,000 square meters of military infrastructure and logistics facilities had been erected by the Polish forces in the thick mud and rain, as part of the first major exercise by the Multinational Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), a non-Nato European military force, led by France and the United Kingdom, which is to be ready to deploy to Ukraine once a ceasefire has been announced. Named Koalicja (coalition in Polish), the exercise had attracted scores of journalists, some as far away as Japan, as well as high-ranking officials and defence ministers from Estonia, France, Lithuania, Poland, and the United Kingdom. Koalicja exercise near Nowa Dęba. Source: Nikolaj Nielsen With its 2,800 troops and jet fighter flybys of French Rafales, British RAF Typhoons, and Tiger helicopters, the MNF-U intends to provide reassurance for a Ukraine that was itself pounded overnight by a large-scaled Russian air barrage, targeting bridges in Kyiv and killing at least eight people. noticias.titulo: Italy’s hard definition of antisemitism will shield Israeli crimes and harm free speech
noticias.resumen: Italy's Meloni has doubled down on her populist and performative claims to care about Jewish minorities, by imposing a hardline definition of antisemitism that risks gagging debate.
noticias.texto: Anti-Jewish discrimination and legitimate criticism of Israeli state actions became conflated into one offence by Italy’s parliament on Tuesday (17 November). Adopting the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance’s ( IHRA ) official definition of anti-semitism, Rome’s bill will apply across schools, universities, social-media platforms, and beyond. The move has raised serious concerns about what this will do to freedom of expression and protest. Despite not imposing financial penalties or criminal sanctions for offenders, it shows which side of history far-right prime minister Georgia Meloni’s Italy has chosen. “Branding criticism of Israel’s brutal occupation, its system of apartheid, and its ongoing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza as antisemitic – which could happen under the new law – also risks shielding state policies and practices from legitimate public scrutiny and debate,” said Erika Guevara Rosas, Amnesty International’s senior director for policy and research. Read more Fastest EU citizens’ initiative ever pushes Brussels to end EU‑Israel trade agreement “By blurring the distinction between antisemitism and criticism of a state’s actions, the law also risks undermining efforts to identify and effectively address genuine antisemitisms,” she said. Not only does Tuesday mark a bleak beginning for press and self-censorship on issues of public interest in Italy, following the path of the UK’s persecution of the Palestine Action group, who has now arrested over 4,000 activists involved in peaceful protests against Israel’s offences in the occupied territories. Not only does this also indicate the start of an authoritarian slippery slope, which could end in silencing political criticism that is not favoured by the ruling powers, or debate concerning those in office. But it is largely a display of the narrow priorities subscribed to by Meloni’s stagnant government. Read more [Interview] Italy’s Meloni is EU’s best hope of charming Putin at Ukraine peace talks, former Russian spy says Although she has held power for longer than any of her predecessors in the history of the Republic, there is little to show for it, with headline measures that included tightened citizenship rules, anti-rave actions, cuts to welfare benefits, and limited offshoring of migrant processing to an exorbitantly expensive centre in Albania. And stalled economic growth matches the trend. Meanwhile, in a 147-93 vote in Rome’s Palazzo Chigi, supporters of the pro-IHRA definition bill cited soaring anti-Jewish violence and aggression as their main motivation, while forgetting about the abundant relics of fascism that still scar whole cities and regions across Italy, influencing every generation with hatred of minorities. Even the granddaughter of Italy’s late fascist dictator, Rachele Mussolini, has quit Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party for being too rightwing in its treatment of minorities, which should speak volumes on the government’s lack of integrity in its claims to care about Jewish people in Italy. As repression increasingly hits press and NGO freedoms in Europe and beyond , laws that seek to police the vocabulary of crucial democratic debates risk pushing our societies back into dark times, which our grandparents fought to end. In 2024, the German parliament passed a non-binding resolution backing the IHRA definition. Two years later, Germany is considering a law that would make denying Israel’s right to exist a crime, with up to five years in prison.
