noticias.titulo: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
noticias.resumen: Countries from nearly 200 countries are in a deadlock to try and get a new global climate agreement.
noticias.texto:
Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
- Published
Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run through the night, as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
Separately, the Africa Group are fighting to get commitments on more money for adaptation, saying they did not come to the COP "to beg".
A new and potentially final agreement is expected to be published on Saturday.
- More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged 
  - Published1 day ago
Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.
"We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," said France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".
Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.
The BBC understands that a number of other EU nations were asked to join the rebellion but declined, considering it unhelpful to negotiations.
Although one lead negotiator said he sympathised: "How can you have a climate agreement with no mention of the cause."
But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back.
He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.
Away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - contributed the largest share of global energy demand growth, outstripping oil and gas, external.
The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.
Although this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.
The 'worst' COP ever?
It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.
This does not solve one of the other key issues raised by developing nations - the lack of money.
Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn by 2035 - that has now been removed.
"We did not come here to beg we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.
Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.
"I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.
These groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected" said one observer.

noticias.titulo: FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
noticias.resumen: The National Crime Information Center database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information.
noticias.texto:
FBI reportedly investigating apparent hack of its criminal database
- Published
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its criminal information database, US media report citing two people briefed on the issue.
The National Crime Information Center (NCIC) database is used by federal and local law enforcement to share information on warrants and background checks. The BBC has contacted the FBI for comment.
This comes after string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors in the US last week. Officials have said they were not caused by cyberattacks - but the blackouts have sparked scrutiny from lawmakers.
White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired this week, with US President Donald Trump saying he was not good enough.
It would not be the first time hackers have targeted the FBI, the domestic intelligence and security service of the US.
In September, the FBI said it was investigating an apparent breach by a cyber-crime group ShinyHunters, which claimed it had stolen sensitive information on all bureau staff - around 38,000 people.
After that hack, one former FBI agent told the BBC he feared for the safety of current employees, whose personal information could soon become available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
In a separate development, NBC reported an apparent cyberattack against the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) .
Employees were informed on Thursday that its farm payment system had been targeted, NBC said.
The USDA has not publicly commented on the issue.

noticias.titulo: Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
noticias.resumen: The 30-year-old LA resident was convicted of arson leading to wildfires that killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 buildings.
noticias.texto:
Man convicted of starting Palisades fire in Los Angeles
- Published
A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.
Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.
The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial.
Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.
Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.
One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.
"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.
Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.
Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".
"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."
Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.
They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.
They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.
The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

noticias.titulo: Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
noticias.resumen: Brussels sources had previously suggested the bloc might not apply the wider deal until fees were lowered for EU students in Britain.
noticias.texto:
Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says
- Published
A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.
The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.
However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.
Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".
It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.
- What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? 
  - Published19 hours ago
- Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more 
  - Published18 hours ago
- Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow 
  - Published18 hours ago
UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.
The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to Â£17bn a year.
EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.
Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.
"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.
Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."
"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."
Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.
He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".
Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".
He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".
"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.
She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the Â£17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.
Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, the University of Manchester's vice chancellor Professor Duncan Ivison said closer UK-EU relations were a "good thing" but "the issue of tuition fees is something we do have to figure out because there is a cost".
He warned that EU students being allowed to pay domestic university fees would "take Â£500m, we estimate, out of the higher education sector at a time where there's a lot of pressure on the sector".
He added: "If EU students come and are paying domestic fees, it's not clear we'd be able to increase the number of places for EU students anyway."
Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said the Treasury and Department for Education would work with universities to find a solution during negotiations.
She told BBC Breakfast: "I don't think anybody wants to do deals that negatively impact anything. We want win-win deals."

noticias.titulo: Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
noticias.resumen: The 21m tree is Oslo’s annual thank you for Britain’s support during World War Two.
noticias.texto:
Trafalgar Square Christmas tree felled in Norway
- Published
This year's Trafalgar Square Christmas tree has been cut down in a forest outside Oslo, ready to begin its journey to London.
The 21m (69ft) tree, nicknamed Jolly Cheery, is about 75 years old. It was felled on Friday by the Lord Mayor of Westminster, Karen Scarborough, and the Mayor of Oslo, Anne Lindboe.
Norway has sent a tree to the capital every year since 1947 as a thank you for Britain's support during World War Two, when King Haakon VII and the Norwegian government lived in exile in London.
Its lights will be switched on by the two mayors at a ceremony in the square on Thursday, 3 December.
Scarborough said: "It's my greatest honour to take part in this wonderful tradition for both the cities of Oslo and London.
"This tree is a powerful symbol of friendship and peace, reminding us to be there for one another during the festive period."
Scarborough thanked "the people of Oslo and Norway for this truly fabulous gift" and added: "With the care and dedication of the team, I'm sure it will look magnificent on Trafalgar Square."
Lindboe said: "Oslo has been sending a Christmas tree to London for almost eight decades, and every year we send a tree across the North Sea with the same message: we have not forgotten.
"The tradition has a powerful history, and its message remains just as relevant today.
"I hope Jolly Cheery spreads warmth and Christmas cheer to everyone who passes by, and reminds us how much it means to be there for one another, especially in difficult times."
For the second year running, the tree was chosen with the help of a social media poll.
Organisers said it would travel by road in Norway and England using only electric and biodiesel vehicles, cutting the journey's carbon footprint by 80%. It will cross the North Sea on a regular cargo ship from the port of Brevik.
Once in London, it will be decorated in the traditional Norwegian style, with 25m strings of festoon lighting fitted with energy-efficient bulbs.

noticias.titulo: Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
noticias.resumen: Warsaw accuses Moscow of intentional provocation, but bar for triggering NATO's collective defence clause remains high.
noticias.texto:
Russian missiles hit Poland: What happened, and could NATO respond?
Warsaw accuses Moscow of intentional provocation, but the bar for triggering NATO’s collective defence clause remains high.
Security cameras have captured the moment a suspected Russian missile struck Polish territory during an attack on Ukraine. Poland’s government says it may have been hit by two missiles and a jet-powered drone.
The incidents, which came as European troops held military drills in the country and as the United States pushes to revive talks on ending the war in Ukraine, have raised questions about whether the strike was deliberate.
So what happened, and does this mean Russia has struck Poland, a NATO member?
What happened in Poland?
Poland’s Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference in Warsaw that two missiles and a jet-powered drone fell on Polish territory during Russia’s overnight attack on November 20. The missiles came down at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik nad Sanem, while the jet-powered drone fell at Molodycz, all in the country’s southeast.
One missile is believed to have crashed about 35km (22 miles) from where European troops’ military exercises were taking place. A Kh-101 cruise missile went down about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and what officials believe was a jet-powered drone hit about 30km (20 miles) from the border. No immediate injuries or damage were reported.
That night, Russia launched one of its heaviest bombardments of Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia fired more than 400 drones and at least 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, some with cluster warheads. At least eight civilians were killed and more than two dozen were wounded.
Why did a Russian missile enter Polish airspace?
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it appeared “we are dealing with an intentional provocation” by Russia. He said the incident was likely timed to coincide with the European military exercises in Poland. The unprecedented two-week exercise began on November 9 in southeastern Poland and is preparing forces for a possible post-war mission in Ukraine to help stabilise the country and rebuild its military.
Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at the Clinton Institute, University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera that the incident “fits into a pattern going back for months” of Russia “testing how far they can go”.
“A few months ago, it was flying the drones into airspace, and indeed a couple of times they flew fighter jets across the border into the Baltic states,” he said. “You just test how NATO responds.”
This time, he said, Moscow had “gone a bit further”. “You lob a couple of missiles across and a drone” near where 11 countries are holding exercises.
The Polish Air Force had launched preventive air patrols on September 17 aimed at securing the eastern part of Polish airspace following repeated incursions in the previous weeks.
Harry Nedelcu, partner and senior director for geopolitics at Rasmussen Global, said the testing has not been limited to Poland.
“During the war, there’s been repeated instances of Russia testing NATO allies – Poland, Romania and also non-NATO Moldova as well, which is experiencing – especially over the last few months – increasing numbers of drones and missiles flying over its territory and airspace,” he told Al Jazeera.
He linked the incursions to one of Moscow’s core war aims. “One of the key goals in Ukraine that Russia has had in the full-scale invasion, that has lasted almost five years now, has been to prevent Ukraine from being a part of NATO,” he said. “So their goal clearly is to undermine NATO, to do everything possible to undermine it.
“What Russia is doing with these missiles, drones, that sometimes find their way into NATO territory, tests NATO just under the radar of Article 5 to see how far can they push things. How far can they take hybrid warfare?”
Under Article 5, each member of the NATO alliance understands that if one of them is the “victim of an armed attack, each and every other member of the alliance will consider this act of violence as an armed attack against all members”.
Why has this happened now?
At a meeting on Thursday with European leaders in Germany’s capital, Berlin, US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said he believes Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
Kushner and fellow special envoy Steve Witkoff have been holding talks with Ukraine and Russia in recent days, in a push for peace which has been viewed as sidelining Ukraine’s European allies.
Following the Berlin meeting, French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine’s membership of NATO should be considered again, prompting Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov to push back.
Ryabkov said any form of “quasi membership” for Kyiv of the Western military alliance was totally unacceptable for Moscow, Russian state media reported.
Lucas said the timing of the missile incursion into Polish territory now is very likely tied to the ongoing US-led peace talks.
“The Russians cannot be seen to go through talks and completely exclude Europe,” he said. He described the Kremlin’s push for a “Europe-wide security architecture” as a way to avoid discussing a ceasefire or security guarantees for Ukraine.
“Rather than having a strong Europe at the talks, they want to try to divide Europe, they want to try to unsettle Europe, they want to try to scare Europe,” he said.
He also pointed to Ukraine’s recent strikes on the Kerch Bridge, which links occupied Crimea to Russia. He said these were seen as “a very serious attack on Russian capabilities” with “severe political, military and economic consequences”.
The latest Russian bombardment follows President Vladimir Putin’s pledge to retaliate against those strikes.
How have Poland and NATO responded?
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called the missile incident a “grave violation” of Poland’s airspace. On X, he said the incident was “clearly dangerous” and a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. Rutte is expected to visit Poland this weekend.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham called it “utterly unacceptable”. Germany’s Foreign Ministry called it “yet another example of Russia’s ongoing provocations”.
US President Donald Trump had played down earlier incursions hours before. “Putin has been landing drones in Poland and a couple of little missiles, by mistake,” he said.
Nedelcu said Warsaw’s reaction was “definitely a strong one”, with Polish officials “drawing a parallel between the fact that actually around the same time there were exercises by the Coalition of the Willing [those countries willing to provide support to Ukraine] nearby, and that this may have not been a coincidence”.
He said Poland is now “asking for more NATO support under this Eastern Sentry mission that already exists”.
“It’s not if, but what form that additional support will take – maybe an airborne early warning aircraft, or something of the sort,” he said.
“But what they have stopped short of is invoking Article 4,” he added, referring to the clause under which allies consult each other before invoking Article 5. “It’s unclear whether this was at their own volition. Maybe perhaps allies don’t want to use it too often, because Article 4 is also quite serious. It has been invoked not often, and it loses its value if it’s constantly invoked.”
Lucas said the public condemnation from European leaders was itself the message to Moscow. “It’s a signal to the Russians: look, we know what you’re doing, we see what you’re doing here,” he said.
“But you’re not going to run it up into an all-out military confrontation over a couple of missiles.”
He said he expects the response to be “defensive”, built on “preparedness” of ground forces, air, naval and cyber-defence, and defence against disinformation. “These will be the most intense preparations you will have had, certainly since the 1980s and possibly well before that,” he said.
On the same day, Denmark took action on a separate front. It announced that it was expelling Russia’s defence attache after Danish intelligence concluded that Moscow had orchestrated a plot to assassinate Ukrainian-American rapper Kyivstoner during a concert near Copenhagen.
Could a Russian missile strike on Poland trigger NATO’s Article 5?
Probably not. Article 5 treats an attack on any ally as an attack on all 32 members, but invoking it is a political decision requiring agreement from all members, not an automatic trigger. Poland can instead invoke Article 4, which provides for emergency consultations only. Warsaw did so in September 2025, after Russian drones entered its airspace.
Lucas said NATO members want to stop Russia succeeding in Ukraine without allowing the conflict to escalate. “[That] means you set a very high bar for invoking Article 5,” he said.
“You’re talking about what in effect would be a sustained Russian attack on Poland. That’s when Article 5 gets invoked.”
He said NATO is also handling a delicate diplomatic moment. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are pressing for a negotiated settlement, and “NATO can’t be seen to be the ones to sabotage the talks”.
Those talks remain murky, particularly after Kushner’s comments indicating that Russia would be “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for post-war Ukraine.
“Jared Kushner is going around making statements that make absolutely no sense about what deal is on the table,” Lucas said. He said the US is “so desperate for a deal” that it is “muddying the waters”.
Lucas said Ukraine has no real prospect of NATO membership now, because “bringing Ukraine into NATO would destabilise a ceasefire”. He said the goal should be “security guarantees as if Ukraine was a NATO member”.
Could the incident escalate the Russia-Ukraine war?
Analysts say a direct confrontation between Russia and NATO is unlikely for now.
“The alliance shows every signal that it does not want to show any teeth,” Nedelcu said. “So what will probably happen, Russia will keep on testing the alliance. We should not expect that this is the last instance of this.
“The alliance is not trying to show Russia, you know, enough is enough, so Russia will still keep testing because they want to see where that threshold is,” he said.
Lucas said the bigger danger is a wider campaign of hybrid, or “grey zone”, warfare, including cyberattacks and disinformation, rather than direct strikes. “That’s where the real threat here is right now, rather than direct Russian strikes,” he said.
“I’m not going to say that it couldn’t escalate at some point, because you always have unintended escalation,” he added. “But I don’t want to go to the headlines and say this is it, World War III.”
Inside Ukraine, Nedelcu said, the war is intensifying in the air rather than on the ground. He described the incident in Poland as “a residual, if you will, collateral of the conflict in Ukraine”.
“On the front line, the conflict in Ukraine is pretty much static,” he said. “But what happens in Ukraine is that the air attack has been increasingly amplified, I would say, since the end of the summer.
“Russia is trying to essentially make Ukrainian cities especially unliveable – destroying its energy grid, trying to undermine even water supply, bridges, railways, logistics – in order to, if they cannot break it on the front lines, break it economically and break its civilian population.”
Lucas said any offensive pressure on Moscow would come through Ukraine’s own counterattacks, which he said Europe and NATO back, but the Trump administration does not.
“The more that you limit Russia’s capacity by hitting its refineries, its chemical plants, its engineering plants, by hitting the bridges, the more you increase the pressure on the Russians to try to stop the invasion,” he said.

noticias.resumen: Ex-Australia cricketers Khawaja and Warner taken off air having been most outspoken over 2018 scandal in South Africa.
noticias.texto:
Usman Khawaja and David Warner taken off air over Australia’s Sandpapergate
Ex-Australia cricketers Khawaja and Warner taken off air having been most outspoken over 2018 scandal in South Africa.
Usman Khawaja and David Warner were taken off television commentary duties on Saturday until the “Sandpapergate” storm passes, with both set to miss Australia’s entire Twenty20 series against England.
The retired pair have been the centre of attention since Khawaja claimed in his autobiography more than two weeks ago that the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.
Only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy Warner and Cameron Bancroft – who used the sandpaper – were found to be responsible by a Cricket Australia probe.
The move by Fox Sports, for whom they both work, came after Cricket Australia threw its “unanimous support” behind embattled Test captain Pat Cummins.
Cummins denied he knew what was going on and has been under huge pressure since Khawaja’s claims, which were first backed by Warner and then Bancroft.
“In light of recent events, both Usman and Davey will be rested from our broadcasts over the next few weeks,” Fox Sports Managing Director Steve Crawley told Australian media.
“While we always support all members of our commentary team and welcome a diversity of views which is a feature of our summer of cricket, we also understand the pressure they are under to respond to each and every new comment.
“We think it is increasingly difficult to focus on the game while the situation continues to unfold and think it is unfair on both commentators to put them in that position.
“We will continue to monitor the situation,” Crawley said.
It was unclear when they would return, but Australia play four Tests against New Zealand in December-January after the five-game T20 series that got under way in Melbourne on Saturday.
Fast bowler Josh Hazlewood is the latest player from the 2018 side to deny any knowledge of the use of sandpaper and added on Saturday that he would have considered his future had Cummins been removed as captain.

noticias.titulo: Demolition notices for buildings in Hebron provoke fear among Palestinians
noticias.resumen: Palestinians fear forced displacement as Israeli authorities target legally licensed homes in West Bank.
noticias.texto:
Demolition notices for buildings in Hebron provoke fear among Palestinians
Palestinians fear forced displacement as Israeli authorities target legally licensed homes in a Palestinian-administered area of the occupied West Bank.
Hebron, Occupied West Bank – Amjad al-Qawasmi stood gazing at the eight-storey residential building he constructed 13 years ago in the heart of Hebron. He struggled to understand how it could be reduced to rubble in a matter of moments.
The building in the southern West Bank is one of two upon which the Israeli army posted demolition notices last Sunday morning, even though both are in Area A, which, under the Oslo Accords, is under full Palestinian control.
The buildings are in the Dairat al-Seer area, in the northwest of Hebron. One contains 25 residential apartments, the other has 40, alongside an adjacent home. The Israeli army has set a one-week deadline for filing objections to the demolition orders.
The Israeli authorities justified the decisions by citing the buildings’ proximity to “Settler Road 35”, despite the structures possessing all the necessary permits from the Palestinian Authority and the Hebron Municipality.
Hebron is divided into a larger area under Palestinian administrative control and a smaller area – housing Israeli settlers – in the centre of the city.
Pervasive fear
The affected families are living in a state of anxiety, fearing that the demolition orders will be carried out. Meanwhile, the property owners have filed formal objections in an attempt to halt the demolitions.
Al-Qawasmi told Al Jazeera that his building was constructed in 2013 at a cost exceeding 18 million shekels ($5.6m). He, along with his father and brother, had prepared the apartments for occupancy from the ground up, installing all necessary utilities after obtaining the required permits from the Ministry of Local Government.
He explained that he, his brothers, and their families live on the lower floors of the building.
Most of the other apartments were sold to families who have yet to complete their payments; a situation exacerbated by the difficult economic conditions they are facing, such as salary cuts and the ban on most Palestinian workers entering Israel for employment, which has been in effect since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel and the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
“Like all the residents of the building, we fear the execution of the demolition order. Although we have hired a lawyer to try to freeze the decision, this is an occupation, anything is possible,” said al-Qawasmi.
The families living in the two buildings have begun packing their essential belongings and clothing into cardboard boxes in anticipation of a potential forced eviction to carry out the demolition. However, they remain uncertain about the fate of their furniture and other possessions, should they not be granted the time to clear out their apartments.
A devastating loss
Samer Abu Hadid purchased a plot of land in the area five years ago and built a villa for his eight-member family. The 1,165 square metre property cost an estimated $3m.
Last Sunday morning, he was shocked when Israeli soldiers stormed the villa and served him a demolition notice, granting him a one-week window to file an objection. The order stated that it was a military decision based on “security grounds”.
“I told the officer that the villa is legally licensed and there are no grounds for its demolition. He simply replied, ‘Look at the document carefully, the reasons are security-related ‘ and added that I have one week to file an objection. But what can I possibly do in one week against an already-issued demolition order?” he asked Al Jazeera.
Abu Hadid reached out to local authorities to follow up on the matter, yet he remains deeply concerned that the demolition order might actually be carried out.
“We literally cannot sleep any more; we think about this constantly. We don’t know whether we should move out our furniture and empty the villa, or stay put. Nothing is clear, and we are at a loss as to what to do,” he said.
Blow to the investment sector
According to a report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (covering the period from November 2024 to October 2025), Israel targeted 97 Palestinian structures in Area A either through actual demolition or the issuance of demolition orders. This is in addition to 46 structures in Area B, 1,390 in Area C and 240 in occupied East Jerusalem.
The Palestinian Commission Against the Wall and Settlements has documented the issuance of 9,518 demolition or ‘stop-construction’ notices between 2015 and the end of September 2026.
They include 344 notices issued during the first nine months of this year. Hebron governorate tops the list with 2,697 notices issued in the city.
Hebron Municipal Council member Muammar al-Oweiwi told Al Jazeera that the recent demolition notices set a precedent in Hebron by targeting Area A, which should be under the full civil and security control of the Palestinian National Authority. Demolition and stop-construction orders were also issued for a family guesthouse and another building in the Farsh al-Hawa area in Area C.
Al-Oweiwi said that the Hebron Municipality is addressing the matter, in coordination with the property owners’ lawyers, by submitting documentation, including building permits, and pursuing the necessary legal procedures.
He added that the case is now before the Israeli courts; the lawyers requested an immediate stay or freeze on the demolition orders, but Israel has yet to respond.
“The municipality is not merely seeking to freeze the decision, but to have it overturned entirely and to secure official documentation confirming that the demolition of these buildings is unlawful,” he stated.
According to al-Oweiwi, the targeting of the two buildings goes beyond threatening dozens of families with the loss of their homes; it also strikes a blow to the Palestinian investment and construction sectors. The significant investments involved are now jeopardised, undermining investor confidence and threatening the city’s economic and urban stability.
Al-Oweiwi added that the Israeli justification that the buildings are near roads used by settlers is incorrect. He said the structures are within residential neighbourhoods and pose no threat to the roads.
“What is taking place falls within the framework of a policy of collective punishment and pressure on the Palestinians, and an attempt to undermine the citizens’ trust in their national institutions by encroaching upon their jurisdiction in areas that, under signed agreements, are subject to Palestinian administration,” he concluded.

noticias.titulo: Cavaliers’ Harden passes Bryant, closes on Jordan in NBA 50-point game list
noticias.resumen: James Harden climbs NBA career record list in leading Cleveland Cavaliers to 128-119 win over Indiana Pacers.
noticias.texto:
Cavaliers’ Harden passes Bryant, closes on Jordan in NBA 50-point game list
James Harden climbs NBA career record list in leading Cleveland Cavaliers to 128-119 win over Indiana Pacers.
James Harden scored a season-high 51 points – moving into third place in NBA history with his 26th career 50-point game – while leading the Cleveland Cavaliers to a 128-119 win over the visiting Indiana Pacers.
Harden, 37, made 15 of 26 field-goal attempts, 7 of 11 3-point shots and all 14 of his free throws while breaking a tie with Kobe Bryant on the 50-point list. Wilt Chamberlain holds the NBA record with 118 50-point games, and Michael Jordan is second with 31.
Donovan Mitchell added 20 points for Cleveland on a night when all NBA games were part of the NBA Cup’s group stage. The Cavaliers earned their third win in the past four games overall.
Pascal Siakam and Ivica Zubac each scored 21 for Indiana, which took its third consecutive loss.
Atlanta Hawks 111, Charlotte Hornets 97
Jalen Johnson compiled 26 points, six rebounds and six assists to help Atlanta post a victory over visiting Charlotte.
Aaron Wiggins scored 19 points, and Nickeil Alexander-Walker added 17 for the Hawks, who won their third straight game and their seventh in nine tries. Atlanta trailed by 14 points in the first half.
Moussa Diabate produced 21 points and 15 rebounds while Brandon Miller scored 19 points for the Hornets, who lost their fourth straight game.
Orlando Magic 113, Brooklyn Nets 111
Franz Wagner capped a stellar 35-point performance with a tiebreaking stepback jumper over two defenders with 2.8 seconds left as Orlando outlasted Brooklyn in New York.
Wagner made 13 of 25 shots as the Magic beat the Nets for the 10th straight time. Orlando’s Desmond Bane hit seven 3-pointers for his 21 points.
Julius Randle collected 27 points, nine rebounds and six assists for the Nets, but he missed a last-second 3-point attempt. Day’Ron Sharpe contributed 17 points and 11 boards as Brooklyn took its fourth loss in a row.
Toronto Raptors 105, Detroit Pistons 102
Scottie Barnes had 29 points, including a go-ahead basket in the final minute, and visiting Toronto snapped a six-game losing streak by edging Detroit.
Raptors rookie Allen Graves, making his first start, supplied career highs of 20 points and 10 rebounds while Immanuel Quickley notched 18 points and 10 assists.
Cade Cunningham totalled 23 points and nine assists as the Pistons took just their second loss in six games. Kevin Huerter added 20 points.
Oklahoma City Thunder 126, New Orleans Pelicans 120
Shai Gilgeous-Alexander scored 40 points to lead Oklahoma City past visiting New Orleans, just the Thunder’s second win in the past six games.
Rookie Aday Mara had career highs of 22 points and 16 rebounds for Oklahoma City. The Thunder shot 53.3% from the field, their second-best effort of the season.
Zion Williamson and Jeremiah Fears each scored 22 points for the Pelicans, who took their eighth loss in nine games.
Denver Nuggets 133, Houston Rockets 124
Nikola Jokic had 24 of his 26 points after halftime and added 11 assists as host Denver overcame a triple-double by Alperen Sengun to beat Houston.
Christian Braun and Cameron Johnson scored 19 points each for the Nuggets, who won their second straight contest. The game featured 32 lead changes, the most in the NBA this season.
Sengun finished with 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists for the Rockets, who had won five of their previous six games. Fred VanVleet put up 25 points.
Los Angeles Lakers 106, Sacramento Kings 104
Luka Doncic scored 25 points and dished out eight assists as Los Angeles rallied past visiting Sacramento, avoiding what would have been the Lakers’ first set of consecutive losses this season.
Walker Kessler added 15 points as the Lakers came out on top after their nine-game winning streak ended Wednesday in a loss to the Utah Jazz.
De’Andre Hunter scored 30 points, and Domantas Sabonis added 19 points and 16 rebounds as the Kings dropped their eighth straight game. Sacramento led by as many as 11 points in the third quarter.
Washington Wizards 98, Chicago Bulls 94
Anthony Davis finished with game highs of 36 points and 11 rebounds as Washington rallied from a 15-point deficit to down host Chicago.
Davis also made a key play on defence when he disrupted Norman Powell’s potential game-tying layup attempt with six seconds remaining to force a miss. Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa posted 20 points, 10 rebounds and six assists.
Powell led the Bulls with 16 points but shot just 7 of 18. Buddy Hield contributed 15 points off the bench.
Phoenix Suns 111, Utah Jazz 101
Devin Booker scored 23 points, Dillon Brooks and Miles Bridges added 18 apiece, and Phoenix ran its winning streak to three with a victory over Utah in Salt Lake City.
Collin Gillespie added 16 points and three 3-pointers off the bench, and Jalen Green scored 14 for the Suns, who have won five of seven. At 8-7, Phoenix is over .500 for the first time this season.
Rookie Darryn Peterson had 20 points and set his season highs in rebounds (10) and assists (eight) while recording his first career double-double. Jaxson Hayes added 18 points and a season-best 14 boards for the Jazz, who had won their previous two after a 1-13 start.

noticias.titulo: Nations agree to ‘elaborate’ on rules for AI-run ‘killer robots’ by 2028
noticias.resumen: Members of the UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons fail to agree on swift adoption of legally binding rules.
noticias.texto:
Nations agree to ‘elaborate’ on rules for AI-run ‘killer robots’ by 2028
Members of the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons fail to agree on swift adoption of legally binding rules.
The 128 countries at a United Nations conference in the Swiss city of Geneva have agreed to “elaborate” on a possible accord regulating lethal autonomous weapons, known as “killer robots”, in the next two years.
Saturday’s announcement at the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) came after nearly 100 nations pushed for swift adoption of legally binding rules on the weapons capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.
Key arms-producing nations, including the United States, Russia and Israel, opposed the push. Decisions under the convention require the agreement of all member states.
Diplomats said Russia’s objections over procedure led to some formal sessions being called off. Talks over the final wording then ran through the night.
Julien Thoeni, the Swiss diplomat who chaired the conference, said some countries had rejected the word “negotiate”. The agreed text refers instead to the “elaboration” of an instrument.
He said more than 10 years of talks had produced a significant step for humanitarian disarmament.
“It shows that even in today’s deeply divided world, multilateral diplomacy can still deliver concrete results,” he told reporters as the meeting wrapped up.
He said the process should determine which weapons can be banned under international humanitarian law and which can be permitted but regulated.
‘Watered down’
Stop Killer Robots, a coalition of 300 organisations opposed to the development and use of autonomous weapons, called the mandate “watered down”, saying it offered no clear route to legally binding rules.
Its executive director, Nicole van Rooijen, said autonomous weapons were being deployed in combat, including systems that use artificial intelligence to choose targets.
“Delaying the creation of a legally binding instrument puts civilians and humanity at risk,” she told the AFP news agency.
Verity Coyle, deputy director for arms at Human Rights Watch, said the outcome was disappointing.
“It does not provide the urgent action needed to agree new rules – but the technology is racing ahead,” she told AFP.

noticias.titulo: Verstappen escapes Vegas F1 discipline, takes pole as Antonelli penalised
noticias.resumen: Max Verstappen escapes discipline in Vegas F1 practice after run-ins and takes pole as Kimi Antonelli hit with penalty.
noticias.texto:
Verstappen escapes Vegas F1 discipline, takes pole as Antonelli penalised
Max Verstappen escapes discipline in Vegas F1 practice after run-ins and takes pole as Kimi Antonelli hit with penalty.
Max Verstappen has won the Las Vegas Grand Prix two of its three years but never sat on the pole — until now.
He finally made it to the top spot because of a penalty handed to Kimi Antonelli the day before, giving Verstappen a chance after qualifying second behind the Italian on Friday night.
Antonelli, the 20-year-old who is this year’s Formula 1 champion, put together a time of 1:33.893 in the third qualifying session for Saturday night’s race. But he will start sixth because of a five-place penalty after his Mercedes team exceeded its allocation of engines for the season.
Mercedes — which has already clinched the constructors’ championship — had two of the three fastest cars in qualifying, with George Russell .331 seconds behind his teammate. Russell, who won the Las Vegas Strip two years ago, will start second.
“I think on the whole we’ve been very competitive,” Russell said. “But Max this morning we actually had as the fastest.”
Verstappen, a four-time F1 champion who had quite a combative practice session earlier Friday, was .258 seconds behind Antonelli.
This came after he was summoned by the stewards to explain run-ins with Russell and Franco Colapinto, though no discipline was handed down. Verstappen weaved in front of Russell and then the two went side by side.
They were seated at the post-qualifying news conference with Antonelli between them. Both were asked about coming together on the track.
“Nothing happened,” Verstappen said.
“No confusion,” Russell said. “I think it was pretty clear.”
It had been a rocky couple of days for Verstappen. The Dutch champion let his Red Bull team know twice on the radio in Thursday’s practices that he wasn’t happy with how the car was handling.
“Just trying to get my head around it to try to make the best out of it this weekend,” Verstappen said after qualifying. “I think we had a solid qualifying. We executed well. My first lap in (the third qualifying session) was pretty much as good as it can be. I think to be on the front row is very good for us.”
Antonelli, the youngest series champion ever, has the daunting task of trying to become the first driver to win in Las Vegas by starting third or worse. He has started further back just twice this season — but turned a 15th-place spot on the grid into a victory on July 5 in the British Grand Prix. Antonelli also went from 16th to third on June 14 in Barcelona, Spain.
Even though he posted the fastest lap on Friday, Antonelli was far from pleased.
“It was very weird qualifying for me,” Antonelli said. “First of all, I couldn’t get the tyres working, just zero feeling with the car. The brake pedal was very long, so I was struggling on the braking. It was so unexpected, and that last lap I thought I was screwed because I started one second from the car, but the tow is so big here, I was able to gain from that and put it on board.”
Conditions for the 3.85-mile course (6.2 kilometres) were considerably different from Thursday’s two practices, the first in the rain and the second on the wet surface that remained. The track was dry for Friday’s practice and qualifying sessions.
That better simulated expected dry conditions for Saturday night’s 50-lap race. Drivers also learned more about driving in what is expected to be one of the colder races in F1 history, with a forecast temperature of 47 degrees Fahrenheit (8 degrees Celsius) at race time.
Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc — fourth and fifth in the season standings, respectively — surprisingly failed to get out of the second qualifying session. Leclerc cost himself by not properly handling Turn 7 and didn’t get to the chequered flag in time for a final lap to make the time necessary to make the top 10 for the last session.
Leclerc will start 11th on Saturday and Hamilton 12th.

noticias.titulo: Sandpapergate: Cummins has Australia’s ‘unanimous support’ as Test captain
noticias.resumen: Pat Cummins to remain Test captain after Cricket Australia back cricketer following cheating scandal in South Africa.
noticias.texto:
Sandpapergate: Cummins has Australia’s ‘unanimous support’ as Test captain
Pat Cummins to remain Test captain after Cricket Australia back cricketer following cheating scandal in South Africa.
Cricket Australia (CA) threw its “unanimous support” behind Pat Cummins to remain Test captain on Saturday, rejecting any suggestion his integrity had been compromised by the lingering “Sandpapergate” scandal.
Cummins has been under huge pressure since Usman Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the ball in a Test at Cape Town in 2018.
At a news conference last week, he strenuously denied being aware of what was going on, but his position was undermined when Cameron Bancroft backed Khawaja’s version of events.
Only then-captain Steve Smith, his deputy David Warner and Bancroft – who used the sandpaper – were found to be responsible by a Cricket Australia probe.
With speculation over Cummins’ future rampant and a home four-Test series against New Zealand next month, CA moved to stamp out any further discussion about the 33-year-old’s fate after meeting him to check on his welfare.
It came after Josh Hazlewood earlier Saturday suggested he could quit if any action was taken against his longtime bowling partner.
CA expressed “its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain” following a board meeting.
“We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn,” said Chairman David Boon.
“We’ve expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.
“We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat’s integrity has been compromised.”
The retired Khawaja reignited the controversy in his autobiography, alleging the whole team was in the know, and he was strongly backed by close friend Warner.
After Cummins’ denials, Bancroft dropped a bomb in a newspaper column by also claiming “it was the whole team” while saying he felt “angry and betrayed” by the Test skipper.
Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening its investigation but instead set up a forum for players to share their experiences about 2018.
Hazlewood backs Cummins and denies Sandpapergate knowledge
Cummins said being captain “carries with it an awesome responsibility. I have and never will take that lightly.
“David and Todd (Greenberg) have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018,” he added.
“I support the forum 100 percent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to go and to have their say.
“There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what’s needed. Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth (at the first Test) will be my focus and priority.”
Hazlewood threw his support behind Cummins earlier Saturday and made a veiled threat to call it a day if he was removed as captain.
He reiterated that the bowling group at the time, which also included Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon, were not part of the plan.
They jointly released a statement in 2021 denying any involvement.
“I want to back Pat and everything he said in his press conference last week, everything he’s done for the last five or six years in particular as captain,” Hazlewood told the Sydney Daily Telegraph in his first comments since the story blew up.
“He’s a great leader. If you went around and asked everyone in the team, you’d hear the same response.”
Asked if he would consider quitting in protest if Cummins was removed, Hazlewood said: “I think I’d have to be put in that position to make a decision, but you’d have to think about it, yeah.”
Starc has also reinforced that he knew nothing in recent days. Lyon and Smith have yet to comment.

noticias.titulo: Iran says it downed US drones over Hormuz as bid to end war remains stalled
noticias.resumen: Iran reiterates conditions for Hormuz reopening as US slaps sanctions on four Iranians it says acted as 'oil trustees'.
noticias.texto:
Iran says it downed US drones over Hormuz as bid to end war remains stalled
Iranian foreign minister reiterates conditions for reopening of Strait of Hormuz, as US slaps sanctions on four Iranians it says acted as ‘oil trustees’.
Iranian forces say they have shot down two US drones over the Strait of Hormuz, as the United States steps up its economic pressure campaign against Iran.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Saturday a new air defence system had intercepted and shot down an MQ-9 drone, according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB. It said the incident marked the 58th such drone brought down by Iranian forces since the start of the war nearly nine months ago.
Later on Saturday, the IRGC also claimed bringing down an MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, the 19th such downing.
There was no immediate comment by the US military.
The incidents come days after the US and Iran engaged in direct, tit-for-tat strikes, against a backdrop of increasing Iranian attacks on vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas passed in peacetime.
Launched by the US and Israel on February 28, the war has killed thousands of people and severely disrupted shipping, pushing global energy prices higher and spreading to countries across the region.
The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding in June, but it was never fully implemented because of disagreements over freedom and security of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz, with attacks resuming periodically since July. In August, The Washington Post reported that the US had lost 45 MQ-9 drones, or about 25 percent of its fleet at a cost of more than $1.3bn, during combat operations in Iran.
‘No war, no peace’
As an agreement to end the war remains elusive, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Friday outlined his country’s positions on negotiations with the US, citing a seven-day proposal delivered to the US in September.
In an interview with state media, Araghchi said the seven conditions Iran has put forward “must be implemented for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen”. The conditions include ending the war and lifting sanctions and the naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports.
Araghchi said Iran was prepared to negotiate how the conditions should be implemented, saying its timetable was “flexible”. The negotiations would be “conditional on the American side taking necessary confidence-building measures”, he added.
The top diplomat also ruled out Iran transferring its stockpile of 60 percent enriched uranium abroad, but said a “fair solution” could be reached and a number of proposals by mediators were “worth examining”.
Araghchi said that the current “no war, no peace” state of the conflict was undesirable, but that Iran could not accept an agreement that would “hand victory to the other side”.
At a Friday news conference at the White House, US President Donald Trump told reporters that Tehran “want to make a deal” but not one that is acceptable to him.
“We want to make a real deal, not a fake deal that they’ve been doing for 51 years,” alleged Trump, who had said last week that a deal with Iran on ending the war was unnecessary.
At the same news conference, US Vice President JD Vance, who had previously blamed the war for Republicans losing both chambers of Congress earlier this month, declined to say whether he would have authorised strikes on Iran to prevent the country from developing a nuclear weapon.
Vance said the decision to attack Iran in February was Trump’s call, “and my job is to support the president of the United States.”
Separately on Friday, the US Treasury said it had imposed sanctions on four Iranians it said acted as “oil trustees”, collecting money from illicit international oil sales for Iran to evade sanctions and the US naval blockade on its southern ports.
The Treasury said in a statement that in many cases the trustees have kept oil revenues for personal gain. Among the individuals sanctioned are Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former IRGC intelligence officer, and Majid Taj, brother of the Iranian Football Federation’s President Mehdi Taj, the Treasury said.
The new sanctions put the individuals on the Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control’s Specially Designated Nationals list, freezing any assets they may have under US jurisdiction and effectively prohibiting dollar transactions with them or entities that they control.
The Treasury also said it imposed sanctions on Mohammad Hossein Servati, the son of IRGC Brigadier General Mohsen Servati, who has held positions in companies that brokered and received shipments of Iranian oil for delivery to independent Chinese “teapot” refineries.
Another sanctioned individual is Mojtaba Arabnejad, the son of the sanctioned Mahan Air CEO Hamid Arabnejad. The Treasury said that Mojtaba Arabnejad has purchased aircraft parts for the sanctioned Mahan Air and overseen oil sales that have partly supported the airline.
Defunding offensive activity
Meanwhile, as Republicans grapple with the fallout from the sweeping midterm election losses, Democratic Representatives Yassamin Ansari and Ro Khanna called on Congress to use an upcoming government funding bill to end spending for offensive military operations against Iran.
Citing the mounting costs of the war, they issued a video statement urging fellow legislators to reject any funding package that keeps paying for the war, with a deadline looming next month to adopt a budget.
Failing to pass a spending bill by December 11 could trigger a government shutdown, a risk that has made some Democrats wary of drawing a red line on the war on Iran.
Rosa DeLauro and Patty Murray, the top Democrats responsible for appropriations, have said they would prefer to find ways to end the war without risking a government shutdown.

noticias.titulo: French police officers guilty of Michel Zecler assault: What happens now?
noticias.resumen: Officers dealt more than 30 blows to the Black music producer in what the court ruled was a racially motivated crime.
noticias.texto:
French police officers guilty of Michel Zecler assault: What happens now?
Officers dealt more than 30 blows to the Black music producer in what the court ruled was a racially motivated crime.
A French court has found three French police officers guilty of intentional, racist violence during the 2020 assault of Michel Zecler, a Black music producer, and sentenced them to prison.
The landmark ruling has once again shone a spotlight on the issue of police brutality in France, which activists say is rarely prosecuted despite being systemic and often racially motivated.
Here’s what happened in the case and what it means now:
What was the verdict?
The Paris criminal court convicted three police officers of assaulting Zecler in Paris in 2020, ruling that the attack was racially motivated. The court also found the defendants guilty of falsifying a police report about the incident.
The officers – 29-year-old Aurelien Lapersonne, 50-year-old Philippe Tondeux and 37-year-old Pierre Plantier – were each sentenced to five years in prison, part of which was suspended.
All three have been barred from serving in the police force again.
Who is Michel Zecler?
Zecler is a 47-year-old French music producer who co-founded the independent rap label Black Gold Corp. Zecler has worked in the French hip-hop industry for years, including helping to put together the prominent 2016 rap tour called L’Age d’Or du Rap Francais.
Music journalist Olivier Cachin described Zecler as easy-going and humble. “He just works, staying very much in the background,” Cachin told French newspaper Sud Ouest. “He’s not a ‘look-at-me’ type… He’s just a big teddy bear.”
Why was Zecler beaten by the French police?
Officers stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on November 21, 2020, accusing him of failing to put on a compulsory face mask, as required by France’s COVID-19 restrictions at the time.
The officers then pushed Zecler back into the building and assaulted him – an incident captured by his security cameras.
Over five minutes or so, the officers punched, kicked and used batons to deliver some 30 blows to Zecler, severely injuring him. He suffered head trauma and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon.
Zecler said the officers repeatedly used a racist slur during the beating, and that the assault had left him “completely devastated”.
What happened during the trial?
Officers Lapersonne, Paltier and Tondeux were found guilty of aggravated group assault that was racially motivated.
They were also convicted of falsifying an official police report in which they accused Zecler of being violent towards them – claims unsupported by the security footage.
The presiding judge said the officers had been dishonest in their report “to shield (themselves) from disciplinary and legal consequences, with no regard for the criminal consequences faced by Michel Zecler”.
Officer Lapersonne, who submitted the report, initially claimed that Zecler had attacked the officers and “struck out with his arms and legs”. When the presiding judge asked if he had “made that up”, Lapersonne responded during the trial, “Absolutely.” Lapersonne’s initial police report also failed to mention that the officers landed blows on Zecler.
“I deliberately omitted them. I think out of fear. It was stupid of me,” Lapersonne told the court.
All three of the convicted officers admitted to having used excessive force and apologised to Zecler, though they denied the charges of racism.
Tondeux, the oldest of the officers, said he regretted “the image I have given of the police”.
The judges said Zecler’s testimony, in which he claimed to have heard one of the officers use the racial slur “sale negre”, had been consistent from the beginning, while the officers’ falsified report damaged their credibility.
Speaking to the court, Zecler said he would likely not have been recognised as a victim if not for the security footage recording the incident.
How long have the French police officers been sentenced to prison?
All three were given five-year sentences, but with varying portions suspended.
Lapersonne, who was found to have first stopped Zecler and authored the falsified police report, had three years of his sentence suspended, while Tondeux had three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended and will serve the remaining year under electronic monitoring rather than in prison.
Zecler’s lawyer described the sentences as “falling short”, but said they set an important precedent.
“This precedent shows that even if a police officer lies, someone who comes forward to say the police did the worst to them can be believed,” said the lawyer.
What does the Michel Zecler case reveal about police brutality in France?
Zecler’s case is the latest to draw attention to the issue of police brutality in France, which is rarely prosecuted, as well as racial discrimination, following several high-profile cases in recent years.
In 2023, protests and riots broke out after Nahel Merzouk, a 17-year-old boy of North African descent, was shot and killed by a police officer during a traffic stop outside Paris. Police initially reported that an officer had shot at him because the teenager was driving his car at him, but this version of events was contradicted by a video circulating on social media. In March, a French appeals court ruled that the officer who shot Merzouk should stand trial.
In 2024, a judge handed suspended prison sentences to three officers who caused permanent rectal injuries to a Black man, Theo Luhaka, during a stop-and-search in 2017.
In 2016, Adama Traore, a 24-year-old man of Malian descent, died in custody after being restrained and apprehended by police following a dispute over an identity check. A case against three arresting police officers was dropped in 2023 and, in February this year, France’s top court, the Court of Cassation, ruled against reopening the investigation.
A 2025 report published by France’s Defender of Rights (Defenseur des droits), led by Claire Hedon, found that young men “perceived as Arab, black or from North Africa” are four times more likely to be stopped under police stop-and-search powers than the overall population.
They are also 12 times more likely to be subjected to more severe measures, such as being frisked during checks, the report found.
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) also condemned France last year for identity checks it deemed “discriminatory” following a case brought by six French citizens of African or North African origin.
Will the issue of police brutality be addressed in France?
France is coming under increasing pressure to address this issue.
The country was rocked by protests in September against proposed legislation that would grant additional protections to law enforcement officials using firearms in the line of duty.
The new law, which the French Senate is currently considering, will grant police officers a “licence to kill”, critics say.
“It’s a very dangerous piece of legislation. It’s liberticide,” Rim-Sarah Alouane, a legal scholar and an associate researcher in public law at the University of Toulouse Capitole, told Al Jazeera. “It would create a sense of impunity amongst police officers – which already exists, but this would strengthen that. It would undermine investigations and make access to the justice system even more difficult for victims and their families.
“It raises serious issues regarding equality under the law because it puts a presumption of innocence in favour of people because of their profession as cops.”
But while French officials have acknowledged isolated cases of police misconduct, they have so far pushed back against claims of systemic racism or discrimination by law enforcement.
In 2023, Laurent Nunez, then prefect of the Paris police, said “there is no racism in the police force.”
Activists say the French authorities’ refusal to address the institutional nature of police brutality further endangers minorities.
“The people who are dying are mostly Black or Arab,” French activist Assa Traore, the sister of Adama Traore, said in an interview with the Anadolu news agency earlier this year. “Admitting that racism exists is not a weakness. It’s about saving lives.”
Alouane said that Zecler’s case was obviously “about institutional racism, systemic discrimination and police violence”.
“Everything is connected. Not only are we dealing with police violence against a Black man, but that’s on top of attempting to conceal evidence and falsify a report,” said Alouane. “When these reports are falsified, we’re questioning the integrity of the entire system.”

noticias.titulo: Harry Kane to miss ‘a few months’ after injury as Bayern Munich draw
noticias.resumen: Ballon d'Or winner tears a ligament in his left ankle during Bayern Munich’s 1-1 draw against Cologne.
noticias.texto:
Harry Kane to miss ‘a few months’ after injury as Bayern Munich draw
Ballon d’Or winner tears a ligament in his left ankle during Bayern Munich’s 1-1 draw against Cologne.
England football captain Harry Kane will miss the “next few months” after tearing a ligament in his left ankle during Bayern Munich’s 1-1 draw against Cologne on Friday.
Kane was taken down in the area by Cologne defender Joel Schmied, who reached Michael Olise’s low cross first but knocked into the Ballon d’Or winner’s left leg in his follow-through at the back post.
Kane writhed in pain. Although he gingerly got back to his feet and initially continued playing, he soon hobbled off the field with two physiotherapists after treatment.
A club statement on X said: “Harry Kane suffered a tear of the syndesmosis ligament in his left ankle in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga home match against Köln on Friday evening. This was confirmed by an examination by Bayern Munich’s medical department. The 33-year-old will therefore be out for the next few months.”
Kane is the undisputed star of Bayern. Since joining from Spurs in 2023, he has scored 156 goals in 161 competitive fixtures and won two Bundesliga titles and the German Cup.
He became the first Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or in 25 years last month and, two weeks ago, signed a new contract with Bayern that will keep him in Bavaria until June 2029.
The night was supposed to be a happy one for Bayern, who welcomed coach Vincent Kompany back to the dugout a month after he collapsed while watching the reserve squad train.
However, Kompany saw his team go behind after just 11 minutes when winger Mikey Moore, on loan from Tottenham, started and finished a counterattack.
Just nine minutes later, Kane limped off to be replaced by Tom Bischof, and the German midfielder made a quick impact. Before halftime, he found Nathaniel Brown, who fired a fierce shot into the bottom corner from the edge of the box.
Both sides had chances in a busy second half but it remained goalless and the point was enough for Bayern to edge a point ahead of Borussia Dortmund. Bayern remained the only unbeaten team in Europe’s top five leagues.
Cologne, for which Moore was named man of the match, climbed one place into 14th.

noticias.titulo: Illicit alcohol kills 11, poisons 180 in northeast India’s Manipur state
noticias.resumen: Manipur's chief minister orders a probe into the incident, saying those responsible will be arrested and punished.
noticias.texto:
Illicit alcohol kills 11, poisons 180 in northeast India’s Manipur state
Manipur’s chief minister orders a probe into the incident, saying those responsible will be arrested and punished.
At least 11 people have died after drinking what authorities suspect was spurious alcohol in northeast India’s Manipur state, prompting an investigation.
More than 180 people, who were believed to have consumed toxic liquor, had been admitted to hospitals in Manipur as of Friday.
According to local media, officials have advised locals who have drunk alcohol from Sugnu town in Manipur in the past week to seek medical evaluation. Meanwhile, the deputy police commissioner has advised people not to drink alcohol of unknown origin.
“Over 180 patients have been admitted in the two hospitals so far, while the death toll has reached 11 in the last 48 hours,” Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh said in a statement on Friday.
Illicit alcohol is a lucrative industry in India, attracting customers who are too poor to afford licensed brands. Vendors regularly use chemicals to increase the potency of their alcohol.
Methanol is one of the substances used and can be fatal in doses as low as 60ml. Battery acid has also been found in unregulated alcohol in India.
At least 120 people died in Punjab in 2020 after drinking toxic alcohol.

noticias.resumen: Infantino handed huge boost in re-election campaign as FIFA president as CONMEBOL offers unanimous support.
noticias.texto:
Gianni Infantino’s FIFA re-election backed by South America’s CONMEBOL
Infantino handed huge boost in re-election campaign as FIFA president as CONMEBOL offers unanimous support.
FIFA president Gianni Infantino has “unanimous” backing for re-election as head of world football from CONMEBOL, the 10-country South American bloc.
Infantino faced criticism over his aborted plan to allow private investment into the World Cup, but he also retains support from Africa and Asia for his bid to win re-election next March.
Each country has one vote with 211 members, and the winner will need to secure at least 106 votes in the ballot scheduled for March 18 in Rabat.
CONMEBOL has 10, Africa has 54 and Asia 46.
The CONMEBOL statement late on Friday was made in Barranquilla ahead of Saturday’s Copa Sudamericana final between Brazil’s Atletico Mineiro and Argentina’s Boca Juniors.
CONMEBOL said it appreciated “the leadership of the current FIFA president” and the “positive transformations in football” that he has driven since taking office in 2016.
Having been the sole candidate in 2019 and 2023, Infantino faces two declared challengers: Frenchman Philippe Diallo and Japan’s Kozo Tashima.
Infantino has fended off criticism of the enlargement of the World Cup, giving a FIFA peace prize to Donald Trump and – at the American president’s request – overturning a red card for a US player during the competition.
He is under severe pressure for the first time, but mainly due to UEFA’s reaction to the private investor plan that forced a humiliating climbdown.
UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin has given full backing to Diallo, while Tashima has pledged to restore “integrity” to world football’s governing body.
Tashima, who serves on the FIFA Council, stressed his intention to restore trust in the governing body and make transparency and integrity the hallmarks of his campaign.
He said he decided to run after he was incensed by FIFA’s shock decision to lift the ban on United States player Folarin Balogun.
In October, FIFA confirmed its intention to set up a $6.35bn development fund for the next four years.
The fund would allow money to be distributed to FIFA’s 211 federations, as well as to the regional confederations after a commercially successful 2026 World Cup.
The plan would allow for the payment of $25m to all 211 member federations.

noticias.resumen: The blaze erupted at the Hartha power station and spread to nearby houses.
noticias.texto:
At least four killed, 35 injured in fire at power station in Iraq’s Basra
The blaze erupted at the Hartha power station and spread to nearby houses.
A fire has broken out at a power station in southern Iraq, killing at least four people and injuring 35, according to the Iraqi state media.
The Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported on Saturday that the Civil Defence Directorate had brought the fire under control at the Hartha power station and in neighbouring houses.
Operations at the power station, which has a generating capacity of 800 megawatts, were forced to stop after the blaze.
Footage of the fire shared online shows plumes of smoke and burned-out cars. Crowds of people observing the emergency response could also be seen.
The cause of the fire is yet to be confirmed.
Iraq’s electricity infrastructure has long struggled with decades of underinvestment, inadequate maintenance and an inability to meet peak demand, particularly during the extremely hot summer months.
Fires and technical failures at substations and power facilities have previously disrupted electricity supplies and caused widespread outages.
