noticias.titulo: Three US citizens among 4 convicted in Honduras over sex-trafficking case
noticias.resumen: The defendants face 10 years in jail after being found guilty of recruiting women into a sex-trafficking ring.
noticias.texto:
Three US citizens among 4 convicted in Honduras over sex-trafficking case
The defendants face 10 years in jail after being found guilty of recruiting women into a sex-trafficking ring.
A court in Honduras has convicted four people, including three United States citizens, of criminal association in connection with the 2022 disappearance of a woman whose whereabouts are still unknown.
The Public Ministry said on Friday that it would request the maximum jail term of 10 years for each defendant after they were found guilty of recruiting women into a sex-trafficking ring. The next hearing is due to take place on December 9.
The ministry also said it would appeal the court’s decision to acquit US citizens Harold Green and William James Murdock of human trafficking.
They were found guilty of the lesser crime of criminal association, along with fellow US national Gary Lee Johnston and Honduran national Gustavo Trejo.
Woman’s disappearance
Angie Pena disappeared on January 1, 2022, while jet skiing by the Caribbean island of Roatan, off the northern coast of Honduras.
She was a 22-year-old university student when she went missing and police initially suspected she had drowned. However, her family believed she had been abducted and demanded an investigation.
A trafficking investigation was later launched after the jet ski Pena had used was found in Belize, about 90 nautical miles (170 kilometres) away from Roatan.
Investigators later found she had fallen prey to a sex-trafficking network called “Delta Teams” that has since been dismantled. The Attorney General’s Office determined minors were among the trafficked victims.
“The Public Ministry [Attorney General’s Office] obtained a guilty verdict against four members of the network known as Delta Teams for the violation of criminal association,” the prosecutor’s office said on X.
Three US nationals, identified as Harold Green, William Murdock and Gary Lee Johnston, as well as Honduran national Ramon Trejo, were found guilty of “locating, recruiting, and transporting women via social media”.
Green and Murdock were acquitted of human trafficking on Friday after the court concluded there was insufficient evidence to link them to Pena’s disappearance and alleged trafficking.
The case highlights the struggles women in Honduras face when seeking justice after being violently abused.
The country has a femicide rate of 4.3 cases per 100,000 inhabitants, the highest in Latin America, according to the Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean (ECLAC).
Friday’s trial was not open to the public or media, prompting Pena’s family to question its transparency.
In August, a key protected witness was killed. Following his death, videos were released of Dereck McNeil, in which he accused a special unit in the public prosecutor’s office of corruption.
The ATIC denies it is corrupt and says it was not involved in investigating Pena’s disappearance.
“The ruling indicates to the Public Prosecutor’s Office that it must continue investigating, as the lines of inquiry in Angie Pena’s case have not been exhausted,” said Kenia Paz, a lawyer for the Legal Team for Human Rights, which represents Pena’s family.
“The ruling and what has been done so far by the state do not bring Angie Pena back. They do not tell us where she is, and that is what we need to know: what happened to Angie and when she will return.”
Pena’s aunt Yenely Diaz told the AFP news agency: “They told us it was an accident; everything was conducted through organised crime.”

noticias.titulo: Sudan’s war will end, but will it be too late?
noticias.resumen: Pressure from within Sudan may achieve what international diplomacy has not.
noticias.texto:
Sudan’s war will end, but will it be too late?
Pressure from within Sudan may achieve what international diplomacy has not.
It has been more than three years since war erupted in Sudan, and its consequences continue to worsen. More people continue to be displaced and require basic humanitarian assistance to survive. On the surface, the conflict appears set to continue indefinitely.
At a recent Security Council briefing, a United Nations official noted: “The picture is bleak. … The parties continue to show no credible commitment to compromise or to pursuing a negotiated pause in fighting. They are not moving closer to dialogue.”
This assessment reflects the international consensus so much so that the United States has chosen in recent months to heap sanction upon sanction in a bid to “raise the costs of continued conflict” for the warring sides and force them into ceasefire talks. But what the view from New York and Washington misses and what became obvious after only a few days in Khartoum this month is that the conditions for a ceasefire are rapidly emerging from within the country.
A perfect storm of financial collapse, military advances and humanitarian catastrophe, along with growing civilian demands, is creating the long-elusive pressure for a ceasefire that could well take hold before the fourth anniversary of the war next April.
Khartoum, Sudan’s beleaguered capital, is no longer the ghost town that it was throughout much of the war. International flights now arrive regularly at the city’s modest airport from Cairo, Riyadh and Doha, carrying Sudanese looking to restart the lives the war put on hold and businessmen sensing a ceasefire on the horizon and angling to get in on the ground floor of the country’s rebirth. At one of the city’s leading business hotels, the lobby was buzzing with British, Swiss and Saudi business groups there to close deals on everything from mining to commodity trading to reconstruction.
But Sudan’s leaders don’t just see the opportunities; they are also feeling the pressure of an economy in freefall. The week I was there, the Sudanese pound fell to a then-record low of 9,000 to the US dollar, compared with a pre-war average of 600. (The exchange rate now exceeds 10,000.) Petrol queues stretched for blocks, even for those lucky enough to be able to afford to fill their tanks. Many of Khartoum’s returnees, more than 2 million of the roughly 3.8 million people who fled, are struggling to buy groceries and keep the lights on. Worse still, farmers can no longer afford fertiliser, leaving much of the country’s most productive cropland lying fallow.
A senior official acknowledged to me privately that the war economy, which enabled Sudan’s army to procure the weapons needed to turn the tide of the war, is now the greatest source of pain for the country’s population. The pressure on Sudan’s leaders to reverse the economic decline is real and is creating a new demand to end the fighting.
Friendly states like Turkiye and Saudi Arabia have pitched in, pursuing agreements to secure fuel supplies and rebuild energy infrastructure, but such support remains limited and temporary. Protests over transit costs recently broke out in Atbara, the northern city where protests against skyrocketing bread prices began in December 2018, helping to spark Sudan’s 2019 democratic revolution. Economic protests unified the country before and could do so again, and the military knows it.
Beyond the economy, it is the military’s battlefield gains that are creating the conditions for it to contemplate a ceasefire. Army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has promised to reclaim “every inch” of territory. He has succeeded in pushing back a new offensive in southeastern Sudan’s Blue Nile State and is advancing farther west in West Kordofan, where the army and its allied Joint Forces recently retook the strategic town of el-Khuwei and several surrounding areas, increasing the army’s control to roughly two-thirds of the country.
Fighting for control of the western region of Darfur, the only region almost entirely under the control of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary, could be costly and time-consuming. But a year after the fall of el-Fasher, the capital of North Darfur State, to the RSF amid atrocities that a UN fact-finding mission said bore the hallmarks of genocide, efforts to retake the area would demonstrate that the military’s commitment to unify the country wasn’t just battlefield bravado. Making inroads in Darfur would also paint the RSF into a corner and give the army both tactical gains and a strategic advantage in ceasefire discussions.
The final reason why a ceasefire has become so urgent is the spiralling humanitarian crisis in the country, which has been at crisis levels for months but could well become catastrophic by year’s end. Adding to the internal displacement, restrictions on humanitarian access and lost food production is this year’s “Super El Nino”, which has disrupted Sudan’s annual rains and devastated whatever meagre harvest was expected.
With more than 40 percent of the population already facing “acute food insecurity”, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification hunger monitor, projections suggested that Sudan’s hunger crisis could deteriorate dramatically by mid-2027 when food shortages are expected to be at their most severe. The only way to avoid or even mitigate that outcome would be through a ceasefire in the coming months that enables a massive influx of lifesaving aid.
As conditions on the ground make a ceasefire more urgent, Sudan’s own plans for the day after the fighting are becoming clearer. With each ceasefire proposal the military rejects, public demand for a deal grows as people become increasingly exhausted by the war.
Talk of an inter-Sudanese dialogue, political reconciliation and eventually elections is also becoming more common, creating greater expectations that fighting should soon come to an end and responsibility for day-to-day governance and service delivery be transferred to civilians. While these efforts remain inchoate, the demand for them is building.
Ultimately, it is the attitudes inside Sudan that will create the momentum for peace, not the external pressures and punitive measures employed by the international community. As conditions for civilians inside the country continue to deteriorate and the military’s position stabilises, there is hope on the horizon that a ceasefire could be achieved. The international community should focus on supporting these internal conditions before the dire warnings about the economy and humanitarian situation become reality.
A version of this article first appeared on Al Jazeera Arabic.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Netanyahu is playing with the fire that killed Rabin
noticias.resumen: His attacks on Arab lawmakers echo the incitement that preceded Rabin’s assassination and risk unleashing new violence.
noticias.texto:
Netanyahu is playing with the fire that killed Rabin
His attacks on Arab lawmakers echo the incitement that preceded Rabin’s assassination and risk unleashing new violence.
Politics is not for the faint-hearted, and debate and disagreement are integral to it. A number of politicians believe that the end justifies the means, but most know when they are approaching the red lines and when to stop.
Not Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s current prime minister. His repulsive response to the success of the Arab parties in last month’s general election unleashed his darkest racist demons.
Some might argue that this is simply another cynical tactic in his efforts to derail his political rivals’ attempts to form a government. Whether this is who he really is or simply a cynical politician at his core, governing through division makes little difference.
He is the prime minister, and his words and behaviour matter. When he legitimises and normalises this kind of language, he releases the racist genie from the bottle. Certain segments of his supporters may interpret it as a licence to resort to actual violence, and history has precedent for it.
Accusing all 19 elected members of the Knesset (MKs) representing predominantly Palestinian citizens of Israel, individually and collectively, of being supporters of terrorism and terrorists, while portraying those members of the Jewish/Zionist parties prepared to form a coalition with them as, for all intents and purposes, collaborators with those who support terrorism against Jews and seek the destruction of the “Jewish state”, amounts to declaring open season on them. In doing so, Netanyahu is abusing the protection afforded to him by his parliamentary immunity, making allegations for which there is not a shred of truth.
If anyone should know better, learn from his past mistakes and express profound remorse for such behaviour, it is Benjamin Netanyahu. No one is more closely associated with the atmosphere of incitement that preceded the assassination of Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin on November 4, 1995 than Netanyahu.
Rabin became the principal target of the Israeli right’s hatred after signing the Oslo Accords – in other words, for demonstrating the courage to pursue a peaceful end to the conflict between Israelis and Palestinians. The religious-messianic right, including several rabbis, issued a ruling known as din rodef (the law of the pursuer) against Rabin, accusing him of “ceding parts of the Land of Israel to Gentiles”. Yigal Amir, Rabin’s eventual assassin, cited this ruling as justification for his heinous crime. Amir pulled the trigger, but those who orchestrated and fed the campaign of hatred against Rabin bear considerable responsibility too, at the very least morally.
Netanyahu, who was chairman of the Likud party and leader of the opposition at the time, not only failed to condemn this behaviour but notoriously participated in a protest in Jerusalem during which Rabin’s image was portrayed in a Nazi uniform. Rabin’s widow, Leah, later recalled: “There was a Likud rally in Jerusalem not too long ago. They put the figure of Yitzhak, my husband, in the uniform of a Nazi leader and Mr Netanyahu was there. He later talked against it, but he was there, and he didn’t stop it.”
She never forgave him for that. He never apologised or expressed regret.
Several months later, Netanyahu was elected prime minister. Perhaps, in his mind, this electoral victory exonerated him from any responsibility for creating the atmosphere that led to Rabin’s assassination. It may also have reinforced his belief that divisive politics pays off and can take him where he has always felt he belongs: The prime minister’s office.
Now, caught between a sense of entitlement to remain in power that appears stronger than ever and the fear that relinquishing office could jeopardise his efforts to prevent his corruption trial from reaching its conclusion, Netanyahu is allowing racial hatred to pour out of him unabated.
It began during the election campaign, when he foresaw that his chances of forming the next government were slim. It escalated dramatically on election day, when he once again resorted to his vile dog-whistle tactics in a last-ditch attempt to mobilise his supporters. He warned of surging Arab voter turnout and, by that, at least implicitly questioned the legitimacy of their votes compared with the Jewish ones, as they couldn’t bear their success. But that was only the beginning. The day after the election, Netanyahu and his ultra-right-wing partners turned up the volume, raising allegations of irregularities in Arab communities to advance a narrative of a “stolen” election.
Worse was to come. What should have been days of celebrating Israeli democracy, the swearing-in of the new Knesset, became another opportunity for Netanyahu to abuse his parliamentary privilege. Instead of delivering a speech that might have helped unite the nation after a bruising election campaign, he embarked on a jingoistic horror show.
He accused Gadi Eisenkot, whom President Isaac Herzog had tasked with forming a government because he enjoyed the support of a majority of MKs, and his political partners of seeking to establish a government dependent on parties that, according to Netanyahu, “agree that the Jewish state must be destroyed”. He went on to claim that these parties differed only over the kind of Palestinian state they wanted to see emerge from the ruins of the Jewish state: “Whether an Islamic state in the Muslim Brotherhood mould, like Hamas in Gaza, or a nationalist Palestinian state in the Fatah mould. That is the whole difference.”
This amounts to nothing less than portraying Arab political representatives as a fifth column or traitors, while depicting those prepared to form a government with them as collaborators with this supposed ambition, or as dangerously naive for failing to recognise it.
When Netanyahu and his political partners insist that their accusations are not directed at the Arab population, even though Arab citizens had voted in record numbers for these very parties only days earlier, they are either playing innocent or insulting the intelligence of both Arab citizens and the wider public.
Not so long ago, Netanyahu himself offered Mansour Abbas and his Ra’am party the opportunity to join his own government when it suited his political interests. Yet when his rivals contemplate doing precisely the same thing, he shamelessly incites against them.
Let us not forget that Netanyahu is the politician who legitimised the messianic far right and normalised sharing power with its representatives in government. He appointed Itamar Ben-Gvir, who had been convicted of incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organisation, as minister of national security. This is the same Ben-Gvir who first gained notoriety by stealing the emblem from the car of then-Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, displaying it on television and declaring: “We got to his car, and we’ll get to him too.” Netanyahu is opportunistic and cynical to the very end, but by now the distinction between him and the Kahanist Ben-Gvir has become paper-thin.
The warning signs are there, written on the wall in capital letters. The incitement of 1995 helped create the atmosphere that led to Rabin’s assassination. The scale and intensity of today’s incitement could once again lead an extremist zealot to pull the trigger, this time against an Arab or Jewish politician seeking to work with Arab political representatives. It could also encourage attacks against Arab citizens, potentially escalating into widespread communal violence or even civil war, as extremists convince themselves that they are acting in accordance with their leader’s wishes to prevent the supposed destruction of the Jewish state.
Israel is on the brink of political violence. And Benjamin Netanyahu bears a very substantial share of the responsibility for bringing it there.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

noticias.titulo: Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
noticias.resumen: Eisenkot's fragile alliance must overcome deep ideological divisions to turn its opposition into a government.
noticias.texto:
Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
Eisenkot’s fragile alliance must overcome deep ideological divisions to turn its opposition into a government.
As negotiations over the formation of Israel’s next government approach their first deadline of December 6, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to be seeking to exploit divisions within the opposition “change” alliance trying to oust him.
On Wednesday, he held an undeclared meeting with one of its leading figures, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, in a move that has prompted accusations that Netanyahu is attempting to fracture the bloc from within.
The meeting, which lasted two and a half hours, was described by Netanyahu’s office as a “security briefing”. Sources within the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, however, characterised it as a “strategic disaster”, according to Israeli media.
Bennett had not informed Eisenkot of the meeting in advance, sources told the outlet Ynet. During a subsequent gathering of opposition leaders, Bennett is reported to have argued that they should try to pursue the possibility of a unity government with Netanyahu, Channel 12 reported.
Bennett, a right-winger, is among several prominent figures in the opposition alliance who have previously served in Netanyahu-led governments. Eisenkot himself joined Netanyahu’s emergency unity government following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, serving as a minister without portfolio and a member of the war cabinet.
Avigdor Lieberman, meanwhile – another right-wing member of the opposition bloc – served as Netanyahu’s foreign minister and defence minister.
“Netanyahu is trying to break up the [opposition] bloc for change through Bennett,” a senior figure in the Eisenkot-led alliance told Ynet in an article referencing the numerous pledges by opposition leaders, including Bennett, never to serve within a Netanyahu-led coalition again.
However, given the broad array of ideologies among the coalition leaders, stretching from the hard-right policies of Lieberman to the relatively left-wing platform of Democrats’ leader Yair Golan, and many having previously worked with Netanyahu, it remains unclear how long the bloc can maintain its unity.
Bennett himself was once among Netanyahu’s closest political allies, serving in several of his governments before breaking with him in 2021, when the opportunity arose to form an alternative administration with centrist Yair Lapid. Bennett and Lapid subsequently assembled a cross-party coalition that ended Netanyahu’s 12 consecutive years in office, with Bennett taking the premiership for the first half of its term. But he still shares many policy positions with Netanyahu.
So how cohesive is the opposition coalition, and what could be its potential breaking points?
Here’s what we know:
Is the change bloc united ideologically?
All of the bloc’s members supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – at least at its start – as well as its attacks on several regional states, including Iran and Lebanon.
In terms of domestic policy, however, there are marked differences between members of the alliance.
Both the bloc’s leader, former Israeli military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, and Bennett’s electoral partner, Yair Lapid, are regarded as relatively centrist figures. By contrast, Bennett and Lieberman are firmly on the right, divided largely by their attitudes towards religion: Bennett is a religious nationalist, while Liberman is a staunchly secular politician with a background in Israel’s Russian-speaking community, increasingly at odds with Israel’s powerful religious political currents.
Standing apart is the left-wing Yair Golan, a supporter of a two-state solution with the Palestinians and an outspoken critic of settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, which he has accused the government of encouraging or tolerating.
Is the alliance under strain?
Yes.
Beyond the prospect of Netanyahu – Israel’s longest-serving prime minister – continually attempting to undermine them, Eisenkot faces the formidable task of finding the additional 13 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. His bloc holds just 48 of the parliament’s 120 seats after the October 27 elections, leaving him dependent on bridging deep political divides among his allies if he is to form a government capable of governing.
Golan has already met political leaders from parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel and spoken enthusiastically about forming a government with their support. However, that suggestion has been rejected by the rest of the bloc, and has provoked fierce opposition, with right-wing protesters even threatening civil war at the prospect.
Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beytenu party holds seven seats, has been particularly emphatic in rejecting any government dependent on Palestinian support. However, his longstanding and highly vocal opposition to the de facto exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from military service appears to be softening in the face of another possibility: the 13 seats held by the ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism.
Lieberman’s willingness to compromise on conscription risks undermining one of his central electoral promises, as well as those of other opposition leaders, and could prompt a backlash from supporters.
Have the change bloc’s differences come out in the open?
In August, Bennett dismissed Eisenkot’s proposal to allow limited exemptions from military conscription that would cover the ultra-Orthodox as an “insane mistake”, warning that ultra-Orthodox politicians Aryeh Deri and Moshe Gafni would “run circles around” him. Eisenkot subsequently countered, accusing Bennett and Lieberman of engaging in “old politics” and damaging the opposition’s electoral prospects by refusing to agree that the largest party in the alliance should lead the next government.
Lieberman, just weeks before the election, branded Eisenkot “Gantz 2.0” – referring to former defence minister Benny Gantz, who joined Netanyahu’s government in 2020 despite campaigning against him – accusing Eisenkot of secretly pursuing a deal with Netanyahu and acting out of personal ambition. Golan, meanwhile, told Lieberman several days after the election that, if he was to continue to insist on a government that avoids conscripting ultra-Orthodox men, he was “welcome to form one with Netanyahu”.
What did change bloc leaders say about Netanyahu before entering the opposition?
Their previous assessments of Netanyahu have not always been so harsh.
In 2020, Bennett told reporters that, despite their personal differences, he respected Netanyahu “very much”, adding that Israel had “won a victory” by having him in office for so long and that he had “done great things” for the country.
Lieberman, meanwhile, told The Jerusalem Post in 2019 that he wished Netanyahu “only really good results” and hoped that he would be acquitted on the corruption charges that he has since cited, on numerous occasions, as evidence that the prime minister is unfit for office.

noticias.titulo: Haitians excited but uneasy as El Salvador troops fight gangs
noticias.resumen: Foreign combatants in Port-au-Prince welcomed by many after years of gang control but some fear offensive could exacerbate volatile situation A bullet-peppered mural of the Haitian striker Emmanuel Sanon covers the facade of Port-au-Prince’s main football ground. noticias.texto:
A bullet-peppered mural of the Haitian striker Emmanuel Sanon covers the facade of Port-au-Prince’s main football ground. But more than two years have passed since any sports stars graced the pitch.
In 2024, as the surrounding city was almost entirely captured by heavily armed gangs, Sylvio Cator stadium – where football greats including Brazil’s Ronaldo and Roberto Carlos once played – also fell under criminal control, its dilapidated red and blue stands used as an outpost by fighters working for a gang boss called Izo. Haiti’s national team, the Grenadiers, found itself homeless and was forced to play its World Cup qualifying games abroad.
That changed last week, as Haitian police and troops from El Salvador reconquered the stadium. Nayib Bukele, El Salvador’s authoritarian president, called the development a step towards delivering Haiti from a criminal insurrection that has displaced more than 1.5 million people and killed thousands.
“We now have the upper hand on the ground,” claimed Bukele, who has sent more than 2,000 soldiers to Haiti since mid-October.
Outside the Sylvio Cator stadium, named after an acclaimed Haitian athlete who won a silver medal at the 1928 Olympics, there were joyous scenes as citizens celebrated a foreign politician they hope will prove an unlikely saviour.
“There’s a wind of hope blowing through our country and, thanks to God, we will get through this. Long live Bukele!” said a 55-year-old decorator who asked to be named as Bòs Baton.
Stood by Sanon’s battle-scarred fresco, Baton recalled being driven from an area called Poste-Marchand after criminals set his home ablaze during an armed uprising that started in February 2024. “Today, we are happy because there are places we couldn’t go to before that are accessible – and it’s thanks to Bukele’s intervention that we can be here today,” Baton said.
Identical sentiments have been voiced on the streets of El Salvador’s capital, San Salvador, in recent years as a result of Bukele’s controversial anti-gang crusade, which has freed millions from gang rule – albeit at a high price.
Since that crackdown began in early 2022, more than 90,000 Salvadorans have been jailed as part of a mass incarceration campaign that has slashed murder rates but also fuelled fears that El Salvador’s democracy has died.
Bukele’s domestic clampdown has made the millennial strongman a darling for rightwing politicians and voters across Latin America and the Caribbean, who hold his actions up as proof that, with an iron fist and a malleable approach to human rights, rampant criminality can be tamed.
Now, as Bukele seeks to extend his seven-year presidency in an election in February, he is hoping to burnish his gang-busting credentials overseas.
“It’s an operation that projects force, that projects Bukele’s image as the saviour … and positions El Salvador as a key reference in the region for [how] … to deal with gangs and security,” said Tiziano Breda, a Latin America regional expert from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project.
The extent of Bukele’s ambitions in Haiti is unclear. The operation’s trigger was the 18 October abduction of four Salvadoran aviation technicians who worked for a UN-backed security force. On Monday, Bukele’s vice-president, Félix Ulloa, announced Salvadoran troops would withdraw as soon as the four men were rescued, “because this is not an occupying force – we are not there to stay”.
But Ulloa also said his government was responding altruistically “to a cry for help from the Haitian people and government”, suggesting its mission could be extended.
Bukele has also hinted his plans go beyond short-lived ground operations to recover his citizens, or their remains. “We will triumph. God will give us victory,” the politician vowed this week.
Many Haitians hope his combatants will stay and have been thrilled by cinematic social media clips posted by Bukele showing helicopter strikes on a gang compound and the mansion of a gangster nicknamed Taliban.
Banners and billboards around Port-au-Prince celebrate Bukele as a 21st-century liberator and feature slogans such as “The bandits won’t get a wink of sleep!” and “We’re tired! Give us Bukele!”
Standing outside the liberated football ground, bricklayer Venel Saindor recalled how criminals torched his home in Carrefour-Feuilles three years ago. “It’s impossible to enter my neighbourhood because the thieves are still there. They shoot at us,” the 56-year-old explained, lifting his shirt to reveal a bullet scar above his right nipple.
“We need Bukele to help us return to our homes,” added Saindor, as a Salvadoran soldier with a belt-fed heavy machine gun kept watch from the stadium’s terraces.
Monique Clesca, a writer and activist, echoed the bricklayer’s enthusiasm. “Haitians are elated … [and] I feel elated also … It is a moment of hope,” she said on Tuesday, as thousands of demonstrators poured on to the streets to champion Bukele, chanting: “Viv Bukele!” and “Bukele is not playing games!”
As a sea of protesters swept towards the prime minister’s offices, people from all walks of life spoke of how armed groups had destroyed their lives and their collective hope that Bukele may provide a solution.
“I used to drive an old bus. The bandits burned it. They burned my house down too,” said Wilné Persona, a 50-year-old driver, adding: “Bukele is the one we are waiting for … because we can no longer bear the situation.”
A food vendor called Claudy Mayas urged “Papa Bukele” to stand his ground. “Bukele, I bless you, your wife and your children,” said Mayas, 51. “The Haitian people are with you, just as you are with us.”
Clesca attributed the palpable excitement to the widespread perception that Bukele’s “decisive” action had exposed the incompetence, inefficiency and indifference of Haitian and foreign leaders. “Basically, what Bukele has done is show that leadership is about resolving a problem for your population,” she said, praising how the stadium and other areas were recaptured in less than a month.
Amid the excitement there is also unease. Some fear Bukele’s offensive could exacerbate an already volatile situation in and around Haiti’s capital, much of which resembles a war zone. This week, there was heavy fighting between Salvadoran troops, police and gangs in Village of God, the shantytown that is Izo’s main base. On Thursday, police said officers had killed at least 34 suspected criminals during an operation near the stadium.
Some suspect El Salvador’s president, a social media whiz with 22 million followers on X and TikTok, could be exaggerating his troops’ role in recent successes with help from a strike team of online propagandists and fans. “Nayib Bukele is gang kryptonite,” one US enthusiast gushed this week, calling his intervention “a miracle”.
Others fret over Bukele’s ability to distinguish between gang members and civilians, given the indiscriminate nature of his mass detention campaign in El Salvador, where thousands of innocent people have been jailed without due process.
Clesca downplayed concerns over the toll Bukele’s crackdown has taken on democracy and the rule of law in El Salvador, which now has the world’s highest per capita incarceration rate. Haitian politics was so contaminated with organised crime, she argued, “it’s almost like the mafia has taken over 10 Downing Street”.
“If you’re talking about [an] assault on democracy, Haiti is … almost a case study that is … even worse, more flagrant, than El Salvador,” Clesca said.
The security situation was so dire that urgent action was needed. “Let’s just be honest … in Haiti, we’re being brutalised,” Clesca said. “Girls are being taken as sexual slaves. They’re being gang raped. So somewhere along the line, we have to say: ‘Haiti helped [South American independence hero] Simón Bolívar [who received shelter and support from Haiti in the early 1800s] … and now, Bukele is helping us’.”
At Tuesday’s rally, protesters spoke of El Salvador’s president in divine terms. “Today, we see Bukele as a saviour, as someone sent by God,” said one man, before adding a word of caution that spoke to countless past interventions that have ended in frustration and failure.
“There is one thing I will say to President Bukele,” he said. “He must not start with us and leave us halfway.”

noticias.titulo: China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve
noticias.resumen: Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035 Cop31 live – latest updates China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said. noticias.texto:
China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”
China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.
At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.
But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.
In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”
Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.
While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.
But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.
Last year, electricity made up nearly 30% of China’s energy use and it is on track to make that 35% by 2030. Electricity is several times more efficient than fossil fuels, meaning that it takes far less energy to run electric vehicles, heat pumps and industrial processes than their fossil fuel counterparts.
Wang said China was happy with the 2035 target, but that it would be harder to meet if the electricity was required to come entirely from low-carbon sources. “For this target, no problem. But if you think about ensuring clean electrification, that may be a little bit difficult, even for China. For other countries, it’s even more difficult,” he said.
China still has a large number of coal-fired power stations and is planning some new ones, though fewer than before. Wang said this would be used for back-up during the transition to clean energy.
One of the key issues at Cop31 is the “transition away from fossil fuels”, which was one of the resolutions passed at the Cop28 summit in Dubai in 2023, but which countries have failed to flesh out since. The phrase was included in the first draft of the “cover decision” outcome from Cop31, presented on Monday, but excised from the second draftissued on Thursday, to the dismay of many countries and campaigners.
Wang said: “We agree with paragraph 28 of the UAE consensus [the transition resolution]. But maybe different countries have different roadmaps. It’s very difficult to have only one unified roadmap for every country. So maybe we will help other countries to have their own country-based solutions, to realise their own national way of establishing a new renewable-based power system.”
China is also concerned about trade barriers to its clean technology exports, including the tariffs that the US under Donald Trump has placed on Chinese goods, and the “carbon border adjustment mechanism” (CBAM) imposed by the EU. The CBAM penalises imports from countries with looser regulations on carbon than the EU, which forces companies in high-carbon sectors to pay for their carbon emissions in order to level the playing field.
Some smaller developing countries have criticised the EU for its CBAM, warning that it will hamper their manufacturing industries. The EU said it had processes in place to ensure smaller developing countries were not hurt.
Wang called for more work on trade issues at Cops. “They must come together to find a unified approach,” he said. “China and other developing countries, including the global south, disagree [with the EU] on this. But that’s why we should continue to strengthen our dialogue.”
Jiangwen Guo, a senior research fellow at the Chatham House thinktank, said other countries could learn from China. “China has very consistent top-down policies [and] sets a clear direction with high consistency, then follows with learning by doing,” she said. “In the great energy transition, there is no one ahead of China. China is creating the model for the globe.”
Negotiators at Cop31, which was scheduled to end at 6pm on Friday, were sent home late on Friday after the talks stalled, with a new draft text of a “cover decision” marking the main outcome of the negotiations not thought likely to emerge until some time on Saturday morning. The talks are likely to continue into Saturday and potentially beyond.

noticias.titulo: Teenager allegedly organised arsons and kidnapping on Signal during Melbourne hospitality wars
noticias.resumen: Victoria police say boy, 17, communicated with offenders under username ‘Onepercent’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Victorian police allege a 17-year-old boy tasked others to carry out a series of arsons, home invasions and a mistaken identity kidnapping that resulted in the partial amputation of a victim’s finger during Melbourne’s hospitality wars. The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Victorian police allege a 17-year-old boy tasked others to carry out a series of arsons, home invasions and a mistaken identity kidnapping that resulted in the partial amputation of a victim’s finger during Melbourne’s hospitality wars.
The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal.
He was charged on Saturday with extortion, making threats to kill, three offences of criminal damage by fire, and home invasion. He was remanded to appear in court later on Saturday.
In a statement, police said it would be alleged that Onepercent was involved in tasking an arson at a York Street, South Melbourne licensed premises on 15 April; two home invasions and a kidnapping four days apart in Springvale later that month; and two arson attacks during March at a Williamstown ice-cream store and a car in Moonee Ponds.
The boy was arrested at a house in the Moonee Ponds region, in Melbourne’s north-west, police said.
It is alleged a trafficable quantity of cocaine, three phones and cash were seized during the arrest.
Police allege that when the mistaken identity kidnapping occurred at the Springvale property on 22 April, a 34-year-old victim received serious injuries to his lower body and the partial amputation of one of his fingers.
It is alleged the fire at Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown on 22 March caused $600,000 worth of damage and endangered the lives of residents at the property upstairs.
On 16 November, police appealed for more information about the person behind the Onepercent user name.
“We need the public’s assistance to identify the user of this handle,” Det Insp Graham Banks said at the time.
“There will be people in the wider organised crime network and in our community who will have intimate knowledge of who this person is.
“We are hopeful that those people may now be in a position to come forward and speak to police.”

noticias.titulo: Rejoining EU ‘on the table’ as UK strikes deals on trade and young people
noticias.resumen: All options open in future talks, says Ed Miliband, while prime minister hails ‘a good day for Britain and Europe’ The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said. The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
The UK rejoining the EU could be on the table in informal discussions between Andy Burnham and European leaders in Brussels, Ed Miliband has said.
The foreign secretary said “all options” would be examined in the process, after the prime minister agreed deals on trade and young people with the bloc on Friday.
Agreements on food and drink standards, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme were announced after talks this week.
Under the plans, 100,000 young Britons will be allowed to live, work, study and travel in the EU with similar access for Europeans in the UK.
Burnham said the agreement would add 0.5% to the UK’s GDP, a £17bn boost to the British economy.
Miliband said Burnham would have further “brainstorming” discussions with the EU in the next year about what could happen next.
He said the agreements this week were the limit of what could be done before the next general election.
However, the trio of deals could be derailed in six months, as the EU threatened to block them unless the UK allows European students to pay domestic-level fees to study at British universities.
Miliband said in an interview for the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that “all the options will be on the table” when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding: “we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options”.
Since entering government in 2024, Labour has stuck to the so-called “red lines” in its manifesto, which stated the party would not rejoin the single market or customs union. It also ruled out freedom of movement.
Burnham has previously said he wants to see the UK rejoin the EU in his lifetime.
The prime minister will use the announcement of his 10-year plan before Christmas to explore how the UK could get closer to the EU after the next election. Informal discussions will take place with Brussels before next year’s UK-EU summit.
Miliband said he accepts the result of the 2016 vote but “the world has changed massively”.
“Europe is changing too, so we’ve got to look at what that means,” he said.” “It’s not about this parliament, we’re respecting the red lines in this parliament.”
On Friday, Burnham said the agreement represented a “good day for Britain and Europe”.
He said the agreements answer “the biggest challenges of our times and the biggest worries that people have”, citing the cost of living, lack of economic growth, illegal immigration and challenges facing young people.
“The deal is done. It is there in black and white in front of you,” Burnham said, adding that the legislation would enter parliament next week.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, played down the disagreement, saying she was “confident we are going to find a solution”.
About the further discussions, she said: “We welcome this brainstorming, so count on us.”
The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday the deal was good for farmers.
Eagle said: “(It) will open up new markets. They’ll be able to import and export.
“This is a win-win for the UK. We will dissolve a lot of the friction and costs at the border for UK agriculture and food.”

noticias.titulo: ‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges
noticias.resumen: Despite dodging tears in the tarmac, people are confident in city’s infrastructure – and will not worry about what has not happened yet Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday. Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.
Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.
“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.
Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.
Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.
“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.
Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.
Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.
As of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.
The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.
Dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.
Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.
Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.
Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.
At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.
Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”
It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.
Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.
Additional reporting by Galya Rudyk

noticias.titulo: Tourists are throwing fewer coins into Rome’s Trevi fountain – is €2 entry fee to blame?
noticias.resumen: Charity that collects the coins says donations are down by £200,000 after a barrier was put in place to restrict access When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark. noticias.texto:
When Jeff Clinton, an American visiting Rome with his wife for the first time, found a US one-cent coin on a street close to Termini train station, he knew precisely what he was going to do with it. “I’ll throw it into the Trevi fountain,” said Clinton, holding the copper coin in the palm of his hand as the couple admired the landmark.
He was well aware of the tradition among tourists of tossing a coin over their shoulder and into the waters of the baroque masterpiece, in a ritual fabled to ensure a return visit to the city or make other dreams come true.
But the only thing holding him back from partaking in the gesture was the distance: the steps towards the fountain’s sunken basin are separated by a low barrier and accessible during the day only by Rome’s residents or visitors who pay €2 (£1.64).
The fee, in place since February, has been partly blamed for taking some of the allure out of the coin-throwing tradition. The Rome unit of the church-run charity Caritas, which sweeps up the Trevi fountain’s coins, usually brings in more than €1.4m a year. But it noted a shortfall of about €200,000 between January and September compared with the same period in 2025.
“The closure of the direct access to the Trevi fountain might be a factor,” Giustino Trincia, the director of Caritas Roma, told Il Messaggero. The charity uses the donations to fund food banks and other welfare projects.
Clinton did contemplate asking someone in the basin area to throw the coin into the fountain on his behalf, but in the end slipped it back into his pocket.
The shift towards contactless payments and mobile phone wallets is also believed to have eroded Caritas’s collections.
Eric and Patty, a young couple from New York, said they might have thrown a coin, but did not have any change. Neither did they want to pay the €2 fee to get close to the basin. “It’s such a breathtaking monument, we’re happy just to take it in from here,” said Patty as they posed for selfies.
Alan and Ying, visiting Rome from Australia, did pay the fee. While they had heard that throwing coins “is what people do”, they decided not to indulge because “nobody else was really doing it”.
“I always carry cash with me because you never know when you might need it,” said Ying. “But we didn’t see anyone else doing it, so we didn’t either.”
A spokesperson for Caritas Rome told the Guardian the charity was not making any further public statements about the dwindling coin collection. The spokesperson said the collection so far this year did not take into account foreign currency coins, so the hit might not be so bad.
Still, the matter is understood to have caused friction with Rome’s council, which generated €435,194 from the access fee within the first month of its inception.
The initiative is aimed at curbing overcrowding at the monument while raising funds for the upkeep of the fountain and other Rome monuments. No further figures have been published, but with 4.4 million tourists flocking to the Trevi in 2025, the fee had been forecast to generate a tidy income for the council each year.
A team of stewards staff the ticketing system and monitor the flow of the crowd in the basin area. Nicolas Romero does shifts of seven or eight hours. He said people quite often asked him for change in order to throw a coin. “But many don’t even seem to know about the tradition,” he said. “This might also explain the decline.”
The gesture is believed to have its origins in an ancient pagan ritual offering to the water gods, although the custom of throwing coins only really took off globally after the 1954 romantic comedy film, Three Coins in the Fountain.

noticias.titulo: When you see smoke, run: Rohingya who escaped Myanmar’s genocide tell their stories
noticias.resumen: Survivors recount rivers red with blood and burning nearby villages serving as an urgent warning to flee their homes Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next. In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Smoke was often the signal to run – seen from a distance, it was the indication for Rohingya that a neighbouring village was under attack and that theirs would be next.
In other places, they saw the rivers run red and would pull out the bodies, perform quick burial rites and then flee.
What happened during the escape from Myanmar – a journey through forests and over hills and rivers while being battered by monsoon rains – was a key part of the ruling made this week in The Hague that Myanmar had carried out a genocide against the Rohingya.
The international court of justice (ICJ) said it was not enough to say they had faced ethnic cleansing when soldiers had also killed those trying to escape – Myanmar was trying to destroy the group as a people.
Stories of that violence in 2017, of organised mass killing, sexual attacks and the complete destruction of their villages, came with the refugees who arrived in neighbouring Bangladesh, eventually numbering more than 700,000 and settling in what has become the world’s largest refugee camp.
For months, they would arrive from places such as Tula Toli, where thousands were rounded up, killed and buried in mass graves. In other villages, men were captured and killed by the security forces.
Many survivors had escaped an attack on their own village, only to watch their relatives being killed in the villages where they had sought safety.
Almost a decade later, the majority of Rohingya who arrived in 2017 remain in the refugee camps, joining those who had already been there since the early 1990s, having escaped previous military operations and ever-increasing persecution.
The ICJ ruling has come at a particularly harsh time for Rohingya refugees, in a year in which hundreds have died at sea trying to escape the refugee camps, and in which countries such as Malaysia and India have spoken about returning the Rohingya to Myanmar.
Rohingya campaigners are hoping that this ruling will put an end to that.
Rohingya refugees still live in fragile shelters made of bamboo and tarpaulin sheets. They are denied the right to leave the camps, to work or to seek education.
Below are some of the stories from Rohingya who arrived in Bangladesh in 2017, having escaped Tula Toli and the surrounding area.
Momtaz and Dildar Begum
Sitting in the background, almost unnoticed as Momtaz Begum recollected how Myanmar forces had killed her husband and children and then raped her in front of her lone surviving child, was a woman who seemed to know every word of the story.
It was not because she had heard it before. Dildar Begum had experienced exactly the same violence as her sister had, in their village, Tula Toli.
In fact, they had for months believed each other dead until they discovered that they had both made it to Bangladesh and lived in different parts of the camp.
Each had only one surviving daughter, both of whom had similar scars along the back of their heads.
Anwara Begum
Twice previously Anwara Begum had lived as a refugee in Bangladesh. Once as a child in 1978 and then again in the early 1990s, as a young mother who lost her son to a respiratory disease during a rainy season spent in a flimsy tent.
When she was forced to return to Myanmar, though the persecution she fled there had not stopped, Anwara swore to herself that she would never become a refugee again.
She broke that oath when she saw the river by her village filled with bodies floating from Tula Toli.
Her husband first pulled from the river as many bodies as he could to bury and then they gathered some belongings and headed westwards to the River Naf – the border with Bangladesh.
To cross, she handed over all the gold she owned, equal to US $200 (£150), to a Bangladeshi boatman.
Nur Alam
Elderly people were not spared the Myanmar military’s attacks. Like so many others, Nur Alam had to be carried on the shoulders of his children on his journey to Bangladesh.
His 10-year-old grandson, Mamoon, held his hand. Once in the camp, they stuck to each other.
Alam’s arrival in Bangladesh was his fourth time being a refugee there. He was first expelled from Myanmar – known as Burma until 1989 – during military operations in the 1950s when Bangladesh was not yet an independent country.

noticias.titulo: Black Friday deals for liquid Brazilian butt lifts criticised over safety fears

noticias.texto:
Clinics in England are promoting seasonal deals – including for Black Friday – on liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), despite concerns about the risks of the procedure.
The government is consulting on limiting liquid BBLs, vampire facials and deep chemical peels in England to qualified healthcare professionals. The proposals follow the death of Alice Webb, a 33-year-old mother of five, after a botched liquid BBL in a Gloucester salon in 2024. Her family have called for laws against “cosmetic cowboys” to be introduced before more people die.
A liquid BBL involves injecting dermal filler into the buttocks. Plastic surgeons say it can carry significant risks and requires expert skill and training to perform, with large amounts of filler potentially causing serious side effects such as blood clots, fat embolisms and sepsis.
The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) has already acted against time-limited promotions, concluding that Black Friday offers could rush consumers into deciding on cosmetic surgery without enough time to consider the consequences.
Between April and December 2025, the watchdog found more than 900 ads for liquid BBLs in its advert monitoring system. During that period, only 11.5% of the ads they checked stuck to the ASA’s rules.
It said some ads made claims such as “0% infection rate” or described procedures as “safe”, without properly reflecting the risks involved. Other ads played on body insecurities, promising to “boost your confidence” or “transform your body effortlessly”.
Ashton Collins, the director of Save Face, a government-approved register of accredited non-surgical treatment practitioners, said she was “outraged” by BBLs being advertised as “party-season bargains” with time-limited discounts.
“These are not routine beauty treatments; they are serious medical procedures that can lead to devastating complications,” she said.
“Marketing them this way trivialises the risks, and pressures people to make snap decisions without the time, information or proper consultation they need to make an informed choice.”
She added that Save Face had received 1,004 patient-reported complaints about non-surgical BBLs, hip-dip and breast-augmentation procedures since 2023. More than 50% of the complainants experienced sepsis, 94% required hospital treatment and 43% required surgery.
“The impact on people’s lives can be profound and lasting,” Collins said.
One London provider, Clinic Blvd, recently advertised on social media for a 48-hour deal of 800ml of filler plus 200ml free for £1,300. The post, accompanied by a picture of a woman’s bottom, stated that demand was at “an all time high” and that the deals would not be available to everyone. The clinic also listed breast filler as an option, at £799 for 400ml.
A spokesperson for Clinic Blvd said patient safety and informed consent were its top priorities. “All treatments are subject to individual consultations and clinical suitability assessments,” they said. “We take responsible advertising seriously and remain committed to maintaining appropriate professional standards.”
An Instagram post from De Vere Signature Aesthetics, also based in London, promised 100ml of free filler as a “special limited time offer” added to procedures. Their price for filler falls as the volume rises, from about £5 per ml at the bottom of the scale to about £1.50 at the top, rewarding customers for choosing larger amounts. De Vere Signature Aesthetics was approached for comment.
The Belle Clinic, also in London, advertised a deal online offering 40% off a liquid BBL in autumn to “get ready now for your Christmas party”.
A spokesperson said: “Our current promotion is an autumn and winter seasonal offer … It is not intended to create urgency or pressure anyone into making a decision about an aesthetic procedure. We take the ASA’s guidance seriously and are willing to review our promotional wording to ensure it communicates our approach responsibly.”
Nora Nugent, a consultant plastic surgeon and former president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons (BAAPS), expressed concern over time-limited discounts. “This is a sales ploy that makes people make quick decisions in case they lose out on the offer,” she said, warning that any special offers, even if not time limited, could encourage people to have treatments they might not otherwise choose.
Gerard Lambe, a consultant plastic and cosmetic surgeon and a spokesperson for BAAPS, said: “People encouraging you to have increased volumes and reduced prices, that’s the worst thing that you could ever do. [You] should never ever do that to people. It increases your risk of complications.”
However, Lambe acknowledged that some private plastic surgeons do offer deals on procedures, saying that the issue of finance is complex, and that lack of affordability could lead people to choose cheaper surgery abroad with a greater risk of complications.
The ASA said its rules made clear that adverts for liquid BBLs must be socially responsible.
“We’ve taken widespread and targeted enforcement action against advertisers breaking the rules, including by trivialising the risks of these procedures, using time-limited promotions to create a sense of urgency and exploiting women’s insecurities,” a spokesperson said.
“We support the introduction of further government measures to regulate the sector.”

noticias.titulo: Telegraph departures signal concerns over direction under Axel Springer’s ownership
noticias.resumen: Insiders say they only see cuts, with no discernible long-term strategy, since title’s purchase by German media firm A spate of prominent departures and years of public battling over its ownership have ensured the Telegraph’s newsroom has been no stranger to internal intrigue and speculation in recent times. Even by its own high standards, however, its offices have been fraught with rumours about its leadership this week. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
A spate of prominent departures and years of public battling over its ownership have ensured the Telegraph’s newsroom has been no stranger to internal intrigue and speculation in recent times.
Even by its own high standards, however, its offices have been fraught with rumours about its leadership this week.
Speculation swirled about the future of both its editor, Chris Evans, and his loyal deputy, Rob Winnett. It was accompanied by days of long, hushed meetings between senior figures at the title, now under the ownership of the German media company Axel Springer.
The intrigue was heightened by Evans’s apparent early return from a trip to the US. Suggestions did the rounds that both editor and deputy could be leaving – a rumour dampened by Evans’s continued presence in the newsroom.
In the event, it emerged that only Winnett was departing. Winnett, who led the Telegraph’s coverage of the MPs’ expenses scandal, is heading to the title’s bitter rightwing rival, the Daily Mail. He has been installed as its chief content editor, instantly elevating him as a likely successor to the Mail’s editor, Ted Verity.
However, at the Telegraph, Winnett’s departure is being seen in the light of widespread concerns about the title’s direction under its new owners.
Axel Springer and its all-powerful chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, swept in to buy the titles for an eye-watering £575m earlier this year, with promises of investment and expansion. However, five months into Axel Springer’s tenure, insiders say they are only seeing cuts – and no discernible long-term strategy.
“I don’t think they have a particular plan – they clearly want money saved,” said one staffer. “They’ve clearly given Evans a target of savings to make. In terms of a plan, it’s all very vague.”
Winnett’s departure, one insider said, was “a huge loss”. Winnett had been part of a team who headed to Florida to scope a base for an expanded US operation. So far, solid plans have not emerged.
It follows a recent town hall meeting between journalists and the Telegraph’s new chief executive, Carolin Hulshoff Pol, at which reporters asked a series of questions that they felt went unanswered, and cuts in which large numbers of employees were told they were being made redundant, including senior figures in the newsroom.
Hulshoff Pol said the strategy was to reinvent the reader experience, build new revenue streams and grow internationally.
Reporters asked for more details about the wider plans behind the cuts and what the company meant in its repeated insistence that the Telegraph would become a “global, AI-powered premium media and intelligence business”. Staff remain unclear what the use of AI will entail.
There is also confusion about who is making the cuts. Evans is credited with keeping the Telegraph operation going during three years in which it was without an owner and unable to take major, strategic decisions. He now also appears to have been tasked with making cuts for Axel Springer. Some believe Evans is being used by the company to carry out “the bulk of the current bloodletting”.
A source said the company was having to take “difficult proposals that we believe are necessary for the future of the business”.
Some staff had initially detected a change in the Telegraph’s politics in the months after Axel Springer’s purchase. They presumed the loosening of ties with Reform’s Nigel Farage and the departures of some of its most rightwing writers, such as Allison Pearson and Sherelle Jacobs, were part of a shift towards a global centre-right audience.
However, many now believe the changes so far have been more about costs than politics.
Elsewhere, there has been no such turn to the centre. The Telegraph’s new US podcast, The Right Track with Poppy Coburn, most recently featured the rightwing media host Steve Bannon, an ally of Donald Trump.
It has left Telegraph staff scratching their heads about the takeover. Many had expected Axel Springer to arrive with money to spend. Insiders said executives seemed to be focused on boosting advertising.
The cuts are being made despite the Telegraph making underlying profits. “This is a business that generates healthy margins, healthy profits,” said Alex DeGroote, a media analyst. “So at face value, the restructuring – all these redundancies – is not because of financial pressures.
“Even allowing for the fact that the advertising market this year has probably been a bit soft, both print and digital, the scale of the restructuring would suggest that this is quite a deep strategic rethink. Basically, I’m afraid it points to AI.”
It has all focused attention on the intentions of Döpfner, a billionaire who has made numerous attempts to buy media assets in an attempt to establish himself as a modern media mogul. He made an unsuccessful bid for the Financial Times in 2015 and subsequently bought Business Insider and Politico, and has expressed interest in the Wall Street Journal. It had been assumed he would use the Telegraph as a vehicle to compete against right-leaning media in the US.
There have recently been reports that Döpfner has been interested in acquiring a stake in TikTok’s European operations. He is said to have discussed the idea with the US ambassador to France, Charles Kushner – the father of Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner – in January.
It has made Telegraph staff wonder where they stand in his plans.
“It’s all very well getting rid of the people that come in with stories and write them and produce them and present them to you on a plate, but what are you then going to do?” said one journalist at the town hall meeting. “You don’t get a room full of journalists together and not have answers.”

noticias.titulo: Letby trial doctor barred from treating patients was expert witness in another case
noticias.resumen: Prof Peter Hindmarsh played key role in conviction of two Birmingham parents whose son died after diabetes episode A doctor who gave expert evidence that helped to convict Lucy Letby, and who was barred during the trial from treating patients, was then instructed as an expert witness in another prosecution.
