noticias.texto:
To call it a blue wave, said the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, would be an epic understatement. The midterm elections were “the political equivalent of a meteor strike”. But one state, DeSantis added with pride, was able to “hold the line”. And that state was Florida.
On a night when almost everything else went right for Democrats, David Jolly fell short by 1.3 percentage points against Republican Byron Donalds, who will become Florida’s first Black governor, while Angie Nixon, bidding to become the state’s first Black senator, lost by 2.9 percentage points to Republican Ashley Moody.
Even the losses, however, were remarkable performances in a state that has shifted right in recent years and become the adopted home of Donald Trump, and where two years ago he defeated Kamala Harris by 13 percentage points. In an election where Democrats were winning in Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, Nixon was left asking: did Florida Democrats lose because the party didn’t support them?
“It was a missed opportunity,” the 42-year-old said pointedly. “I’m going to work to bring everybody together so that we don’t miss opportunities like that anymore.”
Democratic party leaders and major national donors made calculated investments in key battlegrounds elsewhere, producing stunning victories in unexpected places. Yet that generosity came at the expense of southern states like Florida and Louisiana, where local candidates were largely left to fend for themselves.
Was that because too many people had written Florida off as a red state? “Folks often write the south off. Now we’ve shown that Florida is in play, the south is in play, and I’m hoping that through my advocacy and me being so vocal that people will take note and will listen and donate to more candidates in the south,” Nixon said.
With nearly 24 million people, Florida is the third most populous state in the US. Covering its vast geographical expanse requires a huge war chest and saturation TV strategy. Nixon had neither. “I would say we were out-fundraised and Florida’s a very big state,” was her simple diagnosis.
Moody had raised $14.5m compared to Nixon’s $11.3m, according to the Federal Election Commission, while outside groups spent $10.4m opposing Nixon versus $3.6m spent opposing Moody.
Without the funds to buy airtime across Florida’s multiple expensive media markets – from Miami and Orlando to Tampa and Jacksonville – Nixon found herself overwhelmed by negative advertising from Moody and her allied political committees. “They hit me hard on it, and we didn’t have enough money to push back until it was too late.”
While conservative groups sought to depict Nixon as a far left extremist (“Angie Nixon is actually a socialist,” said one), she believes it was a more traditional attack that hurt her the most. “Those didn’t necessarily work. What we saw worked was when they were trying to say that I was raising taxes on people.”
By the time Nixon’s campaign could afford to explain her economic platform, the ads had done their damage. Nixon believes that “of course” national Democrats should have intervened sooner. But she is careful not to dwell too long on the blame game.
“I wish more people gave me money, period. I’m going to work to move forward and work to organise and create an environment where, despite whatever the conditions of that year are, that we’ll still be able to win.”
Nixon’s optimism is bolstered by what transpired on election night in other southern contests, where underfunded candidates demonstrated that progressive, community centred campaigns can break through longstanding conservative strongholds.
She points to Scott Colom, the progressive prosecutor who became the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era. The lesson of those races, for Nixon, is that no red state is a monolith and no southern state is permanently out of reach if the party is willing to contest it.
Even with more money, however, any Democrat running in Florida faces a structural barrier erected over successive legislative sessions: the deliberate erosion of voting rights. Nixon points the finger at DeSantis. “That man has done so much as it relates to voter suppression. He’s done so much to suppress voters. Every single year they have attacked voting rights and the election laws and so now we’re dealing with that.”
While turnout rates among registered Democrats remained high, the overall playing field has been warped by the fact Florida now has 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, a huge reversal after Democrats held the advantage for decades.
Nixon argues that this gap did not emerge organically but was engineered by targeted legislation designed to debilitate voter registration drives. In recent years, Florida’s Republican supermajorities have enacted onerous penalties and strict restrictions on grassroots civic organisations.
She continued: “That gap is there because they made it harder for third-party organisations to be able to register voters. Historically, those third-party groups registered more people of colour. That was intentional to make it harder.”
In a state where vote-by-mail (VBM) had long been a secure and convenient staple used by voters of all political stripes, Republicans also changed the rules to require voters to renew their requests for mail ballots after every general election cycle.
Nixon added: “It was also intentional to change up the vote-by-mail laws because again, low-income working families and people of colour vote by mail more often because they’re working.
“They made it hard for that to happen and so we saw a huge drop. Thousands upon thousands of folks who would normally get VBMs did not get them because they didn’t know about the new law.”
In short, does Nixon believe she would have won on a level playing field? “Oh, absolutely, yes,” she replied without hesitation. “I do.”
It follows that Nixon refuses to accept that Florida, once a quintessential swing state but where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 2012, is now a lost cause. “We need to work to close the voter registration gap. We need to continue to organise and go meet people where they are.”
Nixon joined the Democratic Socialists of America over the summer, though she acknowledged some disagreements with the organisation. During her campaign she shared stages with the progressive stars senator Bernie Sanders and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
But Nixon continues to resist easy categorisation. “I’m not interested in labels,” she said. “I’m interested in working with whoever wants to work to advance the agenda for working families.”
That agenda, she believes, is where Democrats can rebuild a working-class coalition that cuts across traditional partisan lines. When asked what the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress should prioritise in Washington, Nixon reels off an ambitious populist legislative platform centred on basic economic security.
“They need to pass comprehensive healthcare: push for Medicare for All. They need to increase the minimum wage. They need to push for comprehensive and compassionate immigration reform. They also need to hold Donald Trump and his people accountable.”
Does the Democratic party possess a coherent, compelling vision for the future? “We need more diverse voices in the conversation for us to get there,” Nixon said candidly. “I don’t think we’re there yet.”
Whether Nixon herself will launch another bid for elected office remains an open question. For now, her focus is on launching a political action committee, Never Scared, so that whoever steps onto the ballot in the future will not face the same structural headwinds she encountered.
“I am deciding right now. What I am doing is working to create the conditions, create the environment where folks will win whether or not the south gets funded by more historical donors.”

noticias.titulo: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says
noticias.resumen: The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day , publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history. The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar said also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms. Continue reading...
noticias.texto:
Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history.
The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar said also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms.
“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement.
The company said the sales set “a new record for entertainment across any medium … becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.”
The figure is nearly five times the roughly $800m that predecessor Grand Theft Auto V attracted during its first 24 hours in 2013.
It also exceeds the entire box office run of Avengers: Endgame, which became the highest-grossing film of all time last month at about $2.9bn worldwide after a rerelease pushed it past Avatar.
The game went on sale Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, launching first in New Zealand and rolling out market by market as each reached midnight local time.
The release quickly became a global phenomenon, generating more social media posts than this year’s World Cup, according to monitoring platform Visibrain.
Critics praised the game, which has a score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic.
Rockstar said that made it the highest-rated game ever.
Like its predecessors, “GTA VI” is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs.
Its busy streets, neon-lit nightlife and beaches are rendered in striking detail, and non-player characters go about their lives whether or not the player is involved.
While critics have raved about the game, it has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities.
With the game’s release on Thursday, police departments across the US reminded people that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets.
There is insufficient evidence supporting a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psycyhological Association. Nonetheless, several police departments took to the internet with warnings – and even jokes – aimed at keeping GTA VI’s lawlessness firmly in the virtual world.
The Atlanta police department delivered one of the clearest messages in a social media post.
“GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department warned. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.”
With the Associated Press and Agence France-Presse

noticias.titulo: COP31: UN Climate summit runs into overtime as deal remains elusive
noticias.resumen: After nearly two weeks of negotiations, countries remain divided on how to fight global warming. A new draft declaration doesn't mention the phaseout of fossil fuels, the main drivers of climate change. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
COP31: UN Climate summit runs into overtime as deal remains elusive
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 21, 2026
What you need to know
- Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey
- A new draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'
- Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached
These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21:
Peru blames 'geopolitical divisions' for lack of COP31 progress
The head of Peru's delegation at COP31, Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, warned that the UN climate summit was unlikely to end with a concrete deal on climate financing or cutting fossil fuel use.
Garrido Sanchez lamented that the outcome "would be very limited."
He reiterated how "geopolitical divisions" were stopping any final deal from mentioning reducing reliance on oil, gas and coal.
The Peruvian delegate singled out major oil producers, such as Gulf Arab states and Russia, as showing significant opposition.
He noted that while Latin American neighbor Panama had also signaled objection to including the term fossil fuels in the final text, Peru was "not so radical" and is keen to attract investment to "ensure our energy security" through renewables.
China throws weight behind '35-by-35' pledge
China has backed a plan proposed by COP host Turkey to raise global electricity demand to 35% by 2035 — up from the current 20%.
In a joint statement with Australia, which is leading negotiations between almost 200 nations at the COP31 summit in Turkey, Beijing said it welcomes "growing international ambition and cooperation ... to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 on a voluntary basis."
The statement goes on to highlight the benefits the transition can bring for the economy, jobs, energy security, public health and households.
The two partners also "acknowledge the importance of inclusive climate action that ensures no one is left behind," the text continued.
Dozens of countries, including EU states, Japan, South Korea and Canada, have so far signaled support for the voluntary goal, which aims to boost clean energy use.
Yet, environmental groups have warned that the draft text doesn't stipulate the use of solar, wind and other renewable energy sources, which could allow power plants using natural gas and coal to be included.
COP31: What to expect today
Good morning, and welcome back to DW's coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries worked through the night to finalize a deal, after a draft text dropped all mention of fossil fuels — the leading cause of climate change.
COP31, being held in the Mediterranean city of Antalya, was due to wrap up on Friday, but has run over time amid deep divisions over fossil fuels.
Hopes are fading that negotiators will finalize concrete plans to drastically slash the use of oil, gas and coal and a deeper commitment to renewable energy.
Stay tuned as we bring you the latest from the closing stages of UN climate summit.
COP31 talks go on — we're taking a break
The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, has gone into overtime, with countries still divided over key issues, including fossil fuels and climate financing.
The talks were scheduled to end on Friday evening, but negotiators have yet to reach an agreement. Germany and several other countries are pushing for a clear commitment to phase out fossil fuels, while poorer nations are demanding more concrete financial support to cope with climate change.
Negotiations are expected to continue into the weekend. We are pausing our live coverage for now and will bring you further updates as talks progress.
WATCH — Turkey's beaches are becoming too hot for sea turtles
While Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya, a growing climate threat is unfolding on its Mediterranean beaches. Rising sand temperatures are causing most newly hatched sea turtles to be born female, raising concerns about the long-term survival of local populations.
Conservationists warn that climate change, combined with pollution, coastal development and fishing-related injuries, is putting increasing pressure on the species.
DW correspondent Julia Hahn follows the people working to protect Turkey's iconic loggerhead turtles and shows how the climate crisis is already affecting wildlife far beyond the COP31 conference halls.
WATCH — COP climate summit under scrutiny over fossil fuel influence
The UN climate summit in Antalya is drawing criticism from activists and campaigners who question whether global climate talks can deliver meaningful change while fossil fuel interests remain influential. Turkey and Australia, both under scrutiny for their energy policies, are leading this year's conference.
Activists, including Greta Thunberg, argue COP summits have become increasingly ineffective, while others defend them as a vital space to pressure governments. Climate policy experts say the talks have helped reduce projected warming, but stress that real progress depends on action taken by countries between summits, not just agreements reached at them.
WATCH — Maldives environment minister: 'We are not going to live in the dark'
For the Maldives, climate change is already affecting everyday life. Heavy rainfall has forced people from their homes, warmer oceans are damaging coral reefs, and changes in fish stocks are putting pressure on the country's fishing industry. Rising sea levels pose another threat to the low-lying island nation. Meanwhile, global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, despite more than three decades of international climate negotiations.
At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, the Maldives' climate minister Ali Sharif discusses why progress has been so slow, what really happens during climate negotiations, and why moving away from fossil fuels is not as straightforward as it might seem.
For island nations like the Maldives, switching to renewable energy comes with practical and financial challenges. So what would it take to accelerate the transition? And can the UN climate process still deliver meaningful results?
COP32 hosts Ethiopia call the conferences a relay, not a single race
The hosts of next year's COP, Ethiopia, found a nationally tailored sporting metaphor to sum up the difficult, ongoing, sometimes tortuous process that the global environmental meetings can prove to be.
Speaking at the end of Friday's plenary to confirm Addis Ababa's intentions to host next year's summit, Gedion Timothewos, the foreign minister and upcoming president of COP32, made reference to Ethiopia's longstanding success in endurance running in track and field.
Referring to the COP process as a marathon, not a sprint, Timothewos said the country was looking forward to picking up the baton from Turkey and leading the next leg of the relay, taking the ongoing process forward into 2027.
His comments came during a late-night plenary session, but more talks are still expected in Antalya.
Late-night plenary session convenes after delay
Shortly after 9 p.m. local time in Antalya, delegates gathered for a plenary session, well past the official closing time.
The Turkish presidency's opening address was partly drowned out by a protester shouting objections in English such as "you are killing the future," and gaining applause within the chamber.
"We've been negotiating for days to find the common ground," COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, told the plenary. He hailed the progress made and said the world "waits for good news from this room."
But the plenary session noted how several of the more ambitious aspects of a political declaration remained incomplete, with no agreement yet reached at the summit.
Several national delegates spoke during the plenary to bemoan the elusive progress or even backsliding during the two weeks of negotiations.
The evening's session, however, has been dealing with technical issues, and the possibility that discussions continue into the weekend remains.
IN DEPTH — Climate science disputes and disinformation hinder action at COP
Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?
The UN's IPCC should have already started work on its next series of multi-year scientific assessments on climate change's progress, but the process is on hold at the urging of countries including fossil fuel-producing giants Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iran.
Read Tim Schauenberg's full report on this obstruction to climate research and other similar issues complicating COP31 here.
IN DEPTH — US is strong at climate talks despite Trump no-show
The US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show that climate action in the US is alive and well.
Head over to this report to learn more about who is representing the US at the summit, even if President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed global warming as a "hoax", didn't send a formal delegation for the second year in a row.
IN DEPTH — Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'
Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.
Learn more about what Uganda's environment minister Beatrice Atim Anywar said about climate financing in this report.
Activist Menotti: Europe has 'learned a few of the Trump tactics'
Veteran climate justice advocate Victor Menotti of the Demand Climate Justice NGO told DW that European governments appeared to be copying US President Donald Trump's negotiating playbook at COP this year.
"We know the US isn't here, but we can see that Germany and other European governments have learned a few of the Trump tactics, maybe in the trade disputes with the US," Menotti said. "And we see them applying here in Antalya, where it's like: Don't admit to anything. Try to dilute your responsibilities. Weaken whatever obligations you have. And then take even more."
He argued these countries were also expecting unreasonable or unfeasible commitments from developing countries, for instance restrictions on what they can spend money on and obligations to report on their expenditures.
"Germany is subsidizing quite a bit of coal still and fossil fuels, LNG expansion infrastructure," he said, arguing that wealthier countries' energy spending also had room for improvement.
"We need the North to act first," Menotti said. "The deal from Paris, the deal from Rio 30 years ago, is that the North will lead. But yet we see too much bullying of the global South and not enough leadership like they agreed to."
Talks formally enter overtime as scheduled close elapses
You can cross off another box on your COP31 bingo cards, dear readers.
As of the top of this hour, the session has officially gone past its scheduled end time of 1500 GMT/UTC on Friday, or 6 p.m. local time on site in Turkey.
This is something of an annual tradition at COP summits, which are always scheduled to finish at the end of a working week but also almost invariably run into the closing weekend. Delegates and members of the media tend to book their travel plans with this in mind.
'Electrification': What to know about the revised draft declaration
The revised draft declaration, which critics have slammed as "watered down" due to the omission of fossil fuels, highlights the "electrification" of the global economy as a central pillar of the energy transition.
"Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels," Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen told reporters.
What are the key points to know about the "35-by-35" electrification target?
- The draft wants to increase electricity's share of global energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035
- The draft highlights electrification as a way to cut emissions and boost energy security — while omitting prior mentions of fossil fuels
- It aims to shift more transport, heating, cooling and industrial activity onto electricity, allowing those sectors to be powered by renewables such as wind, solar and hydro power, rather than by burning coal, oil or gas
But the text does not specify what energy sources would supply the electricity. Some countries are demanding that the text call for "clean" electrification to clearly favor renewable sources over coal, oil or gas.
Bowen, who has been trying to secure compromises, pledged to continue working over the "coming hours, for as long as it takes, to get the job done."
"People have strong views of course — I am not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me let's give up and go home," Bowen said.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle
noticias.resumen: The proposed breakthrough could reshape mathematical research, but still needs independent verification. It's the latest in a string of cases where AI has outpaced humans in solving famous maths problems.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic researcher uses AI to solve math's greatest riddle
November 21, 2026
A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic says he used the company's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.
The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.
Levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Levent Alpoge wrote in a note released Friday.
The proof still has to be verified and confirmed by other mathematicians. If it withstands independent examination, it would be a major milestone both in mathematics and the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research.
The Riemann hypothesis is the latest and most important in a string of famous mathematical problems that were tackled with the help of AI.
What did Alpoge say about the breakthrough?
Alpoge said that the collaboration with AI had generated more than 250,000 pages of mathematical material, adding that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven major mathematical problems, the so-called Millennium Prize Problems, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each of those.
"This is an announcement of historic significance," Martin Bridson, president of the institute, said in a statement quoted by news agency AP.
He added it "holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics."
"But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult."
What is the Riemann hypothesis?
Formulated by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in the 19th century, the hypothesis is about the distribution of prime numbers, which are numbers that can only be divided by themselves and the number 1.
The hypothesis describes a fundamental pattern of how these numbers are distributed as they become ever larger. Confirming that hypothesis is thought to have crucial implications for a wide range of further mathematical research.
The potential breakthrough by Alpoge and Claude AI comes amid a growing number of examples where artificial intelligence systems are making significant contributions to advanced mathematical research.
In September, rival AI company OpenAI said its technology had helped solve a problem involving the Navier-Stokes equations.
The equations, which describe the movement of fluids such as water and air, are another of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, but the claim that they've been solved also still needs independent verification.

noticias.titulo: Germany news: Support for Ukraine military aid waning, survey shows
noticias.resumen: Nearly half of Germany's population wants to reduce military aid to Ukraine, a survey has found. Meanwhile, German consumers are set to pay more in energy bills next year due in part to the Iran war. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
Germany news: Support for Ukraine military aid waning, survey shows
Published November 21, 2026last updated November 21, 2026
What you need to know
- Almost half of people in Germany want the government to reduce or cut support for Ukraine as it fights Russia's invasion, a survey shows
- Many consumers in Germany will be paying more for electricity and gas from next year, partly because of the war in Iran
- US judge rules Germany's agrochemical giant Bayer must pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from US cancer patients
This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:
US court approves Bayer Roundup cancer settlement
A judge in the US state of Missouri has approved a settlement under which Germany-based agrochemical company Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion (€6.6 billion) over the next two decades to resolve lawsuits from cancer sufferers who say they should have been warned that its weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma.
The settlement, which applies nationwide, means both Roundup users who are already ill with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who develop it in future could an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, with factors such as their use of the product, their age at the time of diagnosis and illness severity determining the exact sum.
The decision could be appealed.
For more on this story, head over to our report.
IN DEPTH: The plight of Gen Z in Germany
Young people in Germany, as in many other parts of the world, have been taking to the streets to demonstrate for a fairer, safer world and a greater say in what policies are enacted by politicians.
But despite the fact that many of their complaints are fully justified, with jobs difficult to find despite a high level of study or training, housing that is increasingly unaffordable and a lack of government action against climate change to ensure the world remains habitable, the demonstrations have sometimes been criticized or even labeled as criminal.
DW looks at the problems facing Gen Z and its fears about its future in a world where young people have little say.
Electricity, gas bills to go up for millions
Many consumers who get their gas and electricity under the standard tariff offered by local utility providers will be paying considerably more for electricity and gas next year, according to comparison website Verivox.
Some 3.7 million households are expected to pay more for electricity, with a rise of some 2% expected.
The rise has been cushioned to some extent by coalition's recent agreement to lower the electricity tax rate for 2027 to the European minimum level to protect households and businesses.
Gas will become considerably more expensive for some 1.9 million households, with 361 regional utility providers announcing rises of some 14% for December, January and February.
"The wholesale prices for gas and electricity, which have risen sharply since the Iran war began in March 2026, are only now starting to have an effect on prices for consumers," Verivox energy expert Thorsten Storck said.
Almost half of people in Germany want Ukraine aid cut or dropped
Some 49% of people in Germany would like to see Berlin's financial, military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine amid the Russian invasion either reduced or cut completely, a survey has shown.
In all, 25% of respondents in a YouGov survey wanted aid to Ukraine to be dropped, while 24% were in favor of reducing.
Altogether 30% wanted to retain aid at the current level, and 9% felt it should be raised. Eleven percent were undecided on the issue.
The survey was conducted between November 13 and 16 on behalf of the newspaper Welt am Sonntag.
This week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted a meeting of Ukraine's European allies, known as the "Coalition of the Willing", in a bid to maintain a united front as peace talks in Ukraine continue.
Welcome to our coverage
Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn!
You join us as a survey shows that support for Berlin's help to Kyiv amid the Russian invasion is declinin.
And millions of households will see their electricity and gas bills rise considerably next year amid a number of geopolitical pressures.
Read on for more on these and other stories hitting the headlines in Germany this weekend.

noticias.titulo: 'Killer robots' talks at UN end with no legally binding ban
noticias.resumen: Countries have agreed to extend discussions over controls on lethal autonomous weapons systems for two years.
noticias.texto:
'Killer robots' talks at UN end with no legally binding ban
November 21, 2026
United Nations talks on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems ended on Saturday without an agreement on a legally binding ban.
The negotiations did, however, yield an agreement for further discussions to develop new rules by 2028.
Delegates from 128 states that are parties to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) had been meeting in Geneva since Monday amid rising concerns over the use of the so-called killer robots in global conflicts.
The conference ended early on Saturday in what campaigners deemed a "weakened" outcome, following several hours of overnight parleying.
What happened at the CCW conference?
Nearly 100 nations had called for negotiations on a legally binding agreement on the systems capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Pope Leo XIV and the Red Cross had also supported a ban on killer robots.
However, countries that have the technology, including arms-producing giants like the US, Russia and Israel, were among those opposing the mandate.
Ultimately, the 128 countries "agreed to launch the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, which should be conducted over the next two years", the conference's Swiss chair, Julien Thoni, told the media on Saturday.
Groups decry a softened mandate on 'killer robots'
But while Thoni hailed a multilateral diplomacy delivering "concrete results" even in "today's deeply divided world," rights groups expressed disappointment at the minimal agreement.
"States adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument," news agency AFP quoted Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of over 300 organizations, as saying.
"Over 95 states expressed their support for a treaty. In the final hours, a small number of states weakened the mandate introducing uncertainty about the legal status of the final document," it added.
The group had earlier said that autonomous weapons systems were already reaching the battlefield and such systems had been tested or deployed, including in the Ukraine war.

noticias.titulo: US judge jails Indian national in foiled Sikh separatist murder plot
noticias.resumen: New Delhi has denied any role in the plot to kill Sikh separatist Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York. Meanwhile, over 200 people have been hospitalized after consuming spurious liquor in Manipur state. DW has more.
noticias.texto:
US judge jails Indian national in foiled Sikh separatist murder plot
Published November 21, 2026last updated November 21, 2026
What you need to know
- Indian man is sentenced to 19 years in prison over plot to assassinate Sikh separatist leader
- Over 200 people are hospitalized after consuming toxic liquor in Manipur state
- India's men get a 118-run lead at stumps on day 3 of test against New Zealand
Here is a roundup of the main headlines from India on Saturday, November 21 and Sunday, November 22:
Rahul, Gill put India 118 ahead of New Zealand on day three in Wellington
India closed day three of the first Test against New Zealand on 486-4, a lead of 118 runs. KL Rahul made 136, Shubman Gill 98 and Rishabh Pant was unbeaten on 55 as every one of India's top five passed 50.
Rahul reached his 13th Test hundred off 207 balls, batting for more than eight hours and sharing stands of 165 with Devdutt Padikkal (80) and 91 with Gill. It completed a set of Test centuries in every major Test-playing nation outside the subcontinent for the Indian wicketkeeper-batsman.
"It feels really awesome, actually, to be able to achieve something like that," Rahul said.
He survived an LBW appeal on 5 that was given not out and New Zealand chose not to review. "Those 15 seconds were probably the slowest 15 seconds of my life," he said of the review process.
Gill and Pant added 100 in the final session before Gill was bowled by Jacob Duffy just before stumps. Duffy finished with 1-180 from 29 overs, the fourth most expensive figures in New Zealand's Test history, AFP said.
The pitch, green on day one, flattened out. "We expected a lot of grass on the wicket, we expected a lot of movement and it has probably not panned out that way," Padikkal said.
New Zealand were all out for 368 in their first innings.
The two-match series ends next week in Christchurch.
Death toll from suspected spurious liquor in Manipur's Chandel rises
At least 14 people have died and more than 200 have been hospitalized after drinking suspected adulterated liquor in Manipur's Chandel district.
At least 12 people remain in critical condition, local media reported.
The victims drank the liquor in the Chakpikarong area, about 75 kilometers (47 miles) from the state capital city of Imphal, and deaths were reported between November 18 and 20.
Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh visited the hospitals where most patients were being treated on Friday. He ordered an inquiry and said the culprits would be arrested soon.
Police said the liquor came from Sugnu in neighboring Kakching district, with no known local brewing in Chandel. A case has been filed, and two people have been arrested.
The local administration has advised residents not to drink liquor from questionable sources and asked anyone who consumed liquor from the same source to get a medical check-up, even without symptoms.
US judge jails Indian national in foiled plot to kill Sikh separatist, New Delhi denies involvement
A US federal judge sentenced an Indian national on Friday to 19 years and seven months in prison for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.
Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.
"I'm sorry to Mr. Pannun," he said in court. Judge Victor Marrero said he faces deportation to India after serving his sentence.
Prosecutors say an Indian government employee recruited Gupta in 2023. The government employee remains overseas and is not in US custody.
Gupta paid $15,000 (€13,670) to a person he believed was a hitman, who was actually an undercover US agent.
Prosecutors also said Gupta had told that agent the day after Hardeep Singh Nijjar's June 2023 killing in Canada that Nijjar "was also the target," the Associated Press reported.
His lawyer, Isabelle Kirshner, denied he had any role in the Nijjar killing.
"There is no question he was not the brains behind this operation," she said. Canada has separately alleged India arranged Nijjar's killing, and India dismissed that, with both countries expelling diplomats.
India denies any involvement in the Pannun plot. New Delhi has designated Pannun a terrorist.
Pannun, who leads the group Sikhs for Justice, called Gupta a foot soldier and said outside court: "I'm ready to face India's bullet if that is the price I have to pay."
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to our weekend coverage!
This is Seerat from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest news from and about India.
An Indian national has been sentenced to 19 years and seven months in prison by a US federal judge for plotting to hire a hitman to kill Sikh separatist leader Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York.
Several people have died and more than 200 hospitalized in the northeastern state of Manipur after consuming toxic liquor.
And India has taken a 118-run lead over New Zealand, reaching 486-4 at stumps on day 3 of the first Test against the Black Caps.
For this and more, follow our blog.

noticias.titulo: Man convicted of arson over deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles
noticias.resumen: A 30-year-old man has been convicted of causing one of the most destructive wildfires in the history of Los Angeles. The verdict came after the case was retried.
noticias.texto:
Man convicted of arson over deadly 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles
November 21, 2026
A US-French man has been convicted on federal arson charges connected with the 2025 Palisades fire in Los Angeles, California, which killed 12 people and devastated the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades.
The weeks-long blaze destroyed some 6,800 homes and other structures, causing estimated property losses of $150 billion (€136.7 billion).
What was the man convicted of in the Palisades fire case?
A US District Court jury in Los Angeles found the man guilty of starting a hilltop brush fire on January 1, 2025.
While the fire was initially suppressed, it continued smoldering underground and reignited days later amid fierce winds to become the highly destructive Palisades Fire.
The man is set to be sentenced on March 17. First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told reporters that he could face up to 40 years in prison.
The man was arrested in October 2025, and already faced one trial five months ago that ended with a hung jury. The judge declared a mistrial in June, prompting federal prosecutors to retry the case under modified charges.
Prosecutors said security camera footage and location data from the defendant's cellphone showed he was the only person nearby when the January 1 blaze began in the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.
At both trials, they characterized the man, a former Uber driver, as a loner who held a deep resentment against society, and particularly the wealthy.
The defense argued that the initial blaze could have been caused by fireworks, while prosecutors said there was no evidence that any had been set off in the area.
In March, the man denied in a court declaration that he had willfully started any fire, though he declined to testify in his own defense at either trial.
Double fire disaster
The Palisades blaze erupted almost at the same time as another wildfire that broke out in Eaton Canyon, some 30 miles (48 km) to the east.
That fire, believed to have been ignited by sparks from an electrical transmission tower, killed 19 people and devastated the Los Angeles suburb of Altadena.
Together, the two blazes rank as the deadliest wildfire disaster ever seen in Los Angeles County.
*Editor's note: DW follows the German press code, which stresses the importance of protecting the privacy of suspects, victims and those who are associated with a criminal case, and urges the media to refrain from publishing their full identities in most cases.

noticias.titulo: Three El Salvador soldiers die in explosives accident in Haiti
noticias.resumen: The soldiers were part of a Salvadoran military contingent deployed to the violence-ridden Caribbean nation last month to rescue four missing airmen. The deployment has widened into an operation against Haiti's gangs.
noticias.texto:
Three El Salvador soldiers die in explosives accident in Haiti
November 21, 2026
Three Salvadoran soldiers were killed in Haiti while handling explosives, El Salvador's military said on Friday.
The incident marks the first officially reported deaths since a 2,000-member Salvadoran military contingent was deployed to the gang violence-stricken Caribbean nation last month.
One of the soldiers succumbed to his injuries while being treated in the neighboring Dominican Republic, where he was airlifted to, the El Salvador military said on X.
Another soldier was wounded in the incident and is out of danger, it added.
It was not immediately clear where the blast took place.
The Salvadoran military's statement also did not give any further details on the type of explosives the soldiers were working with.
"We extend our deepest condolences and solidarity to the families of the three deceased," it said.
Why are El Salvador's troops deployed in Haiti?
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele sent over 2,000 troops and special forces to Haiti to rescue four El Salvador airmen — members of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF)— who went missing after a gang ambush on October 18 in the Haitian capital of Port-au-Prince.
The additional troops dispatched by Bukele are not part of the GSF, and the contingent's remit appears to have broadened to stamp out Haitian gangs.
Bukele, who has been known for his tough approach to the gangs in El Salvador, has posted several videos of strikes on residences of gang leaders around Port-au-Prince.
Haiti announces deal with El Salvador to build new prisons
Meanwhile, on Friday, Haiti announced an agreement with El Salvador to build three new Haitian prisons.
The development follows this week's visit to El Salvador by Haiti's security and justice minister, Patrick Pelissier.
The prisons will be built by a Salvadoran company in collaboration with a Haitian firm, Pelissier said.
Haitian prisons are notoriously overcrowded. In 2024, gang raids in two of the country's biggest penitentiaries saw thousands of inmates being released.
El Salvador, on the other hand, is home to a notorious maximum security mega-prison known as Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT).
The country has imprisoned over 90,000 people with no access to family visits ever since entering a state of exception in 2022.
Pelissier visited CECOT during his trip to El Salvador.
"Once you enter, there is no hope of ever seeing the outside world again," the Haitian minister said as he praised the mega-prison.

noticias.titulo: Brazil ex-President Jair Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
noticias.resumen: Jair Bolsonaro has been hospitalized in Brasilia with intestinal obstruction. The former far-right Brazilian leader is receiving pain medications, his son Carlos said.
noticias.texto:
Brazil ex-President Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
November 21, 2026
Convicted former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt, has been hospitalized with abdominal pain.
Bolsonaro's son Carlos wrote on X that the former far-right leader was taken to the hospital on Friday and was found to have "a near-complete intestinal obstruction."
The DF Star Hospital in Brasília said that Bolsonaro was suffering from "abdominal distension" and was being examined.
Bolsonaro's history of hospitalizations
Bolsonaro, who is 71 years old, has undergone several hospitalizations and surgeries since he was stabbed in the abdomen on the campaign trail for the 2018 elections.
"He is being given medication for pain and an initial attempt to reverse the condition without the need for invasive intervention," Carlos said.
Son blames house arrest for Bolsonaro's health issues
Bolsonaro was in power from 2019 to 2022. He was convicted last year for plotting a coup after his defeat to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election but claims being the victim of a left-wing judicial witch hunt.
Bolsonaro was placed under humanitarian house arrest on medical grounds.
Carlos on Friday railed against his father's detention, which he blamed for Bolsonaro's current health problems.
Carlos said that the senior Bolsonaro's health was "deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility" and what he called "the psychological torture he suffers daily."
Another one of Bolsonaro's sons, Flavio Bolsonaro, recently lost the October presidential election to incumbent President Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil after the vote and now resides in Florida.

noticias.titulo: UK anti-migrant activist jailed for slashing Channel dinghy
noticias.resumen: Daniel Thomas, known as "Danny Tommo," slashed a dinghy with a knife while a French rescue worker was on board. The incident was livestreamed to a large social media audience amid growing tensions over migrant crossings.
noticias.texto:
UK anti-migrant activist jailed for slashing Channel dinghy
November 21, 2026
A British anti-migrant activist has been sentenced to 15 months in prison for slashing a dinghy used by migrants crossing the English Channel while a French rescue worker was still on board.
Daniel Thomas, 37, also known as "Danny Tommo," pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month. He was sentenced on Friday at Portsmouth Crown Court in southern England.
The activist, who founded the anti-immigration group Patriot Platform, livestreamed the September 22 incident on social media, where it was watched by a large audience.
What happened during the English Channel incident?
Thomas had followed an inflatable boat carrying dozens of migrants across the Channel on September 22.
After the migrants were transferred to another vessel and taken ashore, Thomas approached the empty dinghy, which a French rescue worker had boarded.
Video footage showed him repeatedly stabbing the boat with a knife. Judge James Newton-Price said he counted eight cuts.
During the livestream, Thomas could be heard saying "this is what needs to happen."
He also shouted "get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat ... take them back, no more of these," according to prosecutor Joel Smith.
Newton-Price accepted that there was "no immediate danger" to the rescue worker. However, he said Thomas' aggressive behavior would have been highly alarming.
What did the judge say about Danny Tommo's actions?
Sentencing Thomas, Newton-Price said his actions amounted to "flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption" of the legitimate activities of British and French authorities in the Channel.
The judge highlighted the work of Britain's Border Force, Coastguard and volunteers from the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI).
"They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover," he said.
Thomas appeared by videolink from a prison in Winchester, southern England, where he has been held since late September after being denied bail.
He reportedly held his head in his hands when the sentence was announced.
Under current UK sentencing rules, Thomas may serve only a third of his 15-month sentence, including time already spent in custody.
The court also heard that he had five previous convictions, including one for kidnapping in 2016.
Who is Danny Tommo and what is Patriot Platform?
Thomas is a longtime ally of prominent far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.
He has built a large online following and founded Patriot Platform, a group campaigning against migrants arriving in Britain in small boats.
Thomas gained prominence earlier this year by leading confrontational anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth and the southeastern port of Dover.
Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and clashed with police.
The demonstrations have increasingly targeted police officers and rescue workers involved in responding to migrant boats arriving on British shores.
The UK government has condemned the protesters' "intimidating and thuggish behavior."
Thomas is also due to stand trial in London next June over several alleged offenses, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing center in Dover in March.
How many migrants cross the English Channel?
Successive British governments have struggled to stop migrants from making the dangerous journey across the English Channel, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.
More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year.
Although the number of arrivals has since fallen, the crossings remain a major political issue in Britain.
Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration campaigners have continued to demand tougher measures to prevent migrants from reaching the country.

noticias.titulo: 5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
noticias.resumen: Don't let your work troubles follow you home. Psychologist Guy Winch shares techniques to help you stop ruminating about your nine-to-five, so you can focus on what really matters.
noticias.texto:
5 ways to turn off your 'work brain' after the day ends
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
If you're spending your free time spinning your wheels about something that happened at work, guess what? You're still on the clock, says psychologist Guy Winch.
" Your workday only ends when you stop thinking about work," he says.
Winch, author of Mind Over Grind: How to Break Free When Work Hijacks Your Life, says it doesn't have to be this way. In his book, published this year, he shares strategies on how to reclaim your time, energy and attention if work takes up too much of your mental bandwidth.
"Very few of us sit through the evening reliving the glory of the joke that landed in the meeting," he says. "What we do spend hours on are when we get interrupted, dismissed, about the project we're behind on."
That kind of ruminative thinking can have negative effects on our health. Research has shown that it activates our stress response, contributes to poor sleep and eating and, over time, can increase our risks for cardiovascular disease and depression.
Winch, co-host of the podcast Dear Therapists, shares quick strategies you can try if work is taking over your life.
The problem: You can't stop thinking about work
The fix: Take 15 minutes to come up with a solution
Let's say you're trying to focus on your kid's volleyball game but all you can think about is how your colleague keeps taking credit for your work.
Instead of reliving the issue, which is unproductive, take 15 minutes to convert the situation into a problem you can solve, Winch says. "What's the best way of handling it? Do I have a conversation with them? And if I want to have a conversation, what's the outcome I'm trying to get to?"
This approach allows you to create a plan for how to address the situation. "You should feel an ease in stress. Now it will be much easier for you to let go," he says.
The problem: You still can't stop thinking about work
The fix: Distract yourself with a game or a memory task
If you can't stop spinning your wheels about work, try distracting yourself for two or three minutes, Winch says. It can help you reset so you can focus on something else.
"You need something that takes up your mental bandwidth so there's not enough left over for rumination," he says.
He shares a few ideas: Play a puzzle or game like Wordle. Name all the state capitals. Think of whom you sat next to in elementary school. Picture all the items on the top shelf of your fridge.
When you're done, instruct yourself to reengage in whatever you're doing, he says. You might tell yourself, "I really want to enjoy this show now," or "I really want to watch my kid [so I can] talk to her after the game."
The problem: You still feel like you're at work when you're home
The fix: Create boundaries between work and home with immersive rituals
Rituals can train your brain to "shift gears from the mindset of being at work to the family gear, the partner gear, the friendship gear," Winch says.
Your ritual should include as many of your senses as possible, he says. Take a warm shower or a hot bath. Listen to music that puts you in the mood for whatever comes next. Shift the lighting — maybe turn off the bright lights you use at your workstation and light a candle.
One of the most effective things you can do is change your clothing, Winch says. "Clothing makes us feel a certain way. That's why power suits make us feel powerful and leisure wear makes us feel relaxed."
If you work from home and are already in your comfy clothes, change into a different set of comfy clothes when your workday is over, Winch says. It should be something "that your brain can distinguish you wear when you finish working."
The more you repeat these rituals, the more your brain knows when it's time to go from work mode to "being more relaxed and open to engaging with what you're doing when you're home," Winch says.
The problem: You feel drained after work
The fix: Do something that energizes you
One of the mistakes people make after work is they err on the side of relaxing because they feel drained, Winch says. But the things we tend to do while resting, like watching screens or doomscrolling, won't recharge us.
"You have to do something that makes you feel energized, and that's a personal thing," Winch says. If you're an athlete, head to the gym. If you're a maker, create something. If you're an extrovert, get a drink with a friend.
It's a "mental battle to force ourselves" to do these things, especially after a long day at work, he says. But "we're going to sleep better that night and have more pep in our step the next day because of that."
The problem: Work feels like your whole life
The fix: Try this thought experiment
It's OK for work to be a part of your identity, but it shouldn't be the only thing that defines you, Winch says.
If you're losing yourself in your job, try this thought exercise, he says. "If your work disappeared tomorrow, what's left? How would you describe yourself? How would you describe what your life is about?" You may find that your worth likely doesn't come from your job title or salary.
And don't forget what it's all for. If you've got the choice between working for a couple of more hours or watching your favorite TV show with your partner, pick the TV show.
"The only reason why I'm working is to be able to have a life in the first place," Winch says. "And if I end up not having one, then what's the point of it all?"
More Life Kit on work-life balance
Why you feel so guilty when you're not working. When was the last time you had a meal without looking at your phone or took a day off without answering a work email? Journalist Celeste Headlee spoke with therapist Amelia Aldao for her tips on taking a break.
What to do if you're struggling with your mental health at work. Whether it's depression, anxiety, burnout or something else, if you're struggling with your mental health at work, it can be hard to know what your options are and how to seek help. Here's a look at the stigma around mental health at work, how to spot an issue and what to do about it.
Do less, ask for more: How to make life easier as a working parent. Going back to work after having a baby can be overwhelming. You're juggling all the emotions of being a new parent while getting up to speed at your job. Tips to help you make a smooth transition.
This story was edited by Sylvie Douglis. The visual editor is CJ Riculan. We'd love to hear from you. Leave us a voicemail at 202-216-9823, or email us at LifeKit@npr.org.
