noticias.titulo: Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
noticias.resumen: Critics say now that the AI giant is a public company, its commitment to put safety ahead of commercial success will be tested.
noticias.texto:
Anthropic says it will put humanity first. Will its IPO change that?
As Anthropic executives and co-founders gathered to celebrate the artificial intelligence company's market debut at the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday, CEO Dario Amodei spoke about AI's potential benefits, and risks, to humanity.
"There is a gigantic difference between how AI will go if we pay little attention to safety versus how it will go if we are obsessed with safety," Amodei said before ringing the ceremonial opening bell. "And an obsession with safety and public benefit has been built into Anthropic's DNA from the start."
Anthropic raised a record $81.3 billion from the IPO and a further $26 billion through a separate private placement, surpassing SpaceX and vaulting into the ranks of publicly traded companies worth more than $1 trillion.
The company has built its reputation on the promise that developing safe AI matters more than winning the race for commercial dominance. It has cultivated an image as an AI safety pioneer, presenting itself as a company willing to put humanity's long-term interests ahead of industry competition.
But now that Anthropic is a public company, that commitment faces a new test. The IPO has brought in new investors, greater scrutiny and pressure to deliver returns to shareholders. Some critics question whether the company can stay true to its founding mission.
The commercial demands of being a public company may cloud safety decisions that could negatively impact the company's share price, such as delaying the release of potentially risky models, legal experts told NPR.
Anthropic's concerns about AI safety are not merely part of its public messaging. Amodei has repeatedly warned about the potential threats advanced AI models pose to humanity, particularly if they escape the control of their developers. The company's IPO prospectus echoed those concerns, warning that "sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly."
Anthropic also acknowledged that it may ultimately lose control of its own models.
"There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented," the company warned investors.
Anthropic's founders and employees just got very rich
Anthropic's corporate structure is intended to protect its mission, even as it pursues commercial success. Anthropic is a public benefit corporation (PBC), meaning its board must balance shareholder interests with its social mission.
As part of that structure, the company has installed an oversight body known as the Long-Term Benefit Trust, which has the power to appoint four of the company's seven directors. The founders effectively control the appointment of the remaining three.
The trust can, however, be dissolved. Doing so would require the approval of all seven co-founders, as well as a majority vote among shareholders with voting rights.
That arrangement could create a potential route for founders and shareholders to override the trust's influence over company decisions, legal experts interviewed for this article said.
"If there is a fight about some important safety decision, such as 'Are we satisfied that this super-advanced model is safe for users and society, or should we hold off for a couple of months to do extra tests or for whatever other safety reason?,' there's the possibility for the founders and the employees to basically ally against the trustee and neutralize their control rights," said Roberto Tallarita, an assistant professor at Harvard Law School.
The listing has also made many Anthropic employees wealthy. Each of the company's seven co-founders hold a stake in the company currently worth more than $20 billion. Its 5,300 employees hold an estimated $232 billion in combined equity. Non-founder employees were able to sell up to 10% of their holdings on the first trading day.
Those substantial financial stakes could influence how Anthropic's staff approaches decisions around safety and risk, said Tallarita.
"If they make decisions that are driven by safety considerations, but are bad for the bottom line, the stock price will react, and private investors will have reasons to exert some pressure on the company," he said.
The financial rewards could also change Anthropic's internal culture, said Sarah Kreps, a professor and director of the Tech Policy Institute at Cornell University.
"And now so many of these people will be multimillionaires too, which I think will just raise the temperature and egos and sense of stakes," Kreps said.
In his comments on Thursday, Amodei addressed these concerns.
"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control. We will not bend to either business nor political pressure," he said. "Today puts the company in a stronger financial position and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing."
Commercial and competitive pressures may compete with safety
Competition between AI companies is fierce.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described the rivalry between major AI developers as a "race dynamic in the fog of war" while speaking at The New York Times DealBook Summit this week.
That dynamic is "a bad thing," Altman said. "I think this is a time where more caution, not less caution, is warranted."
OpenAI also plans to go public, and filed preliminary IPO paperwork with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June, shortly after Anthropic. But Altman said in September the company has delayed those plans.
In an essay the same month, Amodei discussed the need for AI companies to carefully "pace" the development of frontier models.
"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless," Amodei wrote. "We have sought a middle way: to show that it's possible to build carefully and succeed commercially, and to make safety something on which AI companies compete."
"Anthropic has done a fairly good job of investing in analysis of what its models can and can't do, and the vulnerabilities that it creates, and publishing at least some version of this analysis," Kreps said.
In April, Anthropic announced that it would restrict access to its Claude Mythos model after internal testing revealed its powerful cybersecurity capabilities. The company said Mythos could identify and exploit previously unknown vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, making it a potential tool for hackers.
On June 9, less than three months later, Anthropic introduced Fable 5, a Mythos-class model, for general use with additional safeguards to restrict certain high-risk cyber, biological and chemical capabilities. The original Mythos model remains restricted to selected partners.
"In the past, the fact that the trust and the founders were aligned helped them delay the release of Mythos for several months," said Stavros Gadinis, faculty director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business at the University of California Berkeley's law school. "But this was at a moment when they felt they were leading the pack."
Anthropic's decision to enter the defense contracting space has raised questions about how its commercial relationships align with its stated mission, said Kreps.
In November 2024, Anthropic announced a partnership with defense contractor Palantir, whose software is used in military intelligence and targeting operations. Under the agreement, Anthropic made its Claude models available to U.S. defense and intelligence agencies through Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform.
However, Anthropic earlier this year resisted allowing the Pentagon to use its technology for autonomous weapons and mass domestic surveillance. Negotiations broke down in February, resulting in the U.S. government designating Anthropic a "supply chain risk to national security."
"It does seem to raise a set of concerns about partnering with Palantir, which is contracting with the Pentagon for targeting. What part of that is AI for humanity?" said Kreps. "A lot of people who work there went there because safety was the guiding light."
AI development is accelerating
Questions over Anthropic's promise to prioritize safety over commercial success are becoming more pressing as the technology itself advances. Anthropic is entering the public markets at a moment when its own research suggests the pace of AI development could be accelerating dramatically.
A November 2026 assessment by AI research nonprofit METR concluded that Anthropic's AI capabilities were improving at about twice the previous rate. Researchers estimate that a majority of this acceleration is now driven by Anthropic's use of AI tools to assist its own researchers. METR found no clear bottlenecks that might slow this progress, such as limits on data and computing power.
This could bring the company closer to a future in which increasingly capable AI systems help build even more advanced systems — a process known as autonomous recursive self-improvement. The prospect has fueled fears that Anthropic and other AI developers could lose control of their most advanced models, with potentially significant consequences for society.
"I'm scared myself, but it's very hard to imagine AI technology stopping or pausing," said Gadinis. "We are in a situation where these companies know better than anyone their models to the extent that someone understands them. So we have to work with them as a society."
A federal regulatory vacuum
Society is left relying heavily on AI company executives to make consequential decisions about the risks posed by their own products, experts interviewed for this story said.
Since there are few government safeguards in place to shape how AI companies make decisions about safety and security, the industry's power is going largely unchecked, they said.
At the federal level, the AI sector remains largely unregulated. Under the second Trump administration, the White House has prioritized a deregulatory approach, seeking to limit federal oversight in favor of allowing AI labs to innovate without being encumbered by red tape.
In June, the White House announced its AI framework, which lets developers submit their newest models to federal agencies for cybersecurity and national security evaluations before release. However, the initiative is entirely voluntary.
"I don't think the government knows enough to regulate AI," said Tallarita. "This is a conversation that we should have as a political community, and probably the most serious conversation we should have right now."
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

noticias.titulo: The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms
noticias.resumen: AI stocks — and the broader markets — got pummeled this week, raising major concerns about the financial system and the wider economy. Here's what to know.
noticias.texto:
The AI boom had a really bad week — and it's raising loud alarms
A yearslong AI boom showed signs of unraveling this week in spectacular fashion.
AI-related stocks have powered markets to record highs and helped support the broader economy. But investors now fear that a potential bubble in the sector could be bursting, which could spark wider financial repercussions.
Here's what to know about the week in AI and why alarm bells are ringing
What happened with stock markets this week?
Investors were hoping the stock market debut of AI giant Anthropic this week would provide a boost to the markets. Instead, the entire stock market got pummeled on Friday, sparking one of the worst weeks that Wall Street has seen in quite some time.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq dropped 10% for the week, its worst performance since the onset of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns in March 2020. Even Anthropic, which gained 17% on its debut, ended up slumping more than 8% to close near its IPO price on Friday.
Meanwhile, both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average entered a correction as of the close of trade on Friday, meaning a drop of 10% from their recent highs.
What's behind the steep drops?
It's the culmination of weeks of fears that have been building up about the sustainability of the AI trade.
Back in September, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in over three years. That poses a big challenge to AI companies because they still need to borrow billions of dollars to do things like build out data centers that power the growth of their technologies. Higher interest rates make borrowing more expensive for them.
Democrats also took over both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, vowing to take a tougher regulatory approach toward the AI sector and slow down the build-out of data centers, which have been unpopular with voters.
Democrats were also elected as governors in states that have been key to the data center build-out, like Texas, where Gina Hinojosa stunned the political world by winning her race.
And then there's the turmoil at Nvidia, the top AI chip company. Its CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned this month after being suspected of having had an affair with a woman who's believed to have been spying for China.
All this has exacerbated investors' worries about the sustainability of an AI trade into which investors have sunk billions of dollars.
Hank Smith, the head of investment strategy at Haverford Trust, thinks it's unlikely the markets will recover quickly, the way they have previously bounced right back after AI shares dropped.
"I think it has taken the market the better part of the last two or three weeks to realize it is not going to be like the previous sell-offs," Smith said, adding that AI could fall "out of favor" through next year.
"It's just going to take a little bit of time to heal," he said of the tech market.
What are the potential financial consequences?
That has been a big source of debate on Wall Street.
Some people fear that the AI sector could be in the middle of a bubble that is bursting, just like tech stocks did during the dot-com bust of 2000. At the time, investors had sunk money into tech companies that often had no profits — and not even revenues — and were wiped out in the bust.
Smith, though, argues that this time around the AI trade is being powered by top companies such as Meta and Apple, and he doesn't see them as likely to go out of business, the way many dot-coms did. Nvidia — despite its leadership shake-up — still posted strong results this week.
The future prospects for AI, Smith said, are "not based on a pie in the sky."
That said, Smith continued, there is still a question about whether investors will see the sizable returns they are hoping to get.
And there's another big fear: how interconnected AI companies have become. Nvidia, for example, not only owns shares in other big AI companies like Anthropic but is also lending a lot of money to them. In turn, they are buying chips from Nvidia.
This circular system of financing also involves lesser-known companies, such as CoreWeave, that are borrowing heavily to build out data centers. Nvidia is a major investor in CoreWeave, in another sign of the interconnectedness.
This close-knit ecosystem is raising concerns that if one or two companies run into trouble, it could kick off a chain reaction that could lead to something like a financial crisis.
What does it mean for the economy if the AI boom falters?
It could be potentially significant. The U.S. economy has effectively become an AI economy.
Building out data centers, for example, may be unpopular with voters, but construction creates jobs, which is why some parts of the U.S. have courted the centers. In fact, AI investments helped the economy grow at an annual rate of 3.4% in the most recent quarter.
Not only that, but AI-related stocks have become an integral part of the broader markets, accounting for a substantial portion of the S&P 500. That means many investors hold these stocks as part of their portfolios, including as components of index funds, pensions or retirement funds like 401(k)s.
So if the AI trade unravels, it could have a ripple effect far beyond the high-tech world.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

noticias.titulo: An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
noticias.resumen: A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
noticias.texto:
An effort to circumvent the Electoral College may be within reach. But hurdles remain
A national effort to ensure that only winners of the popular vote become president could reach a critical milestone soon.
It's a possible outcome of huge Democratic wins in this month's midterm elections.
Next year, Democrats will fully control five states that could sign the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the winner of the nationwide popular vote, not the winner of their respective states.
If they do join other 18 Democratic-led states — plus the District of Columbia — that are in the compact, the effort will have surpassed the needed 270 electoral votes required to go into effect, making an end run around the Electoral College. So far no Republican-led states have joined the compact and the party is largely not unified on the issue.
There are still plenty of political, practical and legal hurdles that this effort would need to clear. But proponents are optimistic many of those hurdles will be cleared – even perhaps in time for the next presidential election.
"I've never been more confident that 63% of American voters can get what they want in the 2028 presidential election, which is a national popular vote for president." Patrick Rosenstiel, a senior consultant to National Popular Vote, the group pushing for the compact in states across the country, told NPR, referencing Pew polling.
Right now, the compact has a total of 222 electoral votes. The five states that will soon be completely in the hands of Democrats – Arizona, Pennsylvania, Michigan, Nevada and Wisconsin – add up to 61 electoral votes. Combinations of at least four of those states would put the compact over 270.
So far, governors and incoming governors in Pennsylvania and Nevada have said they are open to signing legislation that would bring their states into the interstate agreement. But other governors have yet to publicly weigh in.
One of the looming questions over these efforts is whether these states – all presidential battlegrounds – would be willing to give up their immense influence in elections ahead of the 2028 presidential contests.
And leaders in each state will also have to weigh whether they want to be the tipping point in moving forward a movement that could upend how the U.S. decides presidential winners.
Already, some Democrats are more reticent on the issue than they were before. For example, Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, who had previously supported the measure, has not commented recently on whether the state's new Democratic majorities should sign on. NPR reached out to Hobbs' office for comment but did not receive a response before publication.
And then of course, there are the various legal and logistical hurdles.
The practical and legal hurdles
Some legal scholars have observed that this agreement between states could run afoul of the compact clause in the Constitution, which says that "no state shall, without the consent of Congress … enter into any agreement or compact with another state … unless actually invaded, or in such imminent danger as will not admit of delay."
Norman Miller, a constitutional law professor at Willamette University, said that beyond the legal hurdles, he sees a range of practical issues with the compact.
Mostly, he said, it could upend what is a core feature of American presidential elections, which is that they are largely decentralized.
States individually decide who can vote and how they can vote. He said forcing electors from one state to vote according to the tallies in another state could create some tension.
"We would want to have a standardized, uniform set of rules regarding who gets to vote for president, how they vote, how those votes are tabulated, and to have a federal election authority doing that tabulation," he said. "I think trying to nationalize [the current system] and entrusting a national election to 51 separate election administrators would just sow discord and distrust."
But John Koza, the chairman of National Popular Vote, said if the compact works the way it is supposed to, none of that will be necessary.
"We don't need a centralized bureaucracy or a presidentially appointed commission that could be manipulated," he told NPR. "The simple fact is current state and federal law provide for the issuance of a certified vote count from each state. And all that has to be done is add them up."
But mostly, Miller said the biggest question before this effort is whether such a large reform should be done via a constitutional amendment.
Upending the Electoral College, some argue, would be a profound change to how the U.S. chooses the leader of the free world. Opponents of a national popular vote, such as Save Our States, argue that without the incentives created by the Electoral College, American politics will move more toward "toward more regional politics and would exacerbate existing divides."
Miller said even though it will be much more difficult to pull off, it would be worth going through a more fulsome process via Article 5 to get rid of the Electoral College, instead of working around it.
"This is where I think process matters," he said. "If you really want to have a national popular vote for the president and avoid all of the legal and practical difficulties, you need to do that through a constitutional amendment, because only a constitutional amendment can address the legal and practical challenges of conducting a national popular vote for the presidency."
A similar effort to pass an amendment to get rid of the Electoral College in 1969 failed, though. And very few amendments have even gotten close to passing in recent history.
Rosenstiel, the consultant to the National Popular Vote, said this is why he thinks groups like his are seeking a creative solution to something most Americans agree is a problem.
And, he said, he ultimately thinks a national popular vote will solve multiple problems at once. For one, he said, it will force presidential candidates to appeal to most of the country, as opposed to a select group of voters in battleground states.
And, importantly, he said, it would make all voters feel like their vote matters.
"We should have a system where every American citizen feels valued and is valued when they cast their vote," he said. "And there's only one reform that delivers it."

noticias.titulo: Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
noticias.resumen: Efforts to establish rules for AI-powered killer robots and drones have run aground. U.N.-backed talks in Geneva ended Saturday with an agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
noticias.texto:
Nations at UN talks on AI killer robots agree to more talks but no firm commitment to rein them in
Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground Saturday as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years.
Scores of countries ended the week-long U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to "elaborate" a possible accord on such lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. But they didn't commit to binding rules sought by U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres, many countries, and activists.
The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts and major military powers jockeying for dominance.
Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a "significant achievement" but acknowledged a "glass half full or half empty" scenario, citing Guterres' hopes for a legally binding deal this year.
Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language.
Stop Killer Robots lamented a "watered-down mandate," and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounts to "pushing the can down the road for two more years."
They noted most countries supported work toward a new treaty, and Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said: "States have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue, for the 14th year, while these weapons enable atrocities."
Before the meeting, seven countries proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability. That effort fell short.
"Technology is moving faster than diplomacy," said Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama in proposing such negotiations. "Diplomats are very slow."
After years of talks on the issue, advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism largely by Russia, which, like other top AI weapons-developing countries such as the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons.
Guterres, who leaves office at the end of the year, set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems.
Pope Leo XIV and many advocacy and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.
Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn't happened.
Talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus. That means any single country can thwart an agreement, and that any deal was likely to be based on a low common denominator.

noticias.titulo: French President Macron warns of 'new level' of Russian aggression
noticias.resumen: The warning came after a series of airspace violations, reported sabotage attempts and an alleged assassination plot made headlines.
noticias.texto:
The warning came after a series of airspace violations, reported sabotage attempts and an alleged assassination plot made headlines.
French President Emmanuel Macron warned on Friday of a "new level" of Russian aggression following a spate of incidents across Europe this week.
"Over the past 24 hours, several of our European partners and allies have once again faced serious incidents that signal a new level of aggression on Russia’s part," Macron wrote in a post on social media.
The warning came after a series of airspace violations, reported sabotage attempts and an alleged assassination plot made headlines.
On Friday, Polish authorities announced that two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone had crashed in Poland as allied nations held military exercises in the eastern European country.
Denmark's Security and Intelligence Service (PET) also accused Russian intelligence services of being behind an assassination attempt targeting a Ukrainian American citizen north of Copenhagen in September.
For its part, the Estonian government announced its decision to suspend all road border crossings with Russia from 1 December in the wake of what Tallinn said was a "GRU-ordered" sabotage attempt targeting drone manufacturer Threod Systems last week.
Earlier this week, Moldova also shuttered its national airspace after an attack drone was detected heading towards the capital Chișinău. President Maia Sandu said "several Russian drones" had violated Moldovan airspace over the course of Tuesday evening.
Macron on Friday expressed his solidarity with the impacted nations while also condemning Russia.
"By intensifying its war of aggression against Ukraine and pursuing an aggressive agenda on European territory, Russia is taking an irresponsible gamble that can only further isolate it and strengthen the resolve and unity of Europeans - and of all those who wish to work toward peace and stability on our continent," Macron said.
Russian strikes on Ukraine
Macron's comments followed large-scale Russian strikes across Ukraine from Thursday night into Friday morning, which killed at least seven people in Kyiv and damaged key bridges across the Dnipro River.
Zelenskyy said Russia had fired more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles during the assault, which he called "one of the largest attacks" of the war so far.

noticias.titulo: Japan: Autonomous air taxi completes passenger flight without a pilot
noticias.resumen: A pilotless electric flying taxi has carried a passenger during a demonstration, on Friday 20 November 2026, in Japan's Yamanashi Prefecture. The Chinese-built aircraft took off vertically and flew autonomously, offering a glimpse of a possible future for urban transport.
noticias.texto:
With Mount Fuji rising in the distance, a futuristic two-seat aircraft lifted vertically into the air above Yamanashi Prefecture, propelled by 16 spinning rotors along a pre-programmed route without a pilot on board. Inside the cabin, a lone passenger waved through the glass as visitors and journalists crowded around to photograph Yamanashi’s first passenger demonstration of the EH216-S, an all-electric vertical take-off and landing craft built by Chinese firm EHang, during a 380-metre flight along the academy’s runway.
A second, uncrewed sortie later stretched 1,800 metres above the nearby Kamanashi River, showcasing an aircraft engineered to bypass conventional runways altogether, reach speeds of up to 120 km/h and cover roughly 30 kilometres on a single charge. Staged to introduce the public to urban air mobility and test the potential for short-hop flights across Japan, the showcase underscored both the promise of an aerial alternative to congested roads and the regulatory, safety and infrastructure hurdles still standing in the way of commercial rollout.

noticias.titulo: Anthropic worker claims to have solved famed 167-year-old maths problem with help of AI
noticias.resumen: Brian Greene, a professor of physics and mathematics at Columbia University in New York, called Alpöge's proof potentially "one of the greatest mathematical breakthroughs in the past two centuries."
noticias.texto:
Brian Greene, a professor of physics and mathematics at Columbia University in New York, called Alpöge's proof potentially "one of the greatest mathematical breakthroughs in the past two centuries."
A mathematician working for artificial intelligence firm Anthropic claims to have solved one of the world's most important maths problems with the help of AI.
Levent Alpöge posted a four-page note on Friday saying he believed he had found a proof to the Riemann hypothesis by working with Anthropic's Claude AI tool.
"Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," Alpöge wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line."
Formulated in an 1859 paper by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the Riemann hypothesis refers to the distribution of prime numbers as they stretch towards infinity.
"This all happened for me late Sunday night," Alpöge continued, adding that he had contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to ask about announcing his find. His announcement eventually came a day after Anthropic's blockbuster Thursday stock market debut.
In his post, Alpöge linked to computer code written in Lean - a proof assistant for mathematics - that he says verifies his discovery.
Brian Greene, a professor of physics and mathematics at Columbia University in New York, called Alpöge's proof potentially "one of the greatest mathematical breakthroughs in the past two centuries."
"If true utterly astounding: Anthropic claims their AI has proved the Riemann Hypothesis, a towering target in mathematics for nearly two centuries, with profound ramifications," he added in a post on X.
Abhishek Saha, a professor of mathematics at Queen Mary University of London, said he believed the proof had a "very good chance of being correct."

noticias.titulo: Off the Record: Europe shrugs as Trump's Yalta knockoff flops
noticias.resumen: In this week’s newsletter, Euronews Political Correspondent Jorge Liboreiro unpacks the fallout from the much-hyped “Yalta 2.0”, describing the outcome as a political nothingburger.
noticias.texto:
In this week’s newsletter, Euronews Political Correspondent Jorge Liboreiro unpacks the fallout from the much-hyped “Yalta 2.0”, describing the outcome as a political nothingburger.
Hype is, by nature, risky. In diplomacy, it can be deadly.
Just ask Donald Trump, who arrived in Shenzhen, China, amid pomp, pageantry and sky-high expectations for a historic trilateral summit with his Chinese and Russian counterparts. But let's look at what actually happened.
The meeting had been dubbed "Yalta 2.0", drawing an intriguing parallel with the 1945 conference that defined the partition of the world in sphere of influence among the victors of the Second World War: the United States, Britain and Soviet Russia.
As it turned out, Yalta it was not. More like a wannabe knock-off. And the leader of the world's largest economy – who appeared to doze off at times during the proceedings – had the least to show for himself as he left China's technology hub.
For Trump, the main – perhaps only – takeaway was the photo opportunity with the other two leaders and the media frenzy it generated. But Trump has long understood politics as a matter of optics, and the picture alone may have been enough.
The joint declaration against nuclear warfare was about as meaningful as a Miss World contestant calling for world peace at a Trump beauty pageant – a format he once owned, so he knows a thing or two about it.
For Vladimir Putin, it was more of a mixed bag.
The Russian president was visibly side-lined at the preceding dinner, relegated to a second-tier table while Trump and Xi Jinping chummily sat together.
His heavy-handed attempt to push Russia's war against Ukraine to the top of the agenda also fell flat. The conflict was conspicuously absent from the ironically titled "Declaration toward Peace", published by the three countries after their 80-minute meeting.
The meeting allowed Putin to cultivate the illusion that Russia – an economy roughly the size of Italy's – somehow deserves to stand on equal footing to the US and China. But that's only a mirage. The truth is Putin's Russia is a country is decline.
For almost five years, Moscow has waged a devastating war against its neighbour, inflicting immense human suffering while failing to achieve its core objectives: toppling the government in Kyiv and occupying the country in full.
When it comes to Xi Jinping, eager to capitalise on America's rupture with its Western allies, the summit was a home run.
As host, the Chinese president set the pace and controlled the stage. He spoke in grand terms, likening nuclear weapons to "a sword of Damocles hanging over humanity" and urging "major powers [to] live in harmony".
More importantly, he used the occasion to reinforce his central message: an alternative to the Western-led world order is possible – and China intends to help mould it.
So, was it really Yalta 2.0? Or just three ageing men sitting around a table? It's a fair question: together, they are 227 years old.
"As far as a new Yalta goes, what was so bad about Yalta?" Putin said at the end of the talks. "Yalta formalised the existing realities, and in today's conflicts, too, we will have to come to terms with the realities on the ground."
Needless to say, Putin had the most to gain from staging a replay of the 1945 Yalta conference, where Stalin's Soviet Union emerged among the victors of World War II. Xi, by contrast, urged leaders to "abandon Cold War thinking" – somewhat paradoxically, given that Yalta helped usher in the Cold War.
For Europeans, however, the timing turned out to be surprisingly convenient.
Just hours after the Shenzhen summit, they gathered in Berlin for a fresh meeting of the Coalition of the Willing. It gave them an opportunity to project unity, demonstrate that they were taking matters into their own hands and, perhaps most importantly, show that they were getting on with business, seemingly unfazed by the noise elsewhere.
Their closing press conference said it all. To put it bluntly, it was a collective shrug.
"A Yalta-style format will not bring peace," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.
"At Yalta, Europe was divided up. It was parcelled up. And we won't allow anything like that to happen again."
Standing alongside him, French President Emmanuel Macron suggested the Shenzhen meeting lacked the legitimacy to redraw the global order.
"Europeans have taken decisions. They have decided to determine their own fate," he said. "Europe is not a subject on a menu of discussions, but a series of powers who want to build their own future."
Admittedly, there was a tangible sense of relief across European capitals.
For the past two years, Europeans have been on edge, fearing that Trump would lose patience and strike a secret deal with Putin over Ukraine's head.
They have become better at resisting – or building resilience, as we say in Brussels – to that kind of fatalistic thinking. But they remain acutely vulnerable to Trump's penchant for political shockwaves.
The past month has, in fact, been a concerted effort to keep the diplomatic process firmly on track.
European, Ukrainian and US officials have met in Miami, Oslo, Brussels, Abu Dhabi and Berlin, building a close-knit working group to develop security guarantees and recovery plans for Ukraine once the war is over.
It marks quite a turnaround from 2025, when Washington deliberately kept Europe out of the loop and journalists – yours truly included – penned obituaries about Europe's "missing seat" at the negotiating table.
Now, Washington is actively urging Moscow to engage in direct talks with Europe, something Russia has consistently refused to do, despite its seemingly endless fixation with reshaping Europe's security architecture.
Privately, European officials see the US push for multilateral peace talks as evidence that Washington has finally recognised a basic reality: whatever contours a deal has, Europe will have to be involved in both negotiating it and putting it into practice.
And yet, they are under no false hopes. Everybody knows the process is and will remain volatile. Nobody can say what comes next. So far, there is little to suggest that Putin is ready for meaningful negotiations.
In another indication of Moscow's reluctance to engage, Putin invited European leaders to Moscow to discuss their participation in the talks – an offer that hardly inspires confidence. He also declared negotiations with Ukraine over in retaliation for the attack on his prized and heavily defended Crimean Bridge.
And so here we are.
For all the uncertainty, Europeans appear to be increasingly accepting that a resolution to the war may be closer than it once seemed. That means the moment for difficult, potentially painful decisions could be approaching. The question is no longer simply whether Europe will have a seat at the table, but whether it will be ready to make those decisions when the time comes.
Above all, Europeans want to ensure that they – rather than others – get to shape the choices that will determine Ukraine's future.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who was also in Berlin, put it unusually candidly, describing the war as a "lose-lose situation" for all parties.
"We are clear about what we will accept and what we won't accept," he said.
"But we are also clear that we stand with Ukraine today, tomorrow, for as long as it takes until this unjust war is over."
Thank you reading Off the Record. We'll be back next week.

noticias.titulo: Pentagon declassifies new UFO footage filmed by US military
noticias.resumen: The US Department of War has published its eighth release of declassified historical files on unidentified anomalous phenomena, with further documents expected to be made public.
noticias.texto:
The US Department of War published a new batch of declassified files relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAP) on Thursday, marking the eighth release under a government disclosure programme.

The documents are available on the department's website as part of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE).

noticias.titulo: Fossil fuel row sees COP31 talks spill into overtime
noticias.resumen: A number of countries, including France and Panama, released a letter on Friday insisting that a deal include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels."
noticias.texto:
A number of countries, including France and Panama, released a letter on Friday insisting that a deal include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels."
The COP31 climate talks have pushed into Saturday as countries race to secure a deal after a draft text dropped references to fossil fuels, prompting pushback from nations including France and Panama.
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries have struggled to work through deep divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance at the conference, which is being held in Antalya, Turkey.
"We are close to the finish line, but we are not there yet," COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum told an assembly late on Friday.
A new agreement is expected to be published on Saturday.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week had called for a sped-up phasing out of fossil fuels. But a second version released on Thursday removed all mentions of the energy sources, forcing negotiators back to the bargaining table.
The European Union said the revised draft risked "turning this climate COP into a fossil summit."
A number of countries, including France and Panama, shared a letter on Friday insisting that the deal include "a clear transition away from fossil fuels."
Panama has also threatened to walk away from the talks, with its environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro, accusing a "petroleum mafia" of blocking progress.
Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen, who is leading negotiations, said he would work "for as long as it takes, to get the job done."
It came as the OPEC oil cartel said its Secretary General Haitham al-Ghais had met with Russian climate envoy Ruslan Edelgeriev at COP31 to discuss "the importance of inclusive and balanced approaches across all multilateral environmental fora."
"Discussions focused on exchanging views on the UN climate negotiations and enhancing the cooperation between OPEC and the Russian Federation to advance international climate action and sustainable development," it said in a post on X.

noticias.titulo: Second judge blocks construction of Trump's massive 'triumphal arch'
noticias.resumen: Trump, who has embarked on a campaign to remodel Washington since his return to the White House in January 2025, has said the structure would be turned into a "top grade military complex."
noticias.texto:
Trump, who has embarked on a campaign to remodel Washington since his return to the White House in January 2025, has said the structure would be turned into a "top grade military complex."
A second federal judge has blocked US President Donald Trump's plans to build a massive "triumphal arch" in Washington.
District Judge Leonie Brinkema on Friday said she would issue a preliminary injunction temporarily halting construction of the project - a 250-foot-tall memorial arch inspired by Paris' Arc de Triomphe.
The decision comes after fellow District Judge Tanya Chutkan also temporarily blocked the project from getting underway.
Opponents have questioned the arch's purpose and voiced concerns over its proposed location next to the Arlington National Cemetery - the resting place for hundreds of thousands of US veterans - arguing that it would block the view of the site.
Democracy Forward, which is representing the Arlington County Board in the case, has welcomed Brinkema's ruling.
“We are pleased that the court has recognised the irreparable harm that will come to people who live and work in Arlington and stopped the massive vanity project while our case is heard and considered by the court,” Kate Talmor, a senior counsel at Democracy Forward said in a statement released on Friday. “We are honored to work with the Arlington County Board to stop the proposed arch from jeopardising public safety.”
The National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) had voted to approve the project earlier this month.
Trump, who has embarked on a campaign to remodel Washington since his return to the White House in January 2025, has said the structure would be turned into a "top grade military complex."
"I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch, planned since the Civil War Era many years ago, at the Receptive Circle adjoining the Arlington Memorial Bridge, into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch," he wrote in a post on his Truth Social account in September.
He added that it could be used "to house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage."

noticias.titulo: Chronic loneliness linked to higher dementia risks in new study
noticias.resumen: A French research team tracked people’s loneliness and dementia risk over 30 years.
noticias.texto:
A French research team tracked people’s loneliness and dementia risk over 30 years.
People who are almost always lonely may be at higher risk of developing dementia, according to a new study that tracked ageing adults over three decades.
There is no current cure for dementia, which affects 57 million people worldwide. But a combination of genetic and lifestyle factors, such as exercise, alcohol and smoking, can affect people’s risk of developing the condition. According to an expert group convened by the Lancet, social isolation is another risk factor.
Researchers from the University of Bordeaux set out to measure that risk. They found that older adults who were chronically lonely had a 38% higher risk of developing dementia compared to those who never felt lonely.
Notably, occasional loneliness was not significantly linked to dementia risk, according to the study, which was published in the journal Aging & Mental Health.
“This distinction is critical,” said Karine Pérès, one of the study’s authors and a senior researcher at the Bordeaux Population Health Centre.
“While most people experience loneliness at some point in their lives, it is when loneliness becomes chronic and persistent that it may increase the risk of developing dementia,” she said.
The researchers analysed data for 3,777 older adults who were tracked from 1988 to 2018. They classified people as “never lonely,” "occasionally lonely” or “chronically lonely” based on four research visits over an eight-year period. Then they looked at whether the participants developed dementia over the next 20 years.
Roughly one in three people who were never or occasionally lonely went on to develop dementia, compared to about 49% of the chronically lonely group, the study found. Most people in the study did not experience regular loneliness.
Loneliness and social isolation aren’t exactly the same. Loneliness is subjective, and people can experience it even if they live with family or regularly see other people, the Bordeaux team said.
“This vulnerability may also stem from unsatisfying relationships, caregiving burdens, or lack of meaningful activities,” said Yvanna Simon, the study’s lead author.
The study has some limitations. It relied on one question to measure loneliness, rather than a comprehensive assessment, and the researchers may not have accounted for all factors that could influence the relationship between dementia and loneliness. But the findings are in line with previous, bigger studies that found a similar link between dementia and loneliness in midlife and old age.
The Bordeaux researchers recommended that health care workers screen their patients for loneliness and encourage more social activities. More inclusive public spaces that welcome people of all ages could also help, they said.
According to Alzheimer’s Research UK, staying socially engaged in old age can help keep parts of the brain active and reduce changes in the brain that are linked to dementia. But the nonprofit emphasised that no one factor causes dementia on its own.
For example, people who are chronically lonely may also get less exercise and eat a less healthy diet, which may contribute to heart disease and diabetes. Those conditions, in turn, raise the risk of dementia. Social interactions are just another layer.
“Lack of social interactions limits cognitive stimulation, while unresolved social stress leads to an accumulation of biological wear and tear over time,” Pérès said.

noticias.titulo: Putin a 'killer,' Zelenskyy says after Trump calls Russian leader his 'friend'
noticias.resumen: It comes after Russian forces launched a major wave of strikes against Ukraine from Thursday night into Friday morning, killing at least seven people in Kyiv and damaging key bridges across the Dnipro River.
noticias.texto:
It comes after Russian forces launched a major wave of strikes against Ukraine from Thursday night into Friday morning, killing at least seven people in Kyiv and damaging key bridges across the Dnipro River.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has branded Vladimir Putin a "killer" after Donald Trump referred to the Russian leader as his "friend" earlier this week.
"For us, he is an enemy. And of course, for us, he is a killer. And I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer," Zelenskyy told CNN in response to a question about Trump's comment, while also warning that such descriptions could ease pressure on Putin.
Trump called Putin a "friend" as they met on the sidelines of a trilateral meeting with China's Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week, and he continued to talk up their relationship during a press conference at the White House on Friday.
"I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That's a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That's a good thing. And our country is safe because of that," he told reporters.
"You're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he went on, adding that both Zelenskyy and Putin wanted to end the war but "don't know how."
Asked whether Putin was a friend of the US, Trump replied: "I can't speak to America."
It comes after Russian forces launched a major wave of strikes against Ukraine from Thursday night into Friday morning, killing at least seven people in Kyiv and damaging key bridges across the Dnipro River.
Zelenskyy said Russia had fired more than 400 attack drones and over 110 missiles during the assault, which he called "one of the largest attacks" of the war so far.
"Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives. Energy facilities, logistics – bridges across the Dnipro, railway infrastructure," he wrote in a post on social media.
The attacks followed Putin's warning that there would be "no negotiations" on a partial ceasefire with Ukraine following Ukrainian strikes on his prized Crimea bridge this week, which destroyed a large part of the structure.

noticias.titulo: Europe braces for cold winter as polar vortex flips. Can heat pumps help lower energy bills?
noticias.resumen: An unusually early sudden stratospheric warming event has flipped the polar vortex, leaving analysts worried about rising energy prices.
noticias.texto:
An unusually early sudden stratospheric warming event has flipped the polar vortex, leaving analysts worried about rising energy prices.
Europeans brace for what could be a particularly cold winter this year, after an unusually early sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) flipped the polar vortex.
The polar vortex is a ring of westerly winds that keeps freezing polar air locked over the North Pole about 30km above the Earth’s surface.
Sometimes, large atmospheric waves can disrupt this circulation, causing the winds to weaken significantly or even reverse direction. This can cause temperatures in the stratosphere to rise rapidly.
As the cold air from high up in the stratosphere disperses, it can affect the shape of the jet stream as the cold air sinks from the stratosphere into the troposphere, which extends from the ground up to an average altitude of about eight to 15 kilometres.
Europe’s dwindling gas supplies
According to market intelligence provider Montel, forecasters warn that this "heightens the odds of colder temperatures”, more storms, wind and heating demand on the continent over the next month.
However, analysts say this would need to be a “repeated event” to have a sustained effect throughout the winter, as single SSW events are “short-term in nature”.
A severe cold spell could put gas supplies under even more pressure, following warnings from the EU that it may have to curb its gas consumption by seven per cent this winter as stocks hit record lows for this time of year.
Dwindling gas reserves, primarily driven by the war on Iran and subsequent blockade of the Strait of Hormuz – one of the world’s biggest fossil fuel shipping routes – are also set to worsen ahead of a full ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports from January 2027.
The unusually early SSW “might make people a bit nervous”, says Klaas Dozeman, energy forecaster at Brainchild Commodity Intelligence, adding that “most meteorologists remain puzzled on what the effects will be over the coming weeks”.
Can heat pumps save households from spiralling energy bills this winter?
Green technology is cushioning Europe from the ongoing fossil fuel crisis, providing more households with energy security and lower bills.
Solar power, for example, has already saved the EU €44.6 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the US-led war on Iran, which started on 28 February.
But as the days get shorter and darker, it is heat pumps that will offer relief from spiralling energy prices.
Heat pumps, which work by capturing energy from air, water or the ground and turning it into heat or cold air, typically deliver three to four kWh of heat for every one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity they consume.
Each residential heat pump installed displaces around 1,100 m3 of gas and two tonnes of CO2 per year on average, if the small amount of electricity it uses to run is from renewable sources.
Europe’s heat pumps provide as much heat as the LNG carried by more than 200 tankers, according to an analysis from the European Heat Pump Association published in June*.
This is double the amount that arrived in the EU in 2025 from the Middle East and around seven per cent of the EU’s total annual imported LNG – avoiding €9.7 billion in import costs last year.
“Every heat pump installed is another bolt in the door of European energy security,” says Paul Kenny, director general of EHPA.
“LNG is the most expensive energy source and comes from unreliable suppliers, and heat pumps can drastically reduce our need for it.”
Despite myths suggesting that heat pumps do not work in cold countries, which Euronews Earth has debunked here, new research has found that when used effectively, air source heat pumps could help heat homes on a typical winter day for as little as £1.84 (approximately €2.20) a day.
Heat pumps more efficient than gas boilers
The study, from British property developers Barratt Redrow, found that heat pumps can be more efficient than traditional gas boilers because they keep a more constant temperature rather than relying on spikes of heat.
"Heat pumps will run during the cold but consume a lot more power,” Jean-Paul Harreman, Director at Montel, tells Euronews Earth.
“The efficiency is better from a heat pump than from a gas boiler, but if power prices go really high, high costs might still be seen during the worst of the cold. However, that is usually only part of the winter, so a price spike should not be confused with an annual total cost.”
Heat pump sales rose 13 per cent last year, hitting 2.9 million in 21 European countries. This brings the total stock to 29.3 million.
When asked whether heat pumps could help the EU’s dwindling gas supply, Harreman said: “A little yes. We see electrification of heating happening in many countries, but the overall impact on demand is not that large.
“Industrial demand destruction plays a bigger role.”
Industrial demand destruction is a sustained or permanent drop in industrial consumption of energy caused by prolonged high prices or supply constraints.
*EHPA’s data is based on 21 EU member states. You can read the full analysis here.

noticias.titulo: Seeking snow and ski this winter? Try these lesser-known destinations in Asia
noticias.resumen: From ski slopes to snow-covered mountain towns, these Asian destinations offer an alternative to Europe’s winter resorts.
noticias.texto:
From ski slopes to snow-covered mountain towns, these Asian destinations offer an alternative to Europe’s winter resorts.
When it comes to planning a winter getaway, the chances are you might be thinking of heading to Europe's Alpine destinations in France, Switzerland or Austria.
But if you fancy a mid- to long-haul trip away from the continent, Asia has much to offer with snow-covered mountains, ski slopes and a host of resorts worth exploring.
From the landscapes of South Korea, Vietnam, Lebanon and beyond, these destinations deserve a place on your radar for skiing, snowboarding and other winter adventures.
Karakol Ski Resort, Kyrgyzstan
Kyrgyzstan is definitely worth adding to your winter travel bucket list. Picture fresh powder as far as the eyes can see, amid sweeping views of conifer forests.
On the outskirts of Karakol, a Kyrgyz destination for adventure, the Karakol Ski Resort sits at an altitude of 3,040 metres above sea level in the Tian Shan mountain range, which sprawls across the country, as well as China, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. It is also the highest ski resort in Central Asia.
The season usually runs from late November through to April, with the high season being from 31 December to 10 January. During the winter, daytime temperatures rarely drop below -5C, alongside many sunny days.
Aside from the mild climate, there are an array of residences, from hotel rooms to chalet cottages, within the vicinity.
Mzaar Ski Resort, Lebanon
Self-styled as being “above the ordinary”, the Mzaar Ski Resort is perched above the mountain village of Kfardebian and overlooks the breathtaking Lebanese peak, Mount Sannine.
On offer are 115 kilometres of slopes, 19 lifts and a summit at 2,465 metres, making it the largest ski area in the Middle East. Aside from skiing and snowboarding, the winter season is ideal for ziplining over the mountain or riding aboard a snow groomer.
After a long day outdoors, the resort's wellness area is replete with sauna and cold plunge facilities. While there is an outdoor pool, the indoor one is a year-round option for guests to have a swim and unwind.
Accommodation options include the InterContinental Mzaar Mountain Resort & Spa, which has direct access to the 80km Mzaar Ski Domaine, and L’Escale Du Mzaar, which is just 40m from the first chairlift and has chalets and a ski shop.
O2 Ski Resort, South Korea
This resort in South Korea offers speedy rides 1,420 metres above sea level.
Located in the city of Taebaek, O2 Ski Resort has 16 slopes and six lifts, including one which goes up to the top of Hambaek Mountain, where visitors can take in sweeping views.
Facilities include an extreme park, half pipe and a 136m-long snow sledge, with snow made from Han and Nakdong river sources.
Via the gondola, visitors can head to the resting spot at the highest peak, Eutteum Maru, which overlooks the Baekdu mountain range. Beogeum Maru also offers skiers a place to rest, and is easily accessible to novice visitors as it sits between the beginners' slopes.
Sapa, Vietnam
While Southeast Asia isn’t famed for its snowy landscapes, you should also add Vietnam to your winter must-visit lists.
When the temperature drops over the Hoàng Liên Sơn mountain range – the country's highest peaks – frost and the occasional dusting settle over rice terraces.
In Sapa, the town can transform into a snowy sight from December to late January – occasionally extending into early February. During this time, the air becomes crisp, the mountains become capped by snow and the waterfalls also freeze over.
Vietnam Airlines recommends travellers to add Fansipan Mountain to their Sapa itineraries, which stands at 3,143 metres. The country's highest snow-capped peak is accessible via the Sun World Fansipan Legend cable car.
The carrier also suggests paying Bát Xát Commune a visit, as it receives some of Sapa's heaviest snowfall during the winter. The remote retreat's rice terraces and forests become pearly white landscapes during this time.
Meanwhile, Thác Bạc, or the Silver Waterfall, which is on the outskirts of Sapa, is a 200-metre cascade that frequently freezes.
Shahdag Mountain Resort, Azerbaijan
On the outskirts of Gusar city in Azerbaijan’s Greater Caucasus mountain range, the Shahdag Mountain Resort takes its name from Mount Shahdag, which stands 4,243 metres above sea level. This ski and snowboarding playground features 45 kilometres of pristine terrain, including a selection of 37 slopes and a network of 20 lifts.
Winter paintballing, mountain trekking, snow tubing as well as horseback riding are some of the other activities on offer at the resort during the winter. Visitors are also spoiled for choice when it comes to dining with more than 20 venues among five hotels.
At the backdrop of all this are pristine glaciers, deep ravines, stunning canyons and a variety of flora, fauna and wildlife.
Shymbulak Mountain Resort, Kazakhstan
The Shymbulak Mountain Resort is located in the gorge of Trans-Ili Alatau, within the city limits of Kazakhstan's cultural hub, Almaty. The resort itself sits at an elevation ranging from 2,200 metres to 3,180 metres above sea level.
With a total of 10 lifts, adventure travellers are treated to slopes with a total length of up to 20 kilometres and elevation difference of up to 920 metres for both beginners and experts.
The resort features a range of accommodation options, including the Nero Bianca high mountain chalets, which features its own sauna.
Meanwhile, the Le Mont boutique hotel welcomes guests, including those with four-legged companions. It has a viewing platform, with the panorama of Almaty and snow-capped peaks on display. Other options include Shymbulak Resort Hotel and Tenir Eco Hotels.
Zao Onsen Ski Resort, Japan
The Zao Onsen Ski Resort in Yamagata sits amid mountains and vast wilderness, offering a winter playground where the longest run is more than 10 kilometres long.
The Japanese resort features 32 lifts, ropeways and a gondola that goes up to the 1,661-metre summit station. Experienced skiers can enjoy ski jumps, while there are also routes that run through forests for skiers and snowboarders alike.
At the top lifts, keep an eye out for what the locals call "Juhyo", or snow monsters, that the area is known for during the peak of winter in February.
A combination of Siberian winds and heavy snowfall turn the Alpine trees into giant, monster-like figures. There's even a Zao Snow Monster festival where snow monster mascots entertain visitors.
