noticias.titulo: Soil degradation could cost the EU up to €509 billion over its next budget, campaigners warn
noticias.resumen: Soil degradation could cost the EU between €286 billion and €509 billion over its next long-term budget if losses stay at current levels, campaign group Save Soil estimates, urging the bloc to pay farmers for measurable gains in soil health through its next farm subsidy scheme.
noticias.texto:
Soil degradation could cost the EU between €286 billion and €509 billion over its next long-term budget if losses stay at current levels, campaign group Save Soil estimates, urging the bloc to pay farmers for measurable gains in soil health through its next farm subsidy scheme.
Damaged soils could drain €286 billion to €509 billion from the EU economy over the bloc's 2028 to 2034 budget if yearly losses continue at today's pace, Save Soil estimated on Thursday.
The global campaign group wants the next Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), the EU's farm subsidy system, to reward farmers for proven gains in soil health instead of leaving them to bear the cost of restoration.
Save Soil was launched in 2022 by Indian spiritual leader Sadhguru and his non-profit Isha Foundation to push governments into adopting policies that protect and restore soils.
Its estimate builds on research by the European Commission's in-house science service, the Joint Research Centre (JRC), which puts the yearly cost of soil degradation in the EU at €40.9 billion to €72.7 billion.
Save Soil multiplied that by the seven years of the next long-term budget currently being discussed in Brussels.
The range covers erosion, contamination, compaction and soil carbon losses, among other damage, and the JRC has noted the bill could double if costs such as biodiversity loss, floods, droughts and health effects were added.
Farm budget talks
In July 2025, the Commission proposed ring-fencing at least €300 billion for farmers' income and crisis support from 2028. On 26 October, EU agriculture ministers agreed their stance on the CAP rules but left funding to the wider budget talks.
Agriculture negotiations at COP31 in Türkiye, ended without a meaningful outcome, with a decision pushed back to 2027.
"Europe is debating hundreds of billions in agricultural support while soil degradation is already imposing enormous costs on its economy," Rico Rau, the lead author of the group's COP31 report, said in a statement.
"The next CAP should not simply compensate farmers for the pressures they face. It should help them rebuild the productive asset their livelihoods depend on," he added.
Risks to the food industry
According to the Commission, 60% to 70% of soils in the EU are unhealthy, weakening their ability to support farming, hold water and cope with extreme weather.
Poorer soils can cut yields, raise costs and make supply chains more fragile, Save Soil warned. The EU's food and drink sector alone turns over €1.5 trillion a year and employs 4.8 million people, according to industry body FoodDrinkEurope.
Save Soil wants the CAP to pay for measurable soil health gains and to reward farmers whose land is already healthy.
It also called for the Soil Monitoring Law, the EU's first soil law, to provide consistent evidence without duplicating measurements and paperwork. The law took effect in December 2025 but sets no binding restoration targets.
Its other two proposals are for the EU's carbon farming certification scheme to reward verified environmental benefits, and for public bodies to use their buying power to secure steady demand for sustainably grown food.
"If we want to ensure food security, farming has to be lucrative," Sadhguru stated in comments shared by the group, adding that governments must make farming profitable or farmers’ children will not take it up.

noticias.titulo: Five EU countries plan to send migrants to Rwanda. Is it legal?
noticias.resumen: Five EU countries have agreed to a deal with Rwanda to send rejected asylum seekers there from 2027. The agreement is enabled by the EU's new return regulation, which stipulates that such deals can only be made with countries that respect human rights. Does Rwanda meet that standard?
noticias.texto:
Five EU countries have agreed to a deal with Rwanda to send rejected asylum seekers there from 2027. The agreement is enabled by the EU's new return regulation, which stipulates that such deals can only be made with countries that respect human rights. Does Rwanda meet that standard?
Five EU countries have unveiled this week a deal to deport rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda.
Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece will kick off this plan in 2027, with around 100 single men who cannot be deported directly to their home countries being sent to Rwanda.
The agreement is enabled by the EU return regulation, which entered into force last month. This marks the first time a group of EU member states have used the framework to send irregular migrants to a so-called “return hub.”
Article 14 of this law says that deals to deport migrants can only be made with countries that respect human rights, and many have expressed doubts about whether that is the case for Rwanda.
Freedom House, a US-based organisation which measures freedom around the world, gives the country a score of 7 points out of 40 in political rights and 14 out of 60 in civil liberties. Overall, they label Rwanda as “not free.”
The country also received a score of 0 out of 4 on judicial independence, raising questions about whether migrants not receiving proper treatment in Rwanda would be able to challenge their situation in court freely.
The United Nations Human Rights Council has also said this year that Rwandan authorities “suppress opposition and dissent, prosecuting political opponents, journalists and human rights defenders.”
Meanwhile, Amnesty International notes that Rwanda may be implicated in war crimes because of its support of M23, an armed group in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that is allegedly responsible for summary killings and gang rape. War crimes are amongst the worst possible human rights violations.
The EU Parliament itself has proposed to suspend agreements with Rwanda because of these allegations.
Opponents also point to a precedent: a deal between the UK and Rwanda to send people there while their asylum requests were being processed (so not the same as the EU-Rwanda deal, but similar) was blocked by the UK Supreme Court because it found a real risk that Rwanda would send refugees back to the countries they had fled, which is forbidden by international law.
Rwanda’s government has pushed back and says that human rights are respected in the country and that an independent monitoring mechanism, to which the 5 EU countries have committed, will ensure that.
The parties also say that the UN Refugee Agency will have a role in making sure human rights are protected.

noticias.titulo: Costa cuts proposed EU budget by €44B
noticias.resumen: Brussels plans a tax on Big Tech to raise billions for the next budget cycle.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — António Costa aims to shave another €44 billion off the EU’s planned seven-year budget, according to a fresh set of numbers unveiled on Saturday. For the first time since the budget negotiations began last year, EU regional spending, known as cohesion policy, is a target for reductions. The European Council president proposed reducing it by €8 billion compared with the last proposal, while farmers’ subsidies remained untouched. This is a major setback for a coalition of 17 countries from Eastern and Southern Europe — including Poland, Italy and Spain — who rejected potential cuts to cohesion policy only a few days ago. However, the proposal is likely to be welcomed by a German-led group of Northern countries pushing for cuts across the board. “This proposal is fit for tackling the challenges we are facing in our societies, and gives the European Union the necessary capacity to act,” Costa said on Saturday morning. Costa, who is guiding discussions over the 2028-2034 budget which needs to be agreed by all EU governments, suggested the reductions, which are based on current prices, from the previous proposal presented by Ireland , in its role holding the rotating presidency of the Council of the EU, last month. Overall, the cuts amount to a reduction in size of the budget by €204 billion, or 10.2%, from the European Commission’s original proposal in July last year. In another major development, Costa suggested introducing a new tax on large digital companies such as Google and Meta to help finance the budget over the coming years. In recent years, Brussels held back from levying this tax for fear retaliation from Washington, but the Republicans’ bruising defeat in the midterm elections earlier this month created an opening. These ideas set the scene for fraught discussions among the EU’s 27 leaders during a summit next week. Even then the agreed budget will have to be approved by the European Parliament. Despite governments disagreeing over the size of the budget, Costa is confident that governments will reach a deal among themselves during a summit of EU leaders starting on Dec. 17. “I believe this proposal can bring us closer to a final agreement. And I will continue to work with all leaders to reach that objective,” he said. However, the European People’s Party’s budget negotiator Siegfried Mureșan immediately criticized Costa’s cuts. The plan “is unacceptable to the European Parliament and cannot form the basis for our consent. The proposed cuts take the negotiations backwards,” he wrote on X . Big cuts EU governments are split between those that want a smaller budget focused on defense and competitiveness, and those that think it should be larger and spent on traditional priorities such as farming and cohesion. Costa proposed modest cuts to cohesion — which had been spared from previous rounds of cuts due to opposition from many governments — to appease Germany and its allies, the so-called frugals. However, budget savings also came from foreign aid which was cut by €7 billion, and competitiveness which was axed by €20 billion. Another €10 billion savings came from the deferral of the repayments of the EU’s post-Covid debt, which are due to start in 2028. One of the few budget items to receive additional funding was a rainy-day crisis fund that was downsized by Ireland last month. This is seen as a concession to the Commission, which supports more spending flexibility. Going after big tech Costa proposed new taxes and other adjustments to generate €60 billion annually for the EU budget. Crucially, he replaced an unpopular corporate tax proposal known as CORE, which was put forward by the Commission last year, with a levy on tech multinationals with a turnover exceeding €750 million per year globally and over €50 million in the EU. POLITICO first reported the move earlier this week. The proposed digital levy will cover online advertising, digital intermediation services and user-generated data for companies. Most governments opposed CORE — a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — over fears that it would undermine EU competitiveness. To generate additional resources for the budget, Costa also suggested increasing two largely uncontroversial taxes on non-collected plastic and electronic waste that flows directly to the bloc’s budget by levying an additional 25 cents per kilo. The proposal also envisions a higher share of a carbon imports’ tax that flows to the EU cash pot to 100% from the current 75%, and exploring levies on crypto firms and national spectrum auctions. In a further concession, Costa also suggested phasing in two taxes on tobacco products and polluting firms, known as the Emissions Trading System , for countries that are overwhelmingly affected. Costa argued that the new proposed taxes will keep national contributions to Brussels under control. “With this proposal we have managed to come very close to the current level of national contributions,” he said. This article was updated.

noticias.titulo: UK will take its time setting out Brexit options, says minister
noticias.resumen: Hamish Falconer tells POLITICO that discussions around the topic had proved “divisive” and were important to get right.
noticias.texto: BRUSSELS — The U.K. government will take its time when it comes to setting out options for a new relationship with the European Union, the British minister in charge of talks told POLITICO. Speaking on the sidelines of Friday’s EU-U.K. summit, European Relations Minister Hamish Falconer said that discussions around the topic had proved “divisive” and were important to get right. “I think it is right that we take time over this, both because the discussion has been divisive and because so much is at issue,” he said in an interview with POLITICO’s Westminster Insider podcast . Andy Burnham pledged in September to set out “options” to fix the U.K. relationship with the bloc — which he said could include rejoining its single market, customs union, or even the EU itself. But speaking in Brussels on Friday, the prime minister suggested the process could take longer and signaled the start of an “informal brainstorming process” with the European Union to conclude at the next U.K.-EU summit near the end of 2027. It comes after rumbles of Cabinet discontent over the policy shift and speculation the prime minister may be taking a more cautious approach to avoid spooking his own government allies. Defending the length of the process, Falconer said there was “a lot of variation” in the different relationships Britain could have with the EU and detail to work through. “People say, ‘Oh, the options are obvious’ … but I think most people would struggle to describe the precise difference between the different arrangements,” he said. Burnham has said he will be led by the public on the issue and told reporters in Brussels on Friday that he would “not be running ahead of public opinion on the issue.” ‘These things do take time’ But Falconer said there would be more detail next month when the prime minister laid out his ten-year plan for the country. “He’s definitely going to say a lot about the U.K.’s relationship with the EU around the ten year process,” the minister said. Asked why the prime minister had told reporters earlier in the day that the fruits of today’s summit would “probably the limit of what we can achieve in this parliament” on Europe, the minster said implementing the new deals would take time. “We are moving as quickly as we can. There is a reality that implementation does take some time. You’ve got to make sure that you know business is prepared, etc,” he said. “I think what the prime minister was particularly alluding to is the start dates in the joint statement. These things do take time, even once you’ve got agreement, and we’ve got to agreement quite quickly, I think. “But that’s what he meant about the about the rest of the parliament. Obviously, if you are in some areas drawing out implementation in 2028 or latest 2030 then you do start to get towards the end of our parliament.”

noticias.titulo: French billionaire hunter takes fight global after California tax defeat
noticias.resumen: Gabriel Zucman is rallying politicians in Paris behind his campaign to tax the super-rich. But can he overcome the billionaires and political leaders standing in his way?
noticias.texto: PARIS — Gabriel Zucman wants to put the world’s billionaires on notice. The 40-year-old French economist, who has spent more than a decade designing ways to tax the ultra-rich, hosts a summit against “international oligarchy” in Paris on Saturday. It comes less than three weeks after California voters rejected a billionaire tax he backed, in a campaign where Google co-founder Sergey Brin and other opponents spent more than $300 million to thwart the initiative. “Everywhere, we see very, very strong popular support for taxing billionaires,” Zucman told POLITICO this week, arguing that his loss in California was only a minor setback. “That’s true even in the United States.” Zucman sees fresh hope in the results of the U.S. midterms, in which a string of Democrats campaigning to tax the ultra-rich won their races. “Now our party has a choice to make: Are we going to stand with the working class or the tech lords?” said Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), who is flying in for the Paris gathering. “The same inequality is fueling anger and distrust not only in America, but also in France and around the world,” he told POLITICO. Khanna and Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) are due to speak at the Théâtre de la Concorde, a city-owned venue off the Champs-Élysées loaned for the occasion by Emmanuel Grégoire, the socialist mayor of Paris. Left-wing leaders from Italy, Brazil, Spain and the U.K. are also expected to attend. A “Paris Manifesto” published Friday calls for a minimum tax on the largest fortunes, protections for independent media and rules for artificial intelligence. The question is whether anyone outside the theater will buy into Zucman’s ideas. His signature proposal, a minimum annual tax of 2% on the largest fortunes, was rejected by the French Senate last year. “It’s a real program to save our democracy,” said Eva Joly, a former French investigating judge who jailed the boss of oil giant Elf in the 1990s and later served as a European lawmaker for the Greens. Zucman “carries it brilliantly,” she told POLITICO. The fight goes on Global talks on taxing the super-rich have stalled this year under the U.S. presidency of the G20, according to Zucman, who expects the impasse to persist as long as Donald Trump is in the White House. Still, he hopes to revive the debate when Britain takes over the G20 presidency next year. In Brussels, meanwhile, tax legislation generally requires the unanimous agreement of all 27 EU governments, making a bloc-wide solution difficult. Rather than wait for international agreement, Zucman expects individual governments to take the lead, just as France did with value-added tax in the 1950s and several EU countries have done more recently with digital services taxes. Gabriel Zucman gives a press conference on the launch of the European Tax Observatory, on June 1, 2021 in Brussels. | Pool photo by François Walschaerts via AFP/Getty Images Bills to tax the wealthy are in the works in the Netherlands, Belgium and Spain, he said, while the British government has begun looking at the idea. Joly is less ready to write off Brussels, calling the EU “a field of possibilities.” She argued that low taxes on multinationals distort competition with domestic firms and said it was the responsibility of the European Commission and Parliament to address the problem. There are also signs of movement on corporate taxation. European Council President António Costa is weighing a tax on U.S. tech giants to help fund the EU’s next seven-year budget, POLITICO reported Thursday, after Trump’s poor showing in the midterms eased fears of retaliation by Washington. “Europe cannot afford to calibrate its tax policy to America’s mood swings,” said Paul Monaghan, chief executive of the U.K.-based Fair Tax Foundation, which campaigns on corporate tax conduct. At the United Nations, negotiators will meet in Nairobi from Nov. 30 to Dec. 10 for the next round of talks on a global tax convention, with a final text due in 2027. Beyond the left In California, Zucman said, billionaires flooded voters with “disinformation” that the tax would bankrupt the health system, even though 90% of the revenue raised would have gone toward health care. But money was only part of the story. Unions split over the measure, POLITICO reported, and Gov. Gavin Newsom campaigned against it . A state-only wealth tax “creates economic incentives for money and jobs to leave the state,” his chief of staff, Nathan Barankin, said. Zucman rejects the notion that Saturday’s gathering is a rally of the left. He said he had invited former EU competition chief Margrethe Vestager and former Italian Prime Minister Mario Draghi, but both declined. A spokesperson for Vestager declined to comment. Yet in France, the far-left France Unbowed party and the Greens were the only ones to fully embrace Zucman’s proposed 2% annual wealth tax ahead of next spring’s presidential election. MEP Raphaël Glucksmann, who is running for a left-wing coalition that includes the Socialists, has instead proposed to raise the tax rate for inheritances above €1.8 million, and a one-off 5% levy on fortunes over €100 million. François Geerolf, an economist at Sciences Po’s OFCE, has challenged Zucman’s arguments. In a paper updated last month , he argued that Zucman had exaggerated the extent to which billionaires are undertaxed and proposed a remedy that could do more harm than good. Geerolf acknowledged that the ultra-rich can use holding companies to shield income from taxation, but argued for closing the loophole instead of imposing an annual tax on fortunes. He also questioned estimates that the tax would raise €20 billion a year in France, putting the likely proceeds at just €2 billion to €6 billion. His verdict: “A real problem, a false diagnosis, a bad remedy.” Other critics have also been mobilizing. Trop c’est trop (“Enough is enough”), a campaign group backed by business executive Eric Maumy, presented a study Wednesday characterizing Zucman’s tax proposal as confiscatory and unconstitutional. But Zucman believes it is the status quo that is untenable. “Do you think it’s normal that billionaires can pay zero personal tax?” he said. “It’s the current situation that is radical.”

noticias.titulo: [Infographic] Plastics export ban begins: How much more of EU’s 22 million tonne per year trash mountain will go into landfills?
noticias.resumen: With record plastic waste and shrinking recycling capacity, Europe’s new export ban risks quietly diverting mountains of rubbish into incinerators, landfills and poorer neighbours’ backyards.
noticias.texto: From 21 November, the EU will have to find new destinations for half of the plastic waste it currently exports outside the bloc. Under the EU’s new Waste Shipment Regulation , adopted in 2024, exports of plastic waste to non-OECD countries will be banned for at least two and a half years, with the aim of preventing environmental damage and ensuring waste is managed safely. In 2025, non-OECD countries received 735,000 tonnes, around half of the 1.46 million tonnes of plastic waste the EU exported outside the bloc. Turkey, the EU’s largest OECD destination for plastic waste, could absorb much of this redirected volume. However, environmental groups such as the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) have raised concerns about the country’s waste management and enforcement, questioning whether it should continue receiving EU plastic waste. The commission itself expects “a shift in destination countries”: part of the waste will find its way into EU recovery capacity, while “a certain amount will be diverted to treatment in OECD countries outside the EU,” a commission spokesperson said. So, when November ends, where will Europe’s plastic waste go? A ban with a waiting list No non-OECD country will receive EU plastic waste for at least two and a half years. From May 2029, under the Waste Shipment Regulation , countries can apply to resume imports if the commission is satisfied they can manage it sustainably. Exports to OECD countries remain legal but are subject to stricter controls. Since 21 May 2026, all plastic waste exports to third countries have required prior notification and consent, processed through the EU’s Digital Waste Shipment System (DIWASS). The next step comes in May 2027, when exporters will also have to demonstrate that destination facilities have passed independent audits. Read more How the EU lets plastic be labelled ‘recycled’ at just 2.5% re-used content China and Hong Kong received around three-quarters of Europe’s plastic waste exports in 2016, before Beijing’s import ban pushed shipments towards Malaysia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Turkey. Of these, only Turkey will still be able to receive EU plastic waste after 21 November 2026. Can Turkey safely manage Europe’s plastic waste? Turkey was the EU’s largest single destination for plastic waste in 2025, receiving 503,000 tonnes, mostly from Germany (155,000) and Belgium (107,000). Both also rely on markets that close in November: Germany sent almost half of its plastic waste exports outside the EU to non-OECD countries, and Belgium 43 percent. Spain and the Netherlands, also among Turkey’s top suppliers, are even more exposed to the November ban, at 70 and 77 percent. The commission’s assessment of Turkey, published on 18 September, acknowledged that Ankara had strengthened its import controls but highlighted a “lack of transparency” in waste data, insufficient information on enforcement and unclear governance. The commission nevertheless kept exports open, while pledging to continue monitoring the situation. Lauren Weir, Senior Campaigner at the EIA, sees a gap: “We think that there’s a disconnect between the commission’s application of the regulation and what that regulation actually says needs to happen.” “It should not happen, but given the conclusions of this recent commission assessment, it may in the short term,” she said. In Adana, where around 60 percent of imported plastic waste is processed, researchers found up to 132 times more microplastics in irrigation canals downstream of recycling plants than upstream. Fires are another warning sign. Blazes at recycling facilities rose from six a year in 2017 to 125 a year in 2022, according to a policy brief by Sedat Gündoğdu, a marine biologist at Adana’s Çukurova University. “All the fires are happening behind the facilities in storage parts, not the machinery or office parts,” he said. Read more The EU should stop exporting its plastic waste, period Turkey caps each facility’s imports at 50 percent of its certified annual processing capacity, according to the commission’s assessment . But Gündoğdu claims the capacity figures can easily be manipulated. “You can enlarge your area by fencing some places for storage. That’s all,” he explained. Audits may not close the gap. In 2021, a German inspector found that 2BPlast , a recycling plant in Düzce certified to receive German packaging waste, had been dismantled months earlier while shipments kept arriving. “Everything will be based on papers. But the real extent of this business is handshaking business. All things are happening behind the doors,” Gündoğdu warned. If independent auditors start inspecting Turkish plants from May 2027, he expects few to succeed: “I don’t believe that more than 10 percent of the facilities can pass this auditing process.” Turkey already generates around 3.3 million tonnes of plastic waste a year. The government says it recovers 30 percent of its municipal waste, but World Bank data puts the figure at 11.9 percent, according to Gündoğdu’s policy brief . “How can this country soundly manage waste that belongs to other countries? This is pollution transfer,” Gündoğdu said. Can Europe handle its own plastic? This article continues, but the full version is available only to EUobserver.com subscribers. noticias.titulo: COP31 in Antalya: five takeaways from the ‘implementation’ climate summit
noticias.resumen: After three decades of UN climate summits, and little progress on climate finance, this year’s meeting (COP31) in Turkey, is likely to be remembered less for what negotiators agreed than for the deals struck on the sidelines.
noticias.texto: After three decades of UN climate summits, this year’s meeting (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, is likely to be remembered less for what negotiators agreed than for the deals struck on the sidelines. Since the first Conference of the Parties gathered in Berlin in 1995, the annual talks have produced the Paris Agreement’s 1.5C goal, a pledge in Dubai to “transition away” from fossil fuels, and, last year in Belém, a push to turn those commitments into action. But delegates from more than 190 countries remain split over who should pay to help the poorest nations cope with climate disasters, while mentions of a fossil fuel phase-out were barred from the final text. Instead, global leaders leaned on a Turkish-backed goal to boost electrification. Notably, the US did not take part in the talks. “Consensus often only delivers the lowest common denominator,” Linda Kalcher, co-founder of the climate think-tank Strategic Perspectives told EUobserver. But in the context of trade tensions, wars, and conflicts, she said it is positive to see that “multilateralism still delivers.” Turkey, the host country of this year’s COP, is expected to receive billion-dollar investment deals, a preliminary $15bn renewable energy deal with China, $5.1bn in financing from development banks, and accords with Saudi Arabia and Canada . Post-Iran impact Global energy shocks linked to the war in Iran, which effectively saw the Strait of Hormuz shut down, have also complicated energy talks. noticias.titulo: Fresh off China trip, Trump bobs and weaves in freewheeling press conference
noticias.resumen: Fresh off a four-day visit to China and the Philippines, the U.S. president on Friday ...
noticias.texto: Fresh off a four-day visit to China and the Philippines, the U.S. president on Friday held a heavily anticipated press conference at the White ​House, billed as an opportunity to sell the successes of his trip to the American public. A placard beside Trump’s podium listed a series of broad agreements the president had ‌reached with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which included a reaffirmation that nuclear war would be futile for all nations involved. Another poster touted deals the White House said had been inked during the trip. Right off the bat, however, the president pivoted from the topic at hand. He praised the speed of his new Qatari-offered Air Force One, before musing that the COVID-19 vaccine was not rolled out in time to boost his re-election odds during his 2017-2021 term. He then said ​interest rates were too high, before pivoting again, this time to Iran. “They’ve been bullshitting people for 51 years,” Trump said of the Islamic Republic’s leaders, while flanked by top aides, including Vice ​President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and newly installed Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. Trump’s unencumbered and unstructured performance, which lasted 1-1/2 hours, came after the departures of ⁠some of the staffers credited with maintaining message discipline at the White House, including former Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt and, more recently, Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. It amounted to his first major speech aimed at a domestic audience ​since his Republican Party was walloped in the congressional midterm elections earlier in the month. At times, Trump suggested he would be interested in working with Democrats, who will hold significant majorities in the U.S. House of ​Representatives and Senate starting in January. At other times, he seemed unapologetic about the policies that strategists say hurt Republicans in the midterms. He announced he would penalize companies building data centres abroad – even as Americans appear most concerned about them being built at home. And he rejected criticisms that he is too deferential toward Moscow – a view polls show is held by most Americans, including many Republicans – repeating his oft-stated assertion that Putin is ready for a deal in Ukraine. Trump also suggested ​he might be willing to strike an immigration or healthcare deal with Democrats, though his impressionistic style left much to the imagination. “They had jails being emptied out from the Congo, from all over South America, ​from Asia, into our country. Those are the people we focus on, and we focus on them strongly,” Trump said. “Now, other people have broken the law, and I will tell you, I think probably one of the earliest things ‌that Democrats are ⁠gonna see me, are gonna be very hard-working people that came in, in some cases years ago. What are we gonna do?” He added, without elaborating, that he thought he could work with Democratic Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa on border issues after he said they chatted by phone this week. Nice Trump vs mean Trump With both Rubio and Vance in attendance – both of whom are seen as potential presidential candidates in 2028 – reporters pushed Trump to hint at a successor. He did not bite. Asked about a post on X by Vance following the midterms, in which the vice president blamed the Iran conflict for Republicans’ losses, Trump said he had no problem with the ​message. He said he would have only added that ​he would have attacked Iran no matter the ⁠political fallout. He added, in an apparent joke, that Miller was a better public speaker than Vance and Rubio. His new chief of staff is a longtime loyalist whom even fellow Republicans consider a hardliner on immigration and other hot-button issues. “Do you want to run for president?” Trump asked Miller. Trump just seemingly endorsed Stephen Miller for President over JD Vance and Marco Rubio. This exchange is just crazy. pic.twitter.com/VNKwqJEwe7 — Ed Krassenstein (@EdKrassen) November 20, 2026 Trump said he thought deposed Nvidia CEO Jensen ​Huang – who was forced out amid revelations that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy – should be invited back to his job. He added ​that he retained confidence in ⁠Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a close personal friend, despite news reports indicating that Lutnick delayed new restrictions on exports of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips. The administration has come under fire in the past week for its halting response to a series of technology outages. Trump said the various outages were separate events that had been resolved. But he confirmed a Reuters report that White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross had been ousted, saying he “didn’t think that person ⁠was good enough.” Tech outage wave reaches U.S. government; Trump says all is ‘fine’ Trump ​appeared upbeat for most of the briefing, a marked departure from recent exchanges with reporters, during which he has insulted several ​of them on personal terms. He said he appreciated the large crowd of journalists in attendance, and he invited all attendees to a South Lawn reception with refreshments in the afternoon. Yet at the end of the press conference, the pricklier version of Trump briefly reemerged. “You’re a really ​rude person,” Trump told an NBC reporter who attempted to shout a question. “So I’m not talking to you.” With Reuters Caption: US President Donald J Trump (C) with Vice President JD Vance (L) and Secretary of State Marco Rubio (R) hold a press conference in the James S Brady Press Briefing Room of the White House in Washington, DC, USA, 20 November 2026. EPA/YURI GRIPAS / POOL

noticias.titulo: Denmark accuses Russia of plotting assassination of rapper on its soil
noticias.resumen: Danish authorities on 20 November publicly attributed a foiled assassination attempt against a dual U.S.-Ukrainian ...
noticias.texto: Danish authorities on 20 November publicly attributed a foiled assassination attempt against a dual U.S.-Ukrainian citizen to Russian intelligence services, expelled Russia’s defence attaché, and indicated further restrictive measures, including a halt on non-essential visas for Russian citizens. The government described the case as an unprecedented demonstration of Russian willingness to conduct lethal operations on Danish territory and framed it as part of a broader pattern of aggressive hybrid activity across Europe. Police and the Danish Security and Intelligence Service (PET) said they stopped the plot on 25 September, minutes before a scheduled concert north of Copenhagen. Officers intercepted a vehicle carrying men linked to the banned criminal network Loyal to Familia; two loaded pistols and knives were found inside. Two Danish nationals have been charged with attempted murder and assisting a foreign intelligence service; both have denied the allegations and remain in custody. PET assessed that Russian intelligence planned and initiated the operation. The intended target was the Ukrainian-American rapper known as Kyivstoner, whose legal name is Albert Viktorovych Vasyliev (also Slevin Dadyan on U.S. documents). Born in Kyiv in 1991, he first gained notice through short comedic videos while studying in the United States, then returned to Ukraine and became a member of the hip-hop project Griby before launching a solo career. After Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 he left Ukraine with his family, later settling in Bratislava, Slovakia. He has publicly supported Ukraine, including through financial assistance to its military, according to statements from his wife. Russian authorities have separately accused him of involvement in drone attacks on the Moscow region – an allegation he has rejected. An earlier plot against him was disrupted in Poland in August 2026, when Polish services arrested a Russian national; Polish officials described that case as the first known Russian-ordered attempt on an American citizen on NATO soil. In Copenhagen, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen summoned the Russian ambassador and ordered the defence attaché to leave within seven days. He characterized the alleged operation as an effort to intimidate Denmark and weaken its support for Ukraine. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s office issued a statement underscoring that Denmark would not be intimidated and would increase assistance to Ukraine while tightening sanctions. Danish officials have also indicated they are exploring further restrictions on Schengen visas for Russian nationals. Russia has denied organizing the attack or other hybrid operations in Europe, calling the Danish claims unsubstantiated. The case remains under investigation, with court proceedings continuing against the charged men. The episode has reinforced Danish and broader European concerns about Russian intelligence activity on NATO territory amid the ongoing war in Ukraine. Caption: Danish Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen (R) and Foreign Minister Lars Loekke Rasmussen (L) hold a press conference at the Ministry of Justice in Copenhagen, Denmark, 20 November 2026. Two Danish men were formally charged with planning to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper on behalf of Russian intelligence services. EPA/Emil Helms

noticias.titulo: France welcomes Putin’s offer of dialogue but demands a full European role in Ukraine talks
noticias.resumen: France has welcomed Russia’s proposal to formalise dialogue with European representatives, but says the move ...
noticias.texto: France has welcomed Russia’s proposal to formalise dialogue with European representatives, but says the move must translate into a meaningful role for Europe in negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, including at the next meeting with the United States and Kyiv. The position was conveyed by a source at the French president’s office to EUalive’s partner “European Pravda” , following talks in Berlin on 19 November. Paris considers the Russian offer a positive step, but insists that simply inviting European officials to Moscow would not be enough. “France is certainly interested in opening a dialogue with the Russians, in continuing the conversations that we have already started earlier,” the source said, stressing that Paris had never severed contacts with Moscow. The official recalled that France had maintained communication with Russia at several levels, including through the president, diplomatic advisers and the French ambassador in Moscow. The purpose, the source said, had always been to communicate clearly what could and could not be discussed in negotiations. “Therefore, it is positive that today the Russians are offering us to formalise this dialogue,” the official added. However, France expects the move to signal a change in Moscow’s approach to European participation in the peace process. The formalisation of contacts must mean that Russia accepts Europeans as full participants in negotiations and includes them in the next meeting involving the U.S. and Ukraine. The reason, according to the French official, is straightforward: “Peace in Europe is impossible without Europeans.” The source pointed to a similar argument made by U.S. special envoy Jared Kushner. Who would represent Europe? The question of who would speak for Europe in any future negotiations has already been addressed by EU leaders. At an informal EU summit in Dublin on 13 November, they agreed on a seven-member European negotiating team. It is to bring together national security advisers from the five countries known as the E5 – France, Germany, the United Kingdom, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and the European Council. The format is intended to give Europe a coordinated voice in discussions that have so far largely been dominated by Washington, Moscow and Kyiv. It also brings together the main European countries involved in supporting Ukraine with the two EU institutions representing the bloc at the negotiating table. The seven-member team should not, however, be confused with a group of seven political leaders preparing to travel to Moscow. The Russian invitation, announced by President Vladimir Putin on 19 November, was addressed to European representatives, but the Kremlin has not publicly identified those invited or confirmed that a visit has been arranged. Putin said Moscow wanted to hear Europe’s position before deciding how to proceed with negotiations on Ukraine. Speaking in China after meeting U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, he said Russia had proposed through diplomatic channels that European representatives come to Moscow to clarify what they wanted from the talks. The Russian president also acknowledged that discussing European security without European involvement made little sense. But he framed the invitation as a way for Moscow to establish Europe’s position before deciding on the format of further dialogue with Ukraine. European capitals divided on Moscow talks France’s response comes amid debate among European governments over whether to engage directly with Russia. German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius has said Europe should not rule out the possibility of talks in Moscow if they can produce results. His remarks suggest that Berlin is open to considering direct contacts, although the question of what such talks could achieve remains unresolved. “Rejecting the invitation to Moscow would be a completely wrong signal. We must talk. Only those who talk can ultimately achieve results,” the minister said on Friday during his visit to Warsaw. According to him, Europe cannot allow the negotiations to drag on and be just a facade, while people continue to die in Ukraine. Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna, by contrast, has taken a much more sceptical position. Commenting on Putin’s invitation, he dismissed the idea that visits to Moscow would help, warning that no amount of “Kremlin tourism” would solve the problem. “Instead of sending out invitations to Moscow, Putin should answer the only question that really matters: when will Russia stop bombing Ukraine, killing its citizens, and systematically destroying its energy infrastructure?”, the Estonian minister emphasized. The challenge for Europe is how to secure a place in negotiations without allowing Moscow to dictate the terms of its participation or exploit divisions between European capitals. Caption: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, French President Emmanuel Macron, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner leave a press conference during the ‘Coalition of the Willing’ summit on security guarantees for Ukraine in Berlin, Germany, 19 November 2026. About 30 heads of state and government are meeting for the summit. The agenda includes security guarantees for Ukraine, defense, and the next steps in the negotiations. EPA/HANNIBAL HANSCHKE

noticias.titulo: Burnham seeks to close the book on a decade of Brexit drift as EU and UK seal reset deals
noticias.resumen: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Brussels determined to move past what he has ...
noticias.texto: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived in Brussels determined to move past what he has called a decade of post-Brexit drift and division, telling reporters that the status quo was not working and that the British people wanted a better practical deal than the hard Brexit that emerged after 2016. A decade after Britain voted to leave the European Union, the old bitterness has largely faded. Both sides now see a closer partnership as necessary amid a shifting global order shaped by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, U.S. tariffs, China’s grip on critical minerals, and conflict involving Iran. At the second EU-UK summit held on Friday he secured agreements on easing agrifood trade, linking emissions trading systems and launching a Youth Experience Scheme, while leaving university tuition fees for further negotiation. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she welcomed Burnham’s willingness to have a broad debate about future relations with the EU. “We are open for brainstorming, and we welcome this brainstorming, so count on us,” she said. The most ‌significant allows ⁠cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1 billion ($6.7 billion) per year to its economy. A further agreement will link the emissions trading systems of Britain and the EU, which would exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies. On people-to-people ties, the statement confirms conclusion of negotiations on a Youth Experience Scheme (YES). It will allow 100,000 young people from the EU and 100,000 from the UK respectively to reside for up to three years for activities including work, studies, au-pairing, volunteering or travel, under each side’s legal frameworks. The aim is to apply the agreement no later than 2028, with opportunities available no later than January 2030. Denmark is not participating. This builds on UK participation in Erasmus+ in 2027. Tuition fees remain unresolved. The two sides continue to differ, with EU countries wanting their students to be eligible for “home fees” ​at British universities, rather than the international rate, ​which is often three times as much. Britain prefers ⁠to offer only “significantly reduced” fees, and the aim is now to resolve the issue within six months. The deals are to apply from 2028, with the first young people able to benefit from youth mobility by 2030, a joint summit statement said. Broader elements include continued unwavering support for Ukraine’s independence and territorial integrity, with coordinated political, financial, military and humanitarian assistance; deepening of the Security and Defence Partnership (including hybrid threats, maritime security, military mobility and civilian CSDP participation); extension of the TCA Energy Title to 31 March 2028; progress toward possible UK participation in the EU internal electricity market (linked to a financial contribution); and establishment of a Dialogue on Economic Security. The statement reaffirms full implementation of the Withdrawal Agreement (including the Windsor Framework) and the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. European Council President António Costa, speaking at the joint press conference, described a solid EU-UK partnership as “a strategic investment for the security of Europe” and also for shared prosperity, innovation, competitiveness and resilience. “There cannot be a strong defence without a stronger economy. Together we will be stronger in both defence and the economy,” he said. Costa stated that the EU remains open to “the closest possible relationship” with the United Kingdom, while respecting the sovereign decision taken by the British people in 2016 and “whatever decision the UK takes about the future of its long-term relationship with the European Union.” He emphasised EU principles of the indivisibility of the four freedoms of the single market, the balance of rights and obligations, and the integrity of relations with third countries. He also reiterated the shared commitment to Ukraine. Burnham called the outcome “a good day for Britain and a good day for Europe,” arguing that the package addresses everyday concerns such as food prices and growth. UK estimates have previously cited potential economic benefits of around £5.1 billion annually from the agrifood measures alone, with the overall package framed as adding roughly 0.5% to GDP. Full treaty texts were not published with the summit statement; implementation timelines remain “aims” pending ratification and legal processes. The tuition-fee track is the principal outstanding element, and some EU commentary has linked final adoption of the other agreements to progress on it. Further details on alignment mechanisms, exact fee levels, scheme operational rules and parliamentary scrutiny are expected as negotiations and implementation work continue. Nigel Farage, the veteran anti-EU campaigner and leader of the Reform UK party, commented that the deal “was about the first ​steps, incrementally, to taking us back into membership of the European Union,” and again predicted an early election next year. Farage told reporters he would campaign to preserve Brexit. “I ​am ready for this fight.” Caption: (L-R) British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen pose at the end of a press conference during the second EU-UK summit in Brussels, Belgium, 20 November 2026. The second EU-UK summit since Brexit focuses on strengthening the strategic partnership, including cooperation on security, trade, energy, and migration. EPA/OLIVIER HOSLET

noticias.titulo: Italian government reacts to Ukrainian blacklisting of Italian opposition MEPs
noticias.resumen: Eight MEPs from Italy’s Five Star Movement (M5S) have been added to a list of ...
noticias.texto: Eight MEPs from Italy’s Five Star Movement (M5S) have been added to a list of “anti-Ukrainian criminals” on the Myrotvorets website, which has published their names, photographs and personal information. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has instructed Italy’s ambassador to Kyiv, Carlo Formosa, to seek clarification from the Ukrainian authorities. Four days after the first case came to light, however, the profiles remain online. “I don’t have high hopes,” Danilo Della Valle, the Five Star MEP who first raised the alarm about his inclusion in the database, told Focus Europe Italia. “The European Commission, through its spokespersons, has said it was unaware of the blacklist. Evidently, they don’t even read Italian newspapers, which says a lot about the ‘great’ influence our country has in Brussels,” he said. Della Valle took a different view of the Italian government’s intervention. “As for Minister Tajani’s actions, we certainly thank him for taking an interest and for involving our embassy in Kyiv,” he said. “However, we have heard nothing since, and the website is still there, with its list and its hateful language. We expect effective action that respects our freedom as elected representatives of the people.” Kyiv distances itself as Commission says it needs more information Ukraine’s embassy in Rome issued a statement on X on 20 November, following the Italian government’s request for clarification. Myrotvorets, it said, is not “an official source of information of the Ukrainian state”. The embassy stressed that the website is not part of Ukraine’s state institutions, is not authorised to represent their position and that the information it publishes does not reflect the country’s official stance. The European Commission responded a day earlier, addressing the substance of the case. Asked during the midday press briefing by Il Fatto Quotidiano whether Ursula von der Leyen intended to take action concerning an EU candidate country, Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho said more information needed to be gathered and that the issue had not been on the institution’s radar. The European Parliament has also taken steps, although no formal action has yet followed. President Roberta Metsola informed the Five Star delegation that she would seek explanations from the Ukrainian government, while Parliament’s services confirmed they were monitoring threats against MEPs. As of 19 November, Della Valle had not received a written response to his letter of protest. From one MEP’s profile to an entire delegation The controversy began on 16 November, when Della Valle, a member of the European Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, publicly disclosed that his name appeared in the database. The website accuses him of “participation in acts of humanitarian aggression”, information manipulation and propaganda. His profile ends with an appeal to Ukrainian law enforcement authorities to take action against him. The MEP maintains that the accusations are based entirely on his parliamentary work, public statements and votes. In a letter to Metsola, Della Valle called for the launch of a procedure to defend his parliamentary immunity and privileges, the urgent involvement of Parliament’s Directorate-General for Security to assess the threat, diplomatic engagement with Kyiv to secure the removal of his name and action to shut down the website. Around 24 hours after his complaint, the website expanded its listings to include the entire delegation. Alongside Della Valle, the database now features Mario Furore, Pasquale Tridico, Dario Tamburrano, Gaetano Pedullà, Valentina Palmisano, Giuseppe Antoci and Carolina Morace. Seven of the eight face the same allegations: denying Ukraine’s right to defend itself against the Russian invasion, supporting Moscow’s aggression and participating in pro-Russian disinformation. The entries are accompanied by screenshots of articles from Russian media outlets, including TASS. Five Star Movement leader Giuseppe Conte described the entries as outright “proscription lists”, calling on the government to secure the removal of the names to protect the safety of the elected representatives. A blacklist spanning political groups, from the EPP to the League The listings are not confined to one political family. The first group of MEPs entered into the database included, alongside Della Valle, French EPP member Christophe Gomart, Cypriot non-attached MEP Fidias Panayiotou, Finland’s Eero Heinäluoma of the Socialists and Democrats, Bulgaria’s Petar Volgin of Europe of Sovereign Nations, Greece’s Elena Kountoura of The Left and Poland’s Ewa Zajączkowska-Hernik of Patriots for Europe. Panayiotou announced his inclusion in a video, linking it to a visit to Moscow in 2025 and accusations that he had spread Russian propaganda. The database also includes Italian politicians who do not sit in the European Parliament. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini has been listed since 2017 over his positions on Crimea and his past expressions of support for Vladimir Putin. His profile was identified by Il Fatto Quotidiano. Roberto Vannacci has been listed since July 2026, with his email address and passport number published on the website. The database also includes Gianluca Savoini, Salvini’s former spokesperson, whose name emerged in a series of journalistic investigations in 2018 over his alleged involvement in a commercial deal between Russian and Italian companies that could have channelled illicit funding to Italian political parties, particularly the League. The allegations led to a judicial investigation that was eventually closed in 2023. The League called Salvini’s inclusion “extremely serious, intolerable and disgraceful”, dismissed allegations of Russian funding for the party as unfounded and announced a parliamentary question. The Five Star Movement has submitted a similar question to the Foreign Ministry. A website previously flagged by the UN, OSCE and European Parliament Myrotvorets, meaning “peacemaker” in Ukrainian, was launched in December 2014 by activist Georgy Tuka, who later served as deputy minister under President Petro Poroshenko. Its founders also included Anton Gerashchenko, who subsequently became an adviser to the Interior Ministry. In 2015, the website published the home addresses of writer Oles Buzyna and former MP Oleh Kalashnikov, both of whom were murdered days later. In 2016, it released the personal details of more than 4,500 journalists accredited by the separatist authorities in Donetsk. G7 ambassadors called for the information to be removed, while the UN Human Rights Office urged an investigation. The website has faced institutional criticism for almost a decade. In its resolution of 11 February 2021 on the implementation of the EU-Ukraine Association Agreement, the European Parliament called on the Ukrainian authorities to condemn and prohibit the activities of extremist and hate-inciting groups and websites, explicitly naming Myrotvorets over its misuse of personal data. The OSCE had already criticised the publication of journalists’ personal information in 2016, while in 2024 the European Commission confirmed that it had repeatedly raised the disclosure of EU citizens’ personal data with Kyiv. None of those demands has resulted in the website’s closure. On 20 November, the Party of the European Left expressed solidarity with Della Valle and the entire Five Star delegation, calling on EU institutions to take concrete action rather than merely seeking explanations, at a time when Ukraine’s accession to the European Union remains on the Council’s agenda. The article in Italian by EUalive’s partner FocusEurope.it can be found here Caption: Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Antonio Tajani attends the 12th edition of the Mediterranean Dialogues conference at the Royal Palace in Naples, southern Italy, 19 November 2026. The conference, organized by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation (MAECI) in collaboration with the Italian Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI), takes place from 19 to 21 November 2026 in Naples. EPA/ANTONIO BALASCO

noticias.titulo: Italian workers and students protest over wages and public services
noticias.resumen: Tens of thousands of workers ​and students took to the streets across Italy on Friday ...
noticias.texto: Tens of thousands of workers ​and students took to the streets across Italy on Friday as the country’s largest trade union, CGIL, staged a general ‌strike, demanding higher wages and greater investment in public services. The demonstrations coincided with a broader wave of youth mobilisation across Europe. Student protests were also planned in Germany, France, Britain, Austria, Belgium and Spain over rising living costs and military spending. “Today is also a very important day because young people are taking to the streets ​not just in Italy but across Europe,” CGIL leader Maurizio Landini said. “Across Europe and among ordinary people, the demand for change ​is growing,” he added. Other Italian unions, including the grassroots Cobas movement, also called separate strike action, while student ⁠demonstrations were planned nationwide amid simmering discontent over the policies of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government. The CGIL strike was scheduled to last the entire ​working day and involved workers in both the private and public sectors, including schools and healthcare. Air and rail transport services were excluded from the ​general strike, while its impact on local public transport was limited by minimum-service requirements. However, a separate rail strike was due to begin at 9 p.m.on Friday and run until 8 p.m. on Saturday. Addressing a rally in Rome, Landini said more than one million people had taken part in demonstrations across more than 100 ​Italian cities. The Interior Ministry said it was too early to provide its own estimate. The protests come as Italy gears up for a parliamentary ​election due in 2027. ‘We will take our future back’ Friday’s demonstrations follow a nationwide mobilisation on 30 October, when thousands of students joined striking workers to demand more ‌funding for ⁠education and relief from rising living and housing costs. Student groups have since continued protests and occupations at schools and universities, with opposition to higher military spending also emerging as a rallying cry. “We are living under a government that, piece by piece, is cutting healthcare and education, taking away our present and trying to rob us of our future,” said Laura Peritore, 24, a university student. “We are making it clear that we will not ​back down and will take our ​future back.” Parliament is examining Meloni’s €26 ⁠billion budget for 2027, which CGIL says does not go far enough to support incomes and public services. According to Italian financial newspaper ItaliaOggi, only a fraction of the budget is targeted at under-35s. Industry Minister Adolfo ​Urso described Friday’s general strike as a “pre-emptive strike”, saying CGIL leader Maurizio Landini had called it before ​he even knew the ⁠contents of the budget. Urso also said on Sky TG24 he had “great respect for those who are demonstrating and for those who have tabled amendments in parliament, where the budget will then be improved.” The union is demanding wage increases and contract renewals to recover purchasing power lost to inflation, full indexation ⁠of pensions and ​measures to prevent a rise in the retirement age. “People have very basic problems: they ​struggle to make ends meet and therefore need higher wages; they need a healthcare system that works; young people need schools that work,” Landini said. “This budget does not address a ​single one of them.” Reuters Caption: Students protest next to the Coliseum during the rally for the general strike in Rome, Italy, 20 November 2026. A 24-hour general strike, called by Italy’s largest trade union confederation CGIL, alongside other labour groups, is taking place nationwide to protest the government’s budget bill and its economic and social policies. EPA/RICCARDO ANTIMIANI

noticias.titulo: Coalition of the Willing meets in Berlin as counterweight to Putin-Trump diplomacy
noticias.resumen: Leaders and representatives from roughly 37 countries gathered in Berlin Thursday for a high-level meeting ...
noticias.texto: Leaders and representatives from roughly 37 countries gathered in Berlin Thursday for a high-level meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, an informal grouping of mostly European states supporting Ukraine. Co-hosted by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the summit took place on the same day as the first-ever trilateral meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul described the Berlin gathering as the largest meeting of Ukraine’s supporters to date and a strong signal to Moscow that it is time to take negotiations to end the war seriously. He stressed that allies remain firmly behind Kyiv and are prepared to ensure Ukraine can negotiate from a position of strength, while warning that peace talks could still fail. Discussions focused on implementing the European Commission’s proposal for €45 billion in support for Ukraine’s budgetary and military needs in 2027, strengthening air defences (including through the PURL mechanism for U.S.-made systems such as Patriot interceptors), a winter package of anti-ballistic interceptors, new joint European defence capabilities, and preparations for robust, legally binding security guarantees that could include a multinational force after any ceasefire. U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attended, as did Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and EU leaders including European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. According to some reports, Trump briefly joined the meeting online, from Air Force One upon his return from Schenzhen. Participation was substantial but not universal among EU members. Official German listings of the broader Coalition include countries such as Bulgaria and Hungary, yet several Central and Eastern European states have been skeptical. Slovakia is not a member: Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly stated that Slovakia “wasn’t, isn’t and won’t be” part of the Coalition of the Willing and will not participate in further loans for Ukraine. Bulgaria has similarly said it has never officially joined the informal grouping; Rumen Radev’s government has ruled out supplying weapons from national stockpiles and limited further lethal aid. EUalive has also noted opposition from Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria to additional EU financing mechanisms. EU tables €45bn Ukraine loan as Slovakia, Hungary, Czechia and Bulgaria opt out The timing was widely viewed as deliberate. While the three major powers conferred in China on issues including the Ukraine war and nuclear arms control, European allies used the Berlin meeting to reaffirm support and push for a European role in any peace process. Zelenskyy said the talks covered further support and diplomacy aimed at a dignified peace. After the Shenzhen trilateral, Putin told reporters that Russia had invited European representatives to Moscow through diplomatic channels to clarify what Europe would bring to the negotiations. He said the United States was “quite insistently” urging Moscow to accept European participation in talks that had so far mainly involved Russia, the U.S., and Ukraine, and that discussing European security without Europeans was “pointless.” Once European representatives stated their position in Moscow, he added, Russia would decide the format for continuing the dialogue with Ukraine.⁠ At the same time, he restated longstanding maximalist positions. He indicated that Russia would not withdraw from territory it controls in Ukraine, saying both sides must “face up to reality” on the ground; that any deployment of foreign (including European) troops in Ukraine would be unacceptable; that Ukraine’s security should be addressed only within a broader European security framework that also guarantees Russia’s security; and that Kyiv and Europe were not yet ready for the compromises Moscow said it had accepted from earlier U.S. proposals. He also warned that Russian forces would continue operations to create buffer or “security zones” along the border. The Berlin meeting underscored that, even as Putin and Trump disregard Europe when discussing Ukraine, a significant group of countries continues to coordinate military, financial and diplomatic support for Ukraine and to prepare for post-ceasefire security arrangements. Caption: (Front, L-R) Romania’s President Nicusor Dan, Moldova’s President Maia Sandu, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, President of Lithuania Gitanas Nauseda, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, US President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, European Council President Antonio Costa, (Middle, L-R) North Macedonian Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski, Montenegro’s Prime Minister Milojko Spajic, Albania’s Prime Minister Edi Rama, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, Luxembourg’s Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Estonia’s Prime Minister Kristen Michel, (Back, L-R) Turkish Defence Minister Yasar Guler, Portugal’s Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel, Slovenia’s Prime Minister Janez Jansa, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, Ireland’s Taoiseach Michael Martin, Czech Republic’s Prime Minister Andrej Babis, Latvia’s Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, Spains Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares, Cyprus Prime Minister Vassilis Palmas, Canada’s Defence Minister David McGuinty pose for a group picture during the ‘Coalition of the Willing’ summit on security guarantees for Ukraine, at the Chancellery in Berlin, Germany, 19 November 2026. About 30 heads of state and government are meeting for the summit. The agenda includes security guarantees for Ukraine, defence, and the next steps in the negotiations. EPA/HANNIBAL HANSCHKE

noticias.titulo: Elecciones votantes jóvenes
noticias.texto:
Los jóvenes, indecisos ante su primera vez en las urnas el 29N: "Es una oportunidad, pero también una responsabilidad"
- El 63% de los jóvenes entre 18 y 24 años iría a votar en las elecciones, según el CIS
- Cinco chicas y chicos cuentan a RTVE Noticias los temas que le preocupan y cómo se informan de política
La convocatoria de las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre ha caído por sorpresa a todos los votantes, pero sobre todo a aquellos que ya pueden acudir a las urnas por primera vez. Este es el caso de Lucía, Álvaro, Pedro, Mikel y Daniel, que se sitúan en la franja de los 18 a los 24 años y proceden de diferentes puntos de España.
RTVE Noticias habla con ellos y con expertos para entender la importancia de este colectivo, su visión de la política y los temas que les interesan o movilizan. La mayoría de estos chicas y chicos reconocen que aún están indecisos sobre su participación o el partido al que elegirán, ya que ven acudir a las urnas como "una oportunidad, pero también una responsabilidad".
Según el barómetro de octubre del Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS), el 63,6% de los entrevistados en esa misma franja iría a votar a unas elecciones, el porcentaje más bajo del resto de estratos de edad. Si diferenciamos por sexo, un 80% de las mujeres está dispuesta a ir a las urnas, algo que baja levente al 76% en los varones.
Preocupados por la vivienda, la educación y la sanidad
Entre los que tienen decidido ir a votar se encuentran los madrileños Lucía, Daniel y Álvaro, pero solo este último, procedente de un pueblo al sureste de la capital, tiene pensado el candidato. "Para mí es una responsabilidad, lo tengo claro desde hace tiempo", apunta este joven estudiante de Formación Profesional de 19 años, a quien, en política, le interesan temas como la educación, la sanidad pública y la vivienda.
Tanto Lucía —estudiante de 18 años y residente en el barrio de Vallecas— como Daniel —el mayor del grupo con 21 años, y de Leganés, en el extrarradio—, van a esperar a tener más información en la campaña. La indecisión es un fenómeno que le ocurre a casi un 20% de los jóvenes, según el barómetro del CIS que apunta que, entre los que sí lo tienen claro, optan, principalmente, por PSOE, PP, Vox y Sumar. La encuesta, que es del mes de octubre, no incluye al Frente Amplio y también está rodeada de polémica, ya que algunos partidos defienden que favorece al Gobierno.
"Hay mucha incertidumbre y votar es una oportunidad para cambiar las cosas, pero me falta saber las propuestas", sentencia Daniel que espera que su voto pueda contribuir a conseguir "una España de la que todos nos sintamos orgullosos y en la que se pueda llegar a fin de mes".
Lucía, por su parte, reconoce que "no le hace especial ilusión ir a votar". "Lo siento más como una obligación ciudadana porque cada voto cuenta. Pero… no hay ningún partido que me llame, siento que muchos solo buscan el bien para ellos mismos", lamenta esta joven, a quien, además, de la mejora de los servicios públicos, le mueve ir a las urnas los avances en igualdad. "Siento que mis padres tenían los servicios más asegurados y menos peligro. Creo que deberíamos mantenerlo", asevera.
El voto joven es "complejo" porque es "muy diverso", pero para los partidos es muy importante, considera la presidenta de la Asociación de Comunicación Política, Ana Salazar. Primero, según explica, porque los nuevos partidos han usado en ocasiones este segmento de edad "para entrar en las instituciones" y, por otro, porque buscan "su fidelización a medio y largo plazo". "Si alguien emite un voto a un partido por primera vez, puede que se cree un vínculo, luego sigas más sus políticas y que te quedes", afirma, por su parte, el profesor de Ciencia Políticas de la Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Lluis Orriols, aunque también puede haber "trasvases" más adelante si no ven cumplidas sus expectativas.
La abstención, frecuente en el grupo entre 18 y 25 años
Mikel, vecino de una pedanía de Sigüenza, en Guadalajara, lo está viviendo de manera diferente. Al principio pensaba abstenerse, pero ha cambiado de opinión en las últimas semanas debido a la crisis de la vivienda. "Me llamó mucho la atención la acampada en Sol, fui a verlo y a interesarme por lo que estaba ocurriendo. Antes, con la situación en Ceuta, también empecé a comparar lo que decía cada partido y las soluciones que ofrecían cada uno", ha relatado este joven de 18 años, que busca una España que "evolucione a mejor, que sea asequible" y en la que "no se criminalice a todos los migrantes".
La abstención suele ir bajando a medida que aumenta la edad y que el ciudadano "participa más en la sociedad", señala Orriols. "A veces la participación está muy relacionada con los recursos. A medida que una persona se va poniendo en una posición más central en la sociedad (es independiente, trabaja o vive ciertas situaciones) participan más", resalta. En esta misma línea se expresa Salazar: "La identidad política se va desarrollando a lo largo del tiempo", aunque le es difícil generalizar porque "también depende de la persona y su concienciación política".
Desde Cartagena, Pedro lo tiene claro, pero en el otro sentido: "No voy a ir a votar. No creo que ninguna alternativa actual vaya a cambiar las cosas", sentencia por lo que prefiere quedarse en casa estudiando. Aunque sí añade un matiz: "Si hubiera alguna propuesta creíble en vivienda y los servicios públicos, sí que me movilizaría".
A nivel general, los cinco jóvenes consideran que la política cada vez tiene más en cuenta a su colectivo y que se han dado "algunos pasos" como el Bono Cultural o el Verano Joven. "Tienen claro que somos el futuro y por eso cada vez más apelan a nosotros", opina Mikel. No obstante, para Pedro la manera de evitar el desencanto político, más allá de estas medidas, es "cumpliendo sus promesas". "Hacen exactamente lo mismo unos que otros, pero luego dicen que son completamente opuestos. Necesitamos que haya un cambio de verdad", sentencia el cartagenero.
La desafección política, indica el politólogo Orriols, no es exclusivo de los jóvenes, pero puede que en ellos se junten varios factores. "Esta generación es distinta de la mía. Nosotros teníamos un sistema de partidos mucho más estable, unos códigos de oferta política más clara Ahora la oferta es cambiante y tienen un escenario más imprevisible y menos conocido para ellos. Estos votantes jóvenes tienen menos vínculos y eso les hace que sea más difícil para ellos tomar una decisión", afirma.
Mayor seguimiento en redes y del entorno para informarse
Preguntados por su interés en política, la mayor parte de estos jóvenes reconoce que "no la sigue mucho" y que cuando lo hace es a través de las redes sociales o por su entorno familiar o de amistades. En menor medida, se mantienen informado por los medios de comunicación tradicionales (radio, televisión o escrito) o en actos políticos o movimientos sociales. "Hablo de política, principalmente, con mi abuelo. A mis compañeros los veo un poco cerrados, es difícil", expone Álvaro, al igual que Mikel, que asegura que tiene "muy en cuenta" las opiniones de sus padres.
En cambio, para Lucía es lo contrario: habla más con sus amigas que con su familia sobre estos temas. Y Daniel, que ya sigue la política diaria en su trabajo como productor de radio, evita las conversaciones al llegar a casa o con su entorno: "Siempre se suelen dar discusiones si hay una parte que no piensa igual que tú, pero a veces también creo que es necesario ver otras impresiones".
Pedro sigue las redes por sus mensajes humorísticos de política, pero reconoce que este tipo de canales "no son fiables" si te quieres informar. En cuanto a las conversaciones políticas, considera que hay mucha "politización" de los temas, algo que le gustaría que cambiara a futuro: "Que no todo sea rojo o facha, que no todo sea polarización, que se abran espacios para hablar sin que te acusen de un lado u otro".
Sobre las redes sociales, la politóloga Ana Salazar apunta que, aunque siguen ‘teniendo tirón’ también cada vez más personas que están abandonando estas herramientas, por lo que la política debe ir adaptándose. Respecto al contenido, ya sea político o de otros ámbitos sociales, ve que en redes cada vez prima más "una fórmula de movilización a través de la alteración emocional", que apela más a los sentimientos, muchas veces negativos, que al debate. De esta forma, continúa, se provoca la acción y que el contenido se comparta más rápido para llegar a más usuarios.
Para Salazar hay algo "más sencillo" que estas estrategias, pero que cree que es "difícil de meter en las agendas políticas". "Hay que sentarse a escuchar a los jóvenes. Preguntarles qué les pasa, qué necesitan, empezar a crear comunidades y entender que, si son adultos para votar, también lo son para proponer y para tener voz".

noticias.titulo: Feijóo celebra su acto central de campaña en la plaza de toros de Valencia, el escenario talismán del PP
noticias.texto:
Directo: Feijóo celebra su acto central de campaña en la plaza de toros de Valencia, el escenario talismán del PP
- El PP prevé reunir 12.000 personas en el mitin de este sábado
- Sigue en directo el acto del Partido Popular con Feijóo en Valencia
El líder del PP y candidato a la Presidencia del Gobierno, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, viaja a Valencia para tratar de mostrar músculo de cara al 29-N en la Plaza de Toros, escenario emblemático para los 'populares' por ser símbolo de las grandes victorias del partido.
Feijóo clausurará el acto central de la campaña electoral, en el que también intervendrán el presidente de la Generalitat Valencia y del PP valenciano, Juanfran Pérez Llorca; la alcaldesa de la ciudad y candidata número uno al Congreso por Valencia, María José Catalá, y el presidente del PP de Valencia, Vicente Mompó.
Será a partir de las 12:00 horas y el PP valenciano prevé reunir entre 12.000 y 14.000 personas. Para ello, los 'populares' han fletado cerca de 300 autobuses para que los afiliados de toda la Comunitad Valenciana puedan acudir al mitin sin tener que costearse el desplazamiento, según ha anunciado este viernes el portavoz del comité de campaña del PPCV, Gerardo Camps.
El PP llega con la moral alta día y medio después del debate cara a cara entre Feijóo y el candidato del PSOE, un duelo que los 'populares' consideran que ganó su líder.
Un escenario talismán
La plaza de Toros de Valencia se convierte de nuevo este sábado en uno de los escenarios de los grandes mítines del PP. Feijóo vuelve a uno de los recintos que los populares' consideran su particular talismán electoral.
